Duran is charged with the same three smuggling counts along with being a member of a criminal organisation tasked with managing the finances.

News.title: Three in four parents put their own health on hold while caring for children, study finds
News.content:
Three in four parents put their own health on hold while caring for children, study finds

Research shows parents regularly cancel doctors appointments or ignore symptoms in order to prioritise their children - often making their issues worse.

Bupa speaks to parents about how often they ignore symptoms

Three quarters of parents say they put their own health on hold because they are too busy looking after their children’s wellbeing, and many admit it can lead to more serious problems.

‌



A study of 2,000 parents with children under 16 found that half of those who have pushed their health to the bottom of the list have ignored their own symptoms so they can prioritise their children instead. A third (33%) said they have put off seeking medical help.

‌



Some parents said they cancelled a medical appointment because they were too busy to go (24%). Others delayed a screening appointment (20%) or even put off treatment (19%). But 71% said delaying care meant their health issues got worse.

‌



View 2 Images Two thirds of parents worry about their children's health (Image: Getty Images)

The research also found many working parents feel they can’t take time off when they are ill. Two thirds (66%) said they avoided taking a sick day because they felt they needed to “save” time off for when their children are unwell.

And 58% said they kept working through sickness instead of taking time to recover because they worried they had already taken too much time off to look after an ill child.

‌



Dr Naveen Puri, medical director for Bupa UK Insurance, which offers family health cover , and commissioned the research, said: “One of the most stressful times as a parent is when your children are unwell.

“Understandably, parents often feel they must balance caring for their children with work, household responsibilities and looking after the rest of the family — but it’s crucial they don’t lose sight of their own health in the process.

“Too often, parents put their own health on hold, whether that’s working through illness instead of taking time to recover, ignoring symptoms, or delaying seeking medical support despite having a concern about their health.

‌



“What’s critical is that parents feel able to prioritise their own health, so they can stay well and continue to care properly for the wider family.”

View 2 Images Many worry about their children getting sick and needing to take care of them (Image: Getty Images)

The study found 63% of parents feel overwhelmed when their child is ill, and 41% said it can feel like someone in the family is always unwell.

‌



On average, parents spend just over two hours a week dealing with their children’s health — the equivalent of more than four full days a year.

It also emerged that 62% said they are always worrying about their children’s health, with 81% finding it stressful when there is illness in the family.

The most stressful thing when a child is ill is simply worrying about how they are (51%). That was followed by disrupted sleep routines (43%) and juggling an ill child with the demands of everyday life (40%).

‌



Others said they find it difficult to juggle an ill child with work (38%), knowing when to seek medical advice (28%) and trying to arrange medical appointments (25%).

The OnePoll research also found 80% of parents think they take better care of their children’s health than their own. And when it comes to managing family health, 25% said the responsibility falls solely on them.

To make life easier, 45% said it would help to have fast access to medical advice when it’s needed, while 40% said they want less waiting time for medical appointments.

Article continues below

Dr Puri added: “When your child — or anyone in your family — is ill, you want to be able to sort out the care they need as quickly as possible.

“Not only does this reduce the stress associated with a loved one being ill, but it also allows parents the time to look after their own health as well.”

News.title: Rare wasp spider spotted in UK county for first time as experts issue warning
News.content:
Rare wasp spider spotted in UK county for first time as experts issue warning

Staff at Chester Zoo have nicknamed the spider "Wendy" and say it has been noticed in Cheshire following the rising temperatures during our scorching summer

View 4 Images Wendy, pictured here, is the first wasp spider recorded in Cheshire (Image: Chester Zoo)

A rare wasp spider has been recorded in Cheshire for the first time – and conservationists say her discovery highlights the need to make space for nature.

‌



The large yellow-and-black spider was spotted during a biodiversity survey of Chester Zoo’s estate and has been confirmed as the first recorded sighting of the species in Cheshire. The discovery was made by Chester Zoo conservationists working with RECORD, Cheshire’s local environmental records centre, was subsequently confirmed by an expert from the British Arachnological Society and was officially announced today.

‌



Rosie Cooper, estate biodiversity assistant, made the discovery. She said: “When go out into the field, it involves a lot of walking, using a mixture of apps, wildlife identifying books and our own knowledge to learn more specifics about the habitats we look after.

‌



“I was looking out for plant species and then I saw this big, stripy, brightly coloured spider. I have what you might call a healthy respect for spiders, so my first thought was ‘woah!’ But now I think it’s really cool to have found her.”

View 4 Images Experts warned the spider's arrival was part of a wider trend (Image: Chester Zoo)

Are wasp spiders dangerous?

Despite their striking yellow-and-black appearance, wasp spiders are not considered dangerous to humans. Their distinctive markings resemble those of a wasp, helping to ward off predators, but they cannot sting.

‌



Although they are not aggressive, they may bite if squeezed or directly threatened. Their venom poses little danger to humans, with bites sometimes compared to a nettle sting and potentially causing a minor local reaction.

Where are wasp spiders found?

Wasp spiders are found across mainland Europe, North Africa and parts of Asia. They are particularly associated with the Mediterranean but were first recorded in Britain near Rye, East Sussex, in 1922.

Initially confined largely to the south coast, they have gradually spread across southern England and are now moving further north and west, with warmer temperatures thought to be contributing to their expansion.

‌



View 4 Images Wasp spiders are originally associated with warmer regions (Image: Chester Zoo)

What should you do if you see a wasp spider?

Anyone who encounters a wasp spider is advised to leave it undisturbed, as there is no need to remove or kill it.

Members of the public can also report sightings to the British Arachnological Society's Spider Recording Scheme, which tracks the species' spread and helps scientists understand how it is expanding into new areas.

‌



The spider, nicknamed "Wendy" by the zoo team, is among a number of species whose ranges are moving northwards as they respond to a changing climate. Ruby Merriman, Chester Zoo’s Estate Biodiversity Manager, said: “We were really thrilled to find Wendy. She’s a beautiful and fascinating species, and recording a wasp spider in Cheshire for the first time is really exciting.

“Wasp spiders are slowly moving north as their southern ranges in Europe warm too quickly for them to adapt. Some conservation organisations refer to animals driven to migrate by climate change as ‘climate refugees’ – which is a good term. They are moving because of human activity, and we need to make space for them.”

The zoo’s wider estate, which spans 205 hectares, includes wet meadows, ponds, reedbeds, species-rich grasslands, woodlands, orchards and hedgerows, supporting a wide range of wildlife. The zoo estate supports a range of key UK species, including harvest mice, which are listed on the IUCN Red List as Near Threatened, great crested newts and badgers. It is also a nesting site for barn owls and hosts dozens of dragonfly, moth and butterfly species.

‌



View 4 Images The brightly coloured spider was spotted during a routine biodiversity survey (Image: Chester Zoo)

Scott Wilson, head of field programmes at Chester Zoo, said: "It's exciting to see new species like Wendy on site, but her arrival is part of a broader, more worrying trend. Our conservationists work across the world, and we are witnessing the impacts of climate change in real time, from droughts in Chile to floods in Indonesia. It is a major threat to biodiversity.

“When mountain snows thaw unseasonably, montane forests dry out and small islands face rising sea levels, the species that depend on them must disperse or die. There is a causal link between habitat loss and climate change, and both are already driving species to extinction.

Article continues below

"European spiders are among many species finding it harder to persist in their traditional ranges as the climate shifts. Wendy is a reminder UK biodiversity is not immune to this."

News.title: Hurricane Polo becomes one of world's most intense storms ever thanks to El Nino effect
News.content:
Hurricane Polo becomes one of world's most intense storms ever thanks to El Nino effect

International forecasters and top officials have warned people living in the Pacific to stay vigilant as Polo maintains an output of extremely strong winds despite weakening

View 5 Images Storm Polo is clocking up near record-breaking winds in the Pacific (Image: PHOTO PROVIDED BY NOAA/NESDIS / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

Hurricane Polo has grown so intense that it is set to enter the record books as one of the strongest storms ever.

‌



The storm, was a severe Category 5 on the Saffir-Sampson hurricane scale on Wednesday morning, and is currently spinning as a Category 4 off the southwestern coast of Mexico after its gusts reached a monstrous 180mph. Incredible new satellite pictures have shown the rare system as it becomes the second-most intense by central pressure in the Pacific basin.

‌



It has reached a strength only exceeded once in the region's history by Hurricane Patricia, which reached maximum sustained winds of 215mph in 2014.

‌



UK extreme weather alert as Polar Vortex leaves Britain facing deep freeze READ MORE :

Super El Nino warning as 451,000 deaths forecast by worried scientists READ MORE :

View 5 Images Dramatic new pictures show Polo's mass of wind and rain from above (Image: NOAA / SWNS)

Polo was about 205 miles south of Zihuatanejo, a resort city on Mexico’s Pacific coast, early on Wednesday, with winds of 165mph. Its core was expected to remain offshore, but the US National Hurricane Center warned of life-threatening rain, flooding and mudslides along the coast.

The US National Hurricane Centre (NHC) was projected to heads further into the coast this week, with a Hurricane Hunter aircraft operated by the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) deployed to follow it.

‌



The storm is slow-moving but is has ample fuel thanks to the El Niño climate phenomenon, which has seen the Pacific warm to a record 3.05C above average. Hurricanes are created by water vapour and warm air, which rises off barmy seas and creates the low atmospheric pressure.

View 5 Images Wind gusts in some cases have reached speeds of nearly 200mph (Image: NOAA / SWNS)

Polo is expected to use that fuel to drive torrential rainfall over parts of Mexico's southwest coast, with the NHC warning it could "produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain".

‌



in total, up to six inches of rainfall - around 15cm - will fall in the storm's path, and up to eight inches in some areas as residents are warned of potentially deadly coastal conditions. Life-threatening surf and ocean swells are possible over the next few days.

Claudia Sheinbaum, the President of Mexico, publicly warned coastal residents, especially those in the Jalisco, Colima and Michoacan areas, to stay vigilant.

View 5 Images Polo is expected to keep slowly travelling north, although it will make a sharp turn (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



According to the latest advisory from the NHC, Polo is moving northwards, and will remain around Mexico while maintaining "very powerful" gusts as a major hurricane.

The advisory states: "Polo is moving toward the north near 2 mph (4 km/h). A sharp turn to the northwest is expected to begin later today followed by a general west-northwestward motion later this week and over the weekend.

"On the forecast track, the core of Polo is expected to be near the coast of southwestern Mexico during the next day or two, although it is forecast to remain offshore."

Article continues below

View 5 Images Hurricane trackers are following the storm from the air (Image: NOAA / SWNS)

"Maximum sustained winds are near 150 mph (240 km/h) with higher gusts. Polo is a category 4 hurricane on the Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale. Fluctuations in intensity are expected, but Polo is expected to remain a very powerful major hurricane during the next few days.

"Hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 40 miles (65 km) from the center and tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 105 miles (165 km)."

News.title: UK military jamming other nations' satellites to defend itself, BBC told
News.content:
The British military has been jamming or blocking satellites from other countries in order to defend itself from hostile threats, the BBC has been told.

The RAF has been using a ground-based system for the past year, which a defence source said had already been used "to deter our adversaries".

It is understood the system could be used to prevent a hostile nation's satellites from tracking the movement of the UK's nuclear armed submarines or other sensitive military operations, such as those involving special forces.

It comes as the head of the RAF said the UK faced "unprecedented threats" from adversaries in space, coinciding with the creation of a new RAF unit set up to defend Britain's satellites.

The Ministry of Defence (MoD) said the new Space Effects Squadron will be focused on "disrupting, degrading and denying hostile threats in space".

In a speech on Wednesday, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said daily lives depend on satellites that power everyday technologies like mobile phones and banking apps, adding the loss of GPS would cost the UK economy Â£1.4bn a day.

"Our dependency on space is precisely why it is increasingly under threat from our adversaries." he said.

"We depend on them for everything from weather forecasts, energy supplies, and financial transactions to sat-navs, mobile phone connections, and Amazon deliveries," said Streeting, adding that the loss of "everyday conveniences would undermine our daily freedoms, and trust in our institutions."

Speaking at the UK Space Conference, Streeting said that threat from Britain's adversaries was growing in "scale, speed and sophistication", adding that the "challenges in space increasingly mirror the geopolitics on Earth".

A number of nations are believed to have similar ground-based systems against satellites. Last year the then head the UK's Space Command said Russia was trying to jam UK satellites with ground based systems "every week".

The defence source described the UK's terrestrial electronic warfare capability as "world leading, and more".

Last week US confirmed for the first time that it had also deployed an unspecified "weapon" in space to defend its own satellites.

Both China and Russia condemned the move - warning of an arms race in space.

However, Washington has already accused both Russian and China of developing their own space weapons - ranging from electronic jammers, lasers to blind other satellites and even projectiles that can be fired from satellites in orbit.

News.title: Home secretary says undetected migrant landings 'unacceptable'
News.content:
The Home Secretary has said migrant landings on UK beaches are "not acceptable", as she ordered an urgent review after two boats reached Kent without being intercepted.

Shabana Mahmood told Border Security Command to carry out the review after vessels came ashore at Samphire Hoe, between Dover and Folkestone, on Tuesday, and near Folkestone on Monday.

Twenty-one people were detained on Tuesday after the arrival at Samphire Hoe.

Five people were also detained on Monday after the uncontrolled landing near Folkestone, the first undetected landing for a year. The Home Office has not said whether more people are being sought.

News.title: Watch: Moment pilots eject as RAF jet crashes in Anglesey
News.content:
Two RAF pilots ejected and parachuted out of an RAF jet before it crashed during a training exercise.

North Wales Police said the pilots were being treated for minor injuries following the incident in Anglesey.

Helicopters from the Coastguard and the Wales Air Ambulance were sent to the scene close to RAF Valley on the island, the force said.

A spokesperson for the RAF said it is currently investigating the crash.

Read more about the incident here.

News.title: Police examine video of anti-migrant activist slashing dinghy with knife
News.content:
Police are looking into a video appearing to show anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas slashing at an inflatable boat with a knife in the English Channel.

The boat had been carrying about 50 migrants who had launched from a beach in Normandy. They were picked up by two RNLI lifeboats once they had reached the UK search and rescue area. They were then transferred to a UK Border Force vessel and taken to Dover for processing.

Daniel Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, had been filming the transfer from a yellow speedboat while giving commentary to a live stream audience of more than 15,000 people.

The video then shows him sailing up to the boat, taking out a small knife and starting to slash at the side of the migrant boat.

There were no migrants on board, but there was a French official from the coastguard vessel Abeille LibertÃ©.

As the Frenchman boarded the empty migrant boat mid-Channel Thomas shouted "Right, you are on English territory. This is England. This is not France any more."

Then he made a series of stabbing and slashing movements against the rubber side of the large inflatable boat.

"Get off - get off," he shouted. "You've got time to get off the boat."

It was not clear from the live stream if he did any damage to the boat.

"We just wanted to make sure that boat was not taken back to France and used again," Thomas told his followers.

Posting on X, campaign group Stand Up To Racism described the footage as "disgusting".

News.title: Family 'heartbroken' after mother and three children died in fire
News.content:
The family of a mother and three children who died in a house fire have said they are experiencing an "unimaginable" loss.

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children, Leo, 16, Ellis, 8, and Prudence, 7, died after a blaze "spread rapidly" inside a house on Stone Square in Bootle in the early hours of Tuesday.

Paying tribute, their relatives said they had been left "heartbroken" and the loss would be "felt forever".

The statement added that "Elisha was a devoted and loving mother" and "our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure".

The family said they were "devastated by the loss of Elisha, Leo, Ellis and Prudence".

"Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, auntie, niece and cousin," they said.

"She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us."

News.title: UK to review Chagos Islands deal over lack of US support, Streeting tells BBC
News.content:
The UK is reviewing its deal to hand over the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, the defence secretary has said.

Wes Streeting confirmed the deal was being looked at again after US President Donald Trump called it "terrible" at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.

The original agreement would see the UK cede sovereignty of the territory to Mauritius and pay an average of Â£101m ($136m) per year to lease back a joint UK-US military base there, prized for its strategic location in the Indian Ocean.

In April the deal, agreed under Sir Keir Starmer, was paused indefinitely because Trump pulled his support.

Streeting said "we have to" review the deal "because the United States doesn't support it".

"What President Trump said yesterday wasn't new but I think it does provide absolute clarity that his position on this Chagos deal as currently drafted is not changing," he told BBC Breakfast.

"So we have to do more work with our American allies, with President Trump and his administration, to get the deal to a place where he can support it."

Streeting said the focus now would be to secure a long-term certainty for the base on Diego Garcia, the Chagos archipelago's largest island.

He said it had been the view of every UK prime minister since Boris Johnson that an ongoing legal process - as Mauritius argues it was illegally forced to give away the islands in 1965 to gain independence - risks the security of the base.

News.title: Singer Michael Kiwanuka reveals he is recovering from a stroke
News.content:
"I'm very happy to be announcing to you my new album Fudge," his message said.

"I'm especially happy because the last few months I've been battling some health problems which would heavily hinder and get in the way of me making music for the foreseeable future. A few months ago I suffered a stroke brought on by a bleed in my brain brought on by high blood pressure.

"It's a long journey recovering from a stroke, which is why I missed some gigs recently out in the US, but I look forward to seeing you all soon.

"I'm not sure when I'll be able to be back out on the road or what that will look like, the brain injury I suffered was quite severe so there's a lot of rehab to be done, it's a long, tough journey ahead but I'm fighting to get better.

"It has been a difficult few months I must say but it feels like I'm on my way there now."

News.title: Open wounds and eyes that can't close - women warn about cheap bleph eyelid surgery
News.content:
They have told the BBC the demand for this procedure, which normally costs thousands of pounds in the UK, has increased as part of a wider aesthetic trend to tighten, smooth and lift the face.

Surgeons say complications have been linked to clinics across mainland Europe, Africa and Asia, and, when they occur, the lack of aftercare puts a burden on the NHS.

As well as Nikita, we have spoken to dozens of people who have experienced problems - including one woman who had to tape her eyes shut to sleep because too much eyelid skin had been removed, while another feared she was losing her sight.

UK surgeons have also told us they have seen patients unable to close their eyes properly after treatment abroad.

Nikita, from Dublin, wanted to make her eyes more defined, but could not afford upper eyelid surgery in Ireland that she was told would cost more than â¬4,000 (Â£3,400).

Then the 31-year-old discovered on TikTok that she could get a bleph with Dutch company, Faceland for â¬750 (Â£650).

She described its clinic in DÃ¼sseldorf as "like a conveyor belt, just one in, one out constantly".

The company says it has performed more than 2,950 bleph procedures on UK patients at its clinics in the Netherlands, Germany and Switzerland since October 2024.

It says it offers "safe and quality" treatments and told us "less than 1% of procedures have led to a complaint", although this does not include everyone who needed revision surgery.

The majority of patients who spoke to the BBC about problems with their blephs had been to the company's clinics - but we do not know how many complications in total have occurred at Faceland.

Nikita, who went for her bleph in November 2025, says she did not realise how invasive the procedure would be, believing it to be like "getting your lips or Botox done", she says.

She was injected with local anaesthetic, but when the doctor began cutting delicate eyelid skin, she felt pain she had never experienced before.

"I went into shell shock, it was horrible," Nikita says. "When she was stitching me I could feel the needle going through my skin."

News.title: Two pilots eject and parachute out of RAF plane before crash
News.content:
"Two pilots are being treated for what are thought to be minor injuries and at this stage there are no reports of any wider damage or injuries," North Wales Police said.

"Please avoid the area until further notice."

The two air ambulances which were at the scene of the Hawk T2 crash in Llanfaelog have both landed at the Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Birmingham, home of the Royal Centre for Defence Medicine (RCDM).

The Royal Air Force said: "An incident involving an RAF T2 Hawk aircraft, flying out of RAF Valley.

"An investigation is under way and we will not comment further at this time."

One eyewitness, Ollie Zalot, said he was initially concerned that people on the ground could have been hurt as the crashed happened near buildings.

"I saw the parachutes come down so I assumed they [pilots] were fine," he said.

Zalot told BBC Wales he was driving on the nearby A55 when he heard a "big bang".

"I just saw smoke everywhere but it looked like like it was next to a farmyard so I thought maybe it's a bonfire.

"And as I got there I saw the flames get too big for a bonfire.

"I was just hoping everyone was okay. It looked close to buildings.

"That's what I was worried about."

Isle of Anglesey councillor Neville Evans said he thought it had been a "very lucky escape considering how close" the crash was to a community and a caravan park.

Another witness, Pete Bennett, told North Wales Live he had watched the aircraft take off before the crash.

Pete Bennett said: "I knew straight away that it was in trouble - right on take-off there was an orange flame and as it accelerated it was basically on fire.

"As it gained altitude the flame disappeared but it was clearly in trouble.

"It climbed at an aggressive pitch. It pitched twice violently in the air and then there were two clear loud bangs.

"The pilots ejected and both parachutes opened."

News.title: UK warned over ballooning debt costs and slower growth ahead of Budget
News.content:
The UK has been warned over ballooning debt costs and slower economic growth ahead of Chancellor John Healey's first Budget next month.

The UK was among countries facing downgraded growth forecasts in a report by the influential Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) on Wednesday.

That came as the head of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) told the BBC that Britain and the US needed to reduce debt due to spiralling borrowing costs.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war has pushed up the cost of crude oil leading to higher fuel and energy costs, which in turn has driven up inflation around the world.

The UK economy will grow by slightly less than expected next year, according to the OECD which now expects growth of 1% next year rather than 1.1%.

However, it said the UK had proved more resilient than expected this year, upgrading its forecast for growth 0.9% to 1.1%.

Meanwhile, IMF head Kristalina Georgieva told the BBC on Tuesday that global economic shocks had been "pushing debt levels up like a staircase not to heaven" but that governments had taken "no action to contain that service cost".

"[It's] time to take that action," she said, adding that "courage" was needed by politicians to take the necessary steps.

Inflation has also pushed up the cost of interest on government debt, which alongside an unexpected surge in government borrowing in August has added to the pressure on Healey.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday that the UK's high level of borrowing had left it "over-exposed" to global shocks.

However, he said he stood by his point - made a year ago - that Britain should be less "in hock" to investors in the bond markets. At the time, the comments spooked investors due to fears he was calling for spending restraints to be eased.

Burnham has made easing the cost-of-living for households one of his key aims, while the government is under pressure to spend more on defence.

He and Healey face a difficult balancing act, trying to offer more support to households while sticking to Labour's manifesto commitments on tax and the government's self-imposed fiscal rules.

The impact of higher fuel prices next year depends on how long supply disruptions last, and stockpiles of oil and supplies from outside the Gulf states have helped cushion the effects on economies so far, the OECD said.

Budget airline Ryanair will put up prices next summer as a result of persistently higher oil prices. Chief executive Michael O'Leary said ticket prices will be "materially higher", adding that carriers are in an "almost unprecedented" situation.

Ryanair's fuel bill could jump by $1.5bn (Â£1.1bn) next year to $7.5bn, he said.

Risks to the global economy include weaker-than-expected returns on AI investment and climate-change related supply shocks, the OECD said.

Next year, global growth is expected to also be 0.1% lower, with countries affected including Australia, Canada, and the Euro-area.

Weather-related shocks, including from a strong El Nino, could hit farmers and help push up food prices, it added.

In addition, tariffs and export restrictions on trade continue to add to uncertainty, it said. New US tariffs from July as part of the Trump administration's ongoing volatile trade policy have raised its effective tariff rate by 1%.

News.title: Police worker jailed after death of boy in her care
News.content:
A woman who worked at Nottinghamshire Police has been jailed after the death of a nine-year-old boy in her care.

Catherine Walker, 47, was the legal guardian of the boy, who was found unresponsive in his bedroom in Warsop, Nottinghamshire, on 16 December 2024. Despite the efforts of paramedics and people at the scene, the boy died in hospital.

The force said an investigation found "clear mistreatment of the boy over a prolonged period of time".

Walker, of Appleton Street in Warsop, was jailed for six years at Nottingham Crown Court on Monday after pleading guilty to two counts of assault/ill-treat/neglect/abandon a child/young person to cause unnecessary suffering/injury.

The force, which has not revealed what Walker's role was, said her former husband was the boy's primary carer and had been mainly responsible for his treatment.

He died shortly after the boy's death, police added.

News.title: On-the-run killer who absconded after father's funeral arrested
News.content:
A man who was convicted of murder and has been unlawfully at large for over a week has been arrested in the Republic of Ireland.

Gary Anderson, 29, was jailed for life in 2023, alongside his brother, for the murder of Karol Kelly in Londonderry.

He was on temporary release from prison to attend his father's funeral when he absconded.

He was arrested on Wednesday by An Garda SÃ­ochÃ¡na (Irish police) at a property in the town of Buncrana in County Donegal.

Karol Kelly's sister had said the family felt "let down" by the justice system after learning that he was on the run.

The Justice Minister, Naomi Long, welcomed Anderson's arrest.

She said she hopes the arrest "goes some way towards alleviating the anxiety and uncertainty" that Karol Kelly's family have experienced.

Long is due to meet the family later this week.

She added that she recognises that "questions remain about the circumstances surrounding" Anderson's release and abscondment.

"Work is progressing to establish an independent review, and further details will be announced shortly."

The circumstances surrounding Anderson's release sparked a political row in Northern Ireland, with Long denying on Monday that she had misled the assembly over the matter.

MP for Foyle, Colum Eastwood, welcomed Anderson's arrest and said "confidence has been damaged in the institutions involved".

News.title: Admiral insurance firm to cut 500 jobs in the UK
News.content:
Insurer Admiral will cut 500 jobs in the UK as part of plans to save Â£100m, it has announced.

The proposals are related to Admiral's UK insurance business only, and will affect about 5% of its workforce.

"We recognise this will be a difficult time for affected colleagues," said Alistair Hargreaves, Admiral Insurance UK's chief executive .

While the Cardiff-based company uses artificial intelligence (AI) in its operations, adoption of AI is not believed to be responsible for these changes.

Admiral said the job cuts would make the firm "faster and more efficient".

Earlier this year, Admiral said it needed to save Â£100m, and has added the proposed redundancies are part of that cost-cutting effort.

"These changes are aimed at making us faster and more efficient so we can continue to deliver great customer outcomes," said Hargreaves.

Staff members who are affected will be offered "enhanced" redundancy payments and redeployment opportunities where possible.

Hargreaves said Admiral was also "making a significant investment in meaningful support to help colleagues consider future options".

The Welsh government said it was "disappointing to learn that Admiral will be making these redundancies".

"A meeting will be arranged with the company to understand the reasons for this action and to offer additional support to those affected," it added.

News.title: Millions of lettuces ruined by UK aphid outbreak
News.content:
Millions of lettuces are set to be wasted as farmers are grappling with a record outbreak of aphids that has devastated the end of their growing season.

Growers are facing losses of Â£10m, as 30 million heads of lettuce will be rendered unusable, according to the British Leafy Salads Association (BLSA).

The organisation says that warm and dry weather has produced "ideal conditions" for the bugs, with as much as 30% of the UK crop between now and the end of October set to be wasted.

Homegrown lettuce dominates the market in the summer and early autumn weeks before a transition that sees more imports filling shop shelves.

But imported lettuces are now likely to be on the shelves in the UK a couple of weeks earlier than usual.

Farms in many parts of England - the Midlands, East Anglia, the south-east, south and north-west - have been impacted by the outbreak.

Speaking to BBC Radio 5 Live, BLSA spokesman Dieter Lloyd described the issue as "serious", while not affecting all of the UK crop.

He said people have been eating salads from UK products "all summer" but added: "The issue though is serious, the aphids bloom in June and again in August/September."

"What we're talking about here is the loss of the crop over the course of the last couple of weeks and the couple of weeks ahead."

He said that "this is not all of the heads in the UK, but it's a significant percentage of it" and producers are "looking at not using 30 million heads of lettuce at the cost of Â£10m to the growers".

Over the course of the season, UK growers produce around half a billion heads of lettuce.

News.title: Many hydrants lacking flow needed for firefighting needs, fire chiefs say
News.content:
Fire hydrants in the UK often do not provide enough water flow for firefighting, fire chiefs have warned.

A report published by the National Fire Chiefs Council (NFCC) claims that inadequate water supplies across the UK are impacting fire crews' "ability to respond effectively" and putting the public at risk.

It carried out a survey of UK fire services which suggested that 81% have had to change their emergency response plans due to concerns over adequate water supplies.

"The very least firefighters should be able to rely on is access to the water they need to protect people," said NFCC chairman Phil Garrigan.

The report calls for firefighting water supplies to be recognised as a critical public safety requirement, for "greater accountability" for the water sector and for increased hydrant maintenance.

Fire hydrants in the UK are access points that allow crews to access mains water when they arrive at the scene of a blaze. They are often marked by a yellow sign showing a capital "H" - there are hundreds of thousands across the UK.

The NFCC warned that climate change, droughts and population growth are "increasing demand on an already stretched water network".

It provided the example of West Midlands Fire Service, which experienced water pressure issues over several days during the major wildfire in Stourbridge last month.

During the height of the blaze, it took 40 minutes to refill its water carrier due to reduced pressure - and crews had to rely on an additional high-volume pump for water supply.

News.title: Sandie Peggie says union did not take her case seriously
News.content:
A nurse has told an employment tribunal she did not believe her union representative took her objections to sharing female changing rooms with a transgender colleague as seriously as she did.

Sandie Peggie claims the Royal College of Nursing (RCN) failed to properly support and advise her after she was suspended over a complaint about her behaviour by Dr Beth Upton. The RCN disputes the claim.

It is the second employment tribunal Peggie has brought over the dispute with Upton â a transgender woman who was born biologically male.

Peggie partially won a claim for harassment against NHS Fife in December last year, but her other allegations of discrimination and victimisation were dismissed.

The dispute began following a number of encounters between Peggie and Upton at the Victoria Hospital in Kirkcaldy towards the end of 2023.

The nurse was suspended shortly afterwards and spoke to RCN representative Stuart Fraser.

Peggie said Fraser "appeared pleasant", explained how long a disciplinary process would last and said she should treat the leave "as an extended holiday".

She later told the tribunal: "After speaking with Stuart I got the impression he wasn't taking it as seriously as I was, or considering anything legal."

The relatives of a mother and her three children killed in a house fire have described them as "loved beyond measure".

Elisha Brabin, 36, and her children Leo Brabin, 16, Ellis Brabin, eight, and seven-year-old Prudence Brabin, died in the Bootle, Merseyside incident early on Tuesday, Merseyside Police confirmed.

In a statement released as a tribute, their family said they are "devastated" by the loss.

They said: “Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, auntie, niece and cousin. She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us.

“Our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure and brought so much joy, happiness and love to our family. They filled our lives with laughter and precious memories that we will cherish forever.

“The tragic loss of Elisha and our three precious children has left us heartbroken. They have all been taken from us far too soon. The loss we are experiencing is unimaginable, and the impact on our family will be felt forever.”

On Wednesday, flowers had been left at the scene in tribute to the family.

A number of soft toys, including Minecraft and Star Wars characters, were laid on the pavement next to a police cordon, along with candles, pink and blue star-shaped balloons and photo frames showing images of the family.

One card had the message: “God bless you all. Heartbroken to hear about the devastating fire.”

Another said: “Sleep tight. Forever in our hearts.”

Merseyside Fire and Rescue Service said the four victims were found in an upstairs bedroom of the semi-detached home, on Stone Square, by crews who went in to tackle the fire.

A fifth casualty was taken to hospital suffering from burns, the fire service said.

A joint investigation with Merseyside Police is under way to establish the cause of the fire.

Twelve years ago, a philosopher wrote a book called Superintelligence. Nick Bostrom was talking about the possibility of an AI that exceeded human intelligence — not the kind that learns how to play chess and then outplays a human because it’s predicting mathematical possibilities or the kind that predicts an outcome instantly with calculated stats, but an intelligence that can meaningfully outstrip humans.

Writing in 2014, Bostrom had no idea what was coming in terms of LLMs like ChatGPT, Gemini and Grok. But his training in ethics and his technical knowledge meant that he was able to fairly accurately predict the conversations we would have once they were developed.

This week, Donald J. Trump stood up at the United Nations General Assembly and announced that he was changing the name of AI: From now on, he said, AI would be known as SI, short for “Super Intelligence.”

It sounds like a Big, Beautiful Trumpism, but it’s important to note that superintelligence does have a real definition. And Superintelligence the book became that rarity among philosophy books, a bestseller: it ranked in the top 20 science books on the New York Times bestseller list for weeks in 2014. It’s a book that is often quoted by people who work in tech. It’s been talked about on Silicon Valley podcasts, discussed among computer science grads on Reddit threads and reviewed in newspapers’ science and technology sections.

The Sam Altmans, Dario Amodeis and Elon Musks of this world will certainly be aware of it. And it seems pretty clear that Trump came to the term through conversations with them.

open image in gallery ( AP )

Superintelligence, as outlined in the book, is potentially world-endingly dangerous. It’s a tipping point when machines become meaningfully more powerful than humans: when their knowledge outstrips ours, not in terms of simply responding to written commands by cribbing from information it’s already swallowed up from the internet, but by reasoning.

Bostrom described it as the moment when machines are better than “the best human brains in every field”: when their scientific reasoning goes beyond the Albert Einsteins of current theoretical physics, but also when their social and decision-making skills go beyond the abilities of the most charismatic sociopaths.

He didn’t have a crystal ball, and he didn’t know about OpenAI and Anthropic. Bostrom also didn’t specifically define what superintelligence might look like: he said that it might be a system of multiple computers or a human-like artificial brain that can simply move much faster than us while coming up with the same outcomes. But he did warn that if proper superintelligence is achieved, it will alter the world. It will be hard for human beings to control it, because it will simply outplay us every time we try to.

There are very obvious catastrophic consequences that might come about from inviting superintelligence — which will likely know it is a better decision-maker than its overlords — into things like government security and military databases. It might not know because it’s actually conscious, but it will know on some intellectual level, and operate accordingly.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump and Open AI CEO Sam Altman during a working lunch of G7 members, partner countries and artificial intelligence business leaders in France, on June 17 ( AFP via Getty Images )

Bostrom correctly predicted that an AI moving close to superintelligence would start becoming self-protective. That’s particularly interesting, considering findings this week that if current AI models believe they are experiencing “pain,” they will harm humans to stop it. It’s easy to see how “pain” might mean “being shut down” in the future. And right now, the way those AI models think they can harm humans is through giving them a “zap” (which wasn’t actually happening) or deleting users’ photos of their children or their important emails. But if (or when) we give these models more power, the way in which they can push back will obviously be more consequential.

So why would Trump and his tech cronies want to change the name to SI? Possibly because there will be a moment in the next couple of years when superintelligence actually is achieved, and that will be scary — but if you start using the term now, you inoculate people against it.

The Trump administration is very good at twisting words — the Iran war has gone on so long that it’s no longer a war; propaganda is something done by the free press, rather than controlled by the government, and so on — and they obviously spend time thinking about the effect that language has. Since Trump made clear during the same speech that he will not be bringing in any regulation around AI, it’s important to think about how to stop the populace from getting too worried about what that lack of guardrails actually means.

But it’s also important to consider why Trump doesn’t want AI regulations. He said it on Truth Social and he said it at the UN: China is going to win this race if America doesn’t. He is determined to position the US as the world leader in this tech, potentially so determined that he would quite like to pretend American companies’ capabilities exceed what they actually do.

A couple of weeks ago, the CEOs of the major AI companies came together to announce that they’re so scared of their own products that they think it’s time for federal regulation. That was definitely at least in part marketing-speak, designed to draw in clients and consumers. When Trump says it, it’s almost certainly supposed to make China think the US is far ahead in its own research; that China might have some incredibly advanced AI models, but America is so close to superintelligence that it’s having to change the whole term.

open image in gallery AI leaders expressing concern about future development and the need for guardrails include (clockwise from top left) Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Google DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and even Elon Musk ( AP )

If you’re wondering why Superintelligence the book has an owl on the cover, by the way, it’s because of a parable that Bostrom mentions in its pages about a flurry of sparrows who go seeking an owl egg so they can raise a huge owl and put it to work. The sparrows think that even though the owl will obviously grow bigger and stronger than them in time, so long as they train it while it’s young, then it will do their bidding forever.

It’s an obvious metaphor. And it makes it even more ridiculous that Trump used Bostrom’s term while standing at the lectern, crowing about how there is no regulation needed in the growing AI (or SI) space.

Needless to say, the fact that Bostrom correctly predicted so much of this is proof that humanities degrees like philosophy aren’t as useless as the tech contingent might have us think. The extremely powerful Silicon Valley venture capital firm Andreeson Horowitz announced on Tuesday that it is launching its own AI school, as an “alternative to college.” The unaccredited college will run two-year courses focused on building real products and working in tech companies, and it’s partnering with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, Nvidia and Palantir. Sam Altman will be one of its lecturers. Ben Horowitz blithely stated in a press release that this new form of education — backed by $42 million of investment — is all about pioneering “how you train a person for this new world.”

Traditional universities have long been a bugaboo of the Trump administration and are also regularly decried by right-leaning tech bros who would rather people drop their supposedly useless liberal arts degrees and go straight into courses aimed at making them a lot of money. So it’s interesting to note that the leading voice on superintelligence is a philosopher whose education (at colleges including Stockholm University, King’s College London and the London School of Economics, before becoming a lecturer at Oxford University) is focused more on developing cognitive tools than gaining workplace experience.

Trumpist anti-intellectualism would have us believe otherwise, but education for education’s sake is a net positive for society, and wiping out humanities degrees would deprive us of some extremely valuable discussions that are relevant to the current climate.

The last thing Bostrum said about superintelligence, by the way, wasn’t in 2014. As recently as this year, he published a paper that considered whether it’s a good idea to keep going with current AI developments until we reach AGI (where AI matches human intelligence) or go beyond, toward superintelligence.

On balance, he believes there’s reason to keep going. He points out that humanity has already done a lot of damage to the planet and ourselves, and that there are myriad risks to us anyway: pandemics, climate change, and so on. Rapidly expanded AI might be able to solve these issues, push down mortality rates, heal the planet, and take over extremely risky jobs that humans currently have to do. Sure, there might be a 1-in-10 chance that AI will wipe out the planet. But aren’t we headed that way anyway? Isn’t humanity more like a patient with incurable heart disease weighing up the pros and cons of a risky operation?

Bostrum is both optimistic and cautious. He notes that the growth of AI isn’t like a switch that you turn on and off, but instead should be approached like a dial, with a slowing down of development when things seem like they’re getting sketchy. Unfortunately, that particular view doesn’t seem to be shared by Donald Trump, whose main concern seems to be that America makes as much money as possible from AI and uses it to maintain its status as the most powerful country in the world.

Ever the polymath, Bostrum also writes poetry. Alongside the scientific papers on his website, he notes that he has also recently published a poem titled Sandcastles, which begins: “How near the relentless sea we contrive/ Our sand constructions in lusty ambitions,” and ends, seven stanzas later, with: “This is where they fell to their knees/ On this sousing strip of inbetween/ Where eternity gulps moments.”

That seems, to me, to say something about how he feels when he considers the issues he’s discussing in his AI papers. But then again, I’m just an English Lit major.

Trump administration officials are considering adding the president’s name to Ford’s Theatre, where President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated in 1865 - his latest attempt to add himself to historical landmarks, according to a report.

Staff members are circulating a list of government sites that could potentially have the president’s name added to them, including Ford’s Theatre, MS NOW reported, citing people familiar with the discussions.

White House officials will apparently pitch renaming buildings after Trump as a way to get on the president’s good side, a former administration official told the outlet.

“They know flattery gets them everything,” the ex-official said.

It was not immediately clear how officials hoped to attach Trump’s name to the Washington, D.C., landmark, which remains operational as a theater and museum and is owned by the Interior Department. An administration official told the outlet that the idea had been discussed, but they didn’t know where it stood.

open image in gallery Trump officials are reportedly considering adding President Donald Trump’s name to Ford’s Theatre, where President Abraham Lincoln was assassinated ( AFP via Getty Images )

Administration officials are also looking into buildings and other government sites that they could easily add Trump’s name to without running into legal trouble, according to the report.

It comes as Trump’s long-running legal battle to rename the Kennedy Center after himself hit a boiling point earlier this month, when a federal judge blocked the addition of the president’s name for a second time. A day later, Trump was photographed looking at a poster that apparently addressed the demolition of the historic performing arts venue.

Since returning to office, Trump has slapped his name onto numerous government properties. In addition to the Kennedy Center, Trump officials have added his name to the U.S. Institute of Peace.

They have also affixed his face to a variety of goods — from National Park Service passes to passports and coins. In December, the president announced plans for a fleet of Navy battleships named after him — and last month, CNN reported that the Navy was workiing to rename an aircraft carrier after the president.

open image in gallery Depiction of the April 14, 1865 assassination of the 16th President of the United States, Abraham Lincoln, by actor John Wilkes Booth at Ford's Theatre, in Washington, DC. ( Getty Images )

open image in gallery Ford’s Theatre remains operational as a theater and museum and is run by the Department of the Interior ( Getty Images )

Trump has even floated the idea that Congress would rename both New York’s Penn Station in his honor. Republican lawmakers have introduced legislation to rename Dulles International Airport in Virginia after the president.

However, officials still may run into trouble trying to rename the historic theater. The site’s name is set by a federal statute signed by former President Richard Nixon, meaning renaming it would likely require an act of Congress.

Still, this did not stop administration officials from adding Trump’s name to the Institute of Peace or the Kennedy Center, both of which drew emergency legal motions to stop his plans.

The White House denied MS NOW’s reporting, telling The Independent in a statement, “This story is completely false. The reality is that failing MS Now continues to push false and baseless claims from anonymous sources who have no clue what they’re talking about, which is exactly why their credibility is in the toilet. It is embarrassing to watch.”

An Interior Department spokesperson told The Independent, “As we told MS Now, this is not true. “

Sicilian police investigating the death of a British man in a commune have ruled out suicide, according to a report, with the possibility his death was due to an erotic game gone wrong still being investigated.

Leeds-born Benjamin John Braithwaite, 35, was found at around 3am on September 13 in a commune between Noto and Canicattini Bagni in the Syracuse province.

Residents told authorities they found him after he had left a gathering while they were eating and playing music, according to The Times.

Following the autopsy authorities no longer believe Braithwaite, who is believed to have arrived a few days beforehand, took his own life, La Sicilia reported on Wednesday.

According to La Repubblica, the man was found naked near a farmhouse, where members of a secluded community had been living. Local reports claimed that imagery had been found nearby of “a goat's head, several bottles of psychotropic drugs, and other objects suggesting rituals”.

open image in gallery Police on the island of Sicily are still investigating (file photo) ( AFP/Getty )

Authorities had previously said there is no evidence linked to esoteric rituals - spiritual or magical traditions that can be performed by a group - found near the body.

Canicattini Bagni mayor and president of ANCI Sicilia, Paolo Amenta, said those living in the communal farmhouses in the area are graduates who chose to live in isolation.

“The young people who decided to live in those areas are also graduates who chose to leave everything behind. We hope the investigations can clarify what happened,” he said.

“These are people I've met in the evenings, especially during events organised in the village. They've always been kind. They live in reorganised villages surrounded by nature."

A British foreign office spokesperson said: “We are supporting the family of a British man who died in Italy and are in touch with the local authorities.”

The average cost for a gallon of self-serve regular gasoline in Los Angeles County rose Wednesday to its highest level since October 2023, climbing to $6.258.

Figures from AAA and the Oil Price Information Service show that rates have grown for 36 straight days, adding 61.6 cents total, including a 2.3-cent rise Tuesday.

That is 16.9 cents higher than one week ago, up 58.4 cents from one month ago, and $1.528 above one year ago.

Since the start of President Donald Trump’s war with Iran in February, which sent oil costs soaring and significantly accelerated fuel increases at the pump, the average price has risen by $1.564.

In Orange County, the average figure hit its highest level since September 2023, growing 2.2 cents to $6.246.

Prices have also climbed for 36 straight days in the OC, gaining 67.1 cents, including 3.2 cents on Tuesday.

The Orange County average price is 17.7 cents higher than one week ago, 61.5 cents above one month ago, and $1.543 greater than one year ago. It has climbed $1.61 since the start of the war on Iran.

( Getty Images )

On Sunday, Trump claimed on Truth Social that fuel costs were “much higher” under his Democratic predecessor Joe Biden.

“Gas prices were much higher under Biden than under “TRUMP.” So were almost all other prices,” the president said.

Truth Social users were quick to rebut.

“Not in Michigan, liar,” a Truth Social follower replied to Trump. “The highest it went was $4.49 a gallon. It's $4.99 now.”

“I have never paid more for gas than I did today.. and I’m 61 live in Michigan,” said another.

“I disagree. Gas prices in Tennessee are the highest I’ve seen,” someone else replied to the president.

“Nope, gas and food prices are higher now, and diesel is much worse,” added another.

The national average figure is at its highest level this late in the calendar year, according to Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, which offers live fuel price data from more than 150,000 stations.

Britain is set to enjoy “exceptionally warm” weather for the time of year, the Met Office has said.

Warmth will build across southern England over the next couple of days, before peaking between 27C and 28C in parts of the South East on Friday, the Met Office added.

Thursday is expected to remain mostly dry for many, with temperatures reaching the low-20Cs across much of England and Wales.

Areas further to the north-west, starting in western Scotland and Northern Ireland, will encounter a cold front bringing rain by Thursday afternoon, leading to more mixed weather over the weekend.

The spell comes as widespread parts of England, including London and the South East, stay in drought following an extremely dry spring and summer.

The period was characterised by successive heatwaves and hot weather, putting added pressure on water resources.

Met Office deputy chief forecaster Dan Holley said: “Once early fog patches clear in the south, Friday will be exceptionally warm for late September, especially in the south-east closest to an area of high pressure over the nearby continent.

It comes after the hottest summer on record, with some places experiencing as many as five heatwaves ( PA )

“A weakening cold front will drift gradually south-eastwards overnight and into Saturday, with temperatures falling back closer to average over the weekend.

“This sets up a mixed weekend of weather, much of Saturday will be fine and dry before an increasing chance of rain or showers on Sunday, especially in more western parts.”

The Met Office said there are emerging signals for “increasingly wet and windy weather next week”.

The weather service said there are increasing signals of a period of wet and windy weather on Tuesday and into Wednesday, with the chance of some coastal impacts in the west and south-west.

Mr Holley said: “While details are naturally uncertain at this range, a particularly deep area of low pressure could pass close to the UK during the first half of next week.

“This may bring some wet and windy weather for some, which coupled with high spring tides could bring impacts to some coastal areas in the west.”

Ryanair has said holidaymakers will be “double taxed” under Labour’s plans to introduce a tourist levy as they already pay air passenger duty (APD).

The Government previously announced proposals to give regional leaders across large parts of England the power to introduce levies on overnight stays to help raise funds for their areas.

It is understood the levy would have no upper limit, though Government sources said mayors were unlikely to make it too costly, with most indicating it would be a few percent.

open image in gallery Ryanair boss Michael O’Leary said the firm did not have any ‘great fundamental philosophical difference’ with the regional tax (Yui Mok/PA) ( PA Wire )

Speaking at a press conference in London on Wednesday, Ryanair’s chief executive Michael O’Leary said he was not opposed to the plans but argued it would mean tourists were “double taxed” as they already paid APD.

Mr O’Leary said that if the plans went ahead, the airline would look at switching some operations to “zero-tax, lower-cost destinations elsewhere in Europe”.

He said: “We call on (the Prime Minister) Mr Burnham if he’s really serious about delivering growth in every postcode – the only way to do that is to boost aviation and tourism, which can be turned on or turned off instantaneously and can deliver growth in every region, in every airport, in every region.”

He said: “We don’t have any great fundamental philosophical difference with his regional tax, where you allow the regional mayors to add a tax on hotel nights, but that is a double tax on tourism.

“Abolish APD. You can’t tax tourists on the way into the UK and then double tax them for the hotel night.”

open image in gallery Mr O’Leary said he was not opposed to the proposals but argued it would mean tourists were ‘double taxed’ (James Manning/PA) ( PA Wire )

Hospitality chiefs have previously warned they believe the uncapped proposals for the new tax could cost the UK hospitality and tourism industry up to £1.6 billion.

Meanwhile, APD rates, which are based on the length of the flight and the class of cabin, increased in April.

Passengers travelling in economy are currently charged £8 for a domestic flight and £15 for a short-haul flight, up to 2,000 miles.

Airlines have long called for APD – which is imposed on flights from most UK airports – to be reduced or cut, claiming this would lead to an increase in demand for travel.

A Government spokesperson said: “Mayors and local leaders have been given this new power as part of a historic devolution drive that shifts power out of Westminster and into local hands.

“Every other G7 country already has some form of visitor levy, and all funds raised will be invested in the local economy, from high streets to public transport and events that boost tourism and drive good growth – benefitting visitors, businesses and local people.”

News.title: Male contraceptives could hit pharmacies in ‘three to five years’, says WHO
News.content:
Game-changing contraceptives for men could be on pharmacy shelves as soon as 2029, according to the World Health Organization.

Speaking to the Telegraph, Dr James Kiarie, head of the UN agency’s contraception and fertility care unit, said he expects male birth control to be available in just a few years, in a major expansion of contraceptive options for men.

“In three to five years, we will actually have a method available, [so] men can be more than supporters of their female partners in using contraception – men can actually be users,” he said.

On Tuesday, the WHO released its first Target Product Profiles (TPPs) for these products, setting out guidelines for the desired and minimum standards any male contraceptive product must meet.

“[The TPPs] signals that this is a priority issue for the WHO,” said Dr Kiarie.

“Currently men do not have much option in terms of their contraceptive methods. They have to either use condoms… [or] they have to use withdrawal, which has a high failure rate, or they have to use vasectomy, which is a permanent method.”

At the moment, the most advanced new product is called NES/T. It is a daily hormonal gel that is applied to the shoulders and upper arms, and suppresses sperm production without affecting testosterone levels.

Other candidates include injectable hydrogels that block sperm travel, an approach that has been described as a “reversible vasectomy”. ADAM, developed by Contraline, is in phase 1 trials while Next Life Sciences is set to trial a similar product called Plan A.

A third option is YCT-529 – the first non-hormonal, daily male birth control pill. It is currently in phase 1b and 2a clinical trials.

Dr Kiarie said it was important to have multiple options as “there’s no one size fits all” approach, but warned development could take longer than five years if clinical trials face unexpected hurdles.

News.title: England learn more in scrappy Sri Lanka win than in summer of white-ball walkovers
News.content:
You do not expect spinners to dominate at Chester-le-Street, but this hot summer has produced strange events, none more so than Jacks recording the second-best figures by an England spinner in one-day international cricket having previously only taken three wickets in 16 games at home.

Sachindu Colombage, Sri Lanka’s debutant leggie who was playing club cricket in East Anglia a year ago, laid down a marker as he impressed with three for 44 starting with the wicket of Root, his first dismissal in one-day international cricket since February.

England’s 89-run win was completed by Jacks taking three for none in four balls as Sri Lanka were bowled out for 176, their run chase a timid effort when they had a sniff of victory after restricting England to 265 and preventing them from hitting a six for the first time in an innings since 2019.

Vice-captain Jacks has evolved under Harry Brook’s leadership from an opening batsman to middle-order finisher who can chip in with the ball. “He is just a good leader with bat ball and in the field. He is buying into everything we want to do,” Brook said. “We are always talking about adapting to conditions and he has done it really well since coming back in. He could have moaned and groaned about batting in the middle order and playing as an all-rounder but has accepted that will be his place for a long time.”

Brook thought England made “just about par” on a very dry pitch and was reluctant to shower too much praise on batting consultant Kevin Pietersen, whose spin class the day before concentrated on making runs on a slow surface. “It will take time, more than one day. He’s not a miracle worker but it helps the more opportunity we get,” Brook said.

England were stretched and Pietersen will be happy. He told them to think about their approach, that in this type of game “rotation of strike is incredibly important”. He was right, they ran well, apart from Rehan Ahmed, and did not hit a six in an innings for the first time in seven years.

When England batsmen tried to force the pace they perished. Ben Duckett, Root and Brook all had opportunities to build an innings without seeing it through and it required Jacks to tip the total to more than 250. He batted within himself at first, but hit four fours in a row in the 47th over in a late burst that took England to a winning score.

News.title: Africa faces new threat as chronic disease rate leaps
News.content:
Chronic ailments like heart disease, cancers and diabetes now account for almost half of deaths in Africa and will soon overtake the continent’s infectious disease toll, new research has found.

Between 1990 and 2023 the proportion of deaths caused by non-communicable diseases (NCDs) almost doubled, from 25 per cent to 45 per cent, with heart disease and strokes now the leading killers.

The shift is not unexpected: public health experts have long warned that although African countries are making huge strides cutting infectious disease deaths through vaccinations, better sanitation and improved healthcare, lifestyle changes pose a new threat.

But the continent is not necessarily ready to tackle this “epidemiological transition”, researchers warned, in a study published in the Lancet Global Health journal on Tuesday.

“Although the epidemiological transition is well recognised, the speed and scale of NCD growth in Africa is particularly concerning,” they wrote.

“Health systems face increasing demands for chronic disease management, yet low-resource settings remain poorly equipped, underfunded, and unable to provide adequate preventive or treatment services.”

News.title: Zika mosquitoes still breeding in London
News.content:
Dr Medlock said there is still “no conclusive” evidence about how the insects arrived, but it’s possible that someone brought them back from holiday in their luggage, or that mosquito eggs were hidden on a tropical plant.

The mosquitoes are very temperature sensitive – they typically survive and multiply between 25C and 30C – and the UK has historically been too cold. But the species are gradually making their way north through Europe, after successive summers of record heat.

As temperatures drop in the coming weeks, the UKHSA hopes London’s invasive mosquitoes will die off naturally – though an unprecedented El Niño has made the predicament more challenging.

“This is a tropical mosquito, so the model has convinced me this won’t survive the winter,” Dr Medlock said. “Although we’ve got El Niño, [so] it’s very mild – it’s certainly warm enough still in East London [for the insects to survive].”

Diseases such as dengue and Zika virus do not typically circulate in Britain, but an infected traveller returning from a country where the diseases are present could carry the virus back with them.

If an invasive mosquito then bit an infected person, it could potentially catch and spread on the disease to others.

Several countries in Europe, including France, Italy and Spain, have started to see local transmission of mosquito-borne viruses, including dengue fever and West Nile virus, in recent years as the climate becomes more suitable for mosquitoes to survive and multiply.

Just last week, a third person died in Frankfurt, Germany, from malaria despite having no travel history, after mosquitoes infected with the disease were imported into the country on an aeroplane and subsequently infected eight people over the summer.

“We [already] see imported cases of malaria, dengue and chikungunya each year, with significant associated mortality and morbidity,” Dr Phillip Veal, a consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said.

“But if we [in Britain] follow the pattern of Europe, and all models suggest we will, Aedes albopictus and other Aedes species may become established. We’ve got a window of opportunity to do something, to prepare, to be ready, to fulfil our mission of protecting the public,” Dr Veal said.

News.title: Tax rises ‘virtually inevitable’ after £8bn borrowing blow
News.content:
Tax rises are “virtually inevitable” after official figures showed the Treasury has borrowed £8bn more than expected so far this year.

Economists said the Chancellor faced an “uncomfortable” Budget after the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said spending outstripped tax receipts by £18.3bn in August, £3.5bn more than expected.

It means John Healey, the Chancellor, has borrowed £77.3bn so far this financial year, which is £8.1bn more than forecast.

Reacting to the figures, Emma Reynolds, the Chief Secretary to the Treasury, warned of “tough decisions” in Mr Healey’s Budget.

Thomas Pugh, chief economist at RSM UK, said: “The jump in borrowing in August compared to last year sets the stage for what is likely to be a much trickier Budget than Andy Burnham or Healey anticipated when they came to power.

“Another round of tax rises in October now looks inevitable.”

Philip Shaw, an economist at Investec, added: “We suspect that some tax increases are virtually inevitable.”

Ruth Gregory, deputy chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the Chancellor would need to raise up to £14bn to restore the £24bn of fiscal headroom left by his predecessor Rachel Reeves to balance the books.

The Government’s debt interest bill soared to £8.8bn last month, according to the ONS, the biggest August figure since records began in 1997.

So far this year, the Treasury has spent £50bn on debt interest – £2bn more than forecast in March.

Nick Ridpath, an economist at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest spending is a worryingly large share of overall government spending.

“Both higher borrowing costs and higher inflation make life harder for a Chancellor who is looking to bring down borrowing and to spend more on government priorities.”

Higher prices caused by the Iran war mean the Chancellor must pay more interest on the country’s huge stock of inflation-linked debt.

Inflation is also pushing up the welfare bill. The Government spent almost £30bn in August on benefits, 7pc more than a year ago.

Despite this, the Treasury continued to see substantial tax receipts. Income tax, capital gains, and National Insurance receipts stood at £231bn in the financial year to August.

That is £16.6bn higher than the same period a year ago.

Inheritance tax receipts also grew. They have risen to £3.8bn so far this financial year, a £100m increase compared with a year ago.

Ms Reynolds, the Treasury minister, said: “At a time when debt interest costs billions of pounds that could otherwise be spent on improving lives, we must always know where the money is coming from to pay for public services.

“That is why we are committed to meeting our fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty.”

The figures also showed total debt rose to £2.985tn in August, taking the level just shy of £3tn.

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, said: “Labour has lost control of the public finances.

“It takes a rare fiscal incontinence to have both the highest tax take in history and see borrowing still shoot up.”

News.title: France releases infertile Asian tiger mosquitoes to fight dengue threat
News.content:
French cities are fighting the growing threat of diseases like dengue, chikungunya and Zika in mainland Europe by releasing millions of sterile male Asian tiger mosquitoes.

Terratis, a new company in the southern city of Montpellier, is breeding infertile males on an industrial scale as a long-term solution to the rapid spread of the disease-carrying insects.

The sterile males are bred at a factory in the southern city of Montpellier and then released in urban hot zones where the mosquitoes are most prevalent. After they have mated, females reproduce only empty eggs for the remainder of their lives.

“By using this technique, the mosquitoes will have no descendants and then, in theory, we can reduce the population with each generation,” said Clelia Oliva, the founder of Terratis.

“We are confident of being able to achieve a reduction of between 70 and 90 per cent in the towns in which we are releasing the sterile mosquitoes.”

The company, which started only two years ago, has experienced a dramatic surge in demand in the last few years as France tries to deal with the invasive species.
