Sports.title: Florian Wirtz does not look like a £116m player but it is early to write him off
Sports.content:
When Florian Wirtz signed for Liverpool in the summer of 2025, there was only one logical assumption. The Premier League champions at the time had recruited one of the hottest young talents in world football – a key player in the Bayer Leverkusen team that had won the double in 2023-24 and a star in the Germany team. An exciting and productive young attacking midfielder being added to the best team in England? How could this not work?

Football has a habit of flipping the script, though. Last season was difficult for Liverpool for several reasons, and Wirtz, along with other new arrivals, struggled to make the impact expected of a £116m player. There were conversations among fans this summer about how long he and fellow nine-figure signing Alexander Isak should be given before difficult questions needed be asked. The consensus was until Christmas.

As it turned out, the real answer was after the opening game as Wirtz and Isak laboured in Liverpool’s 2-2 draw at Newcastle and loud doubts began to surface. Jamie Carragher spoke on the first Monday Night Football of the season about Wirtz’s signing in 2025 potentially being part of the “worst transfer window in Premier League history”.

The former Liverpool defender was criticising a few players – and Isak has since gone on to score four times in his last four league appearances to quieten his doubters – but Carragher focused his ire on Wirtz again on Sunday in a new podcast for Sky Sports.

“The reason I worry is, I don’t think Wirtz is in poor form since he came to Liverpool. I think what we’re seeing is what he is,” he said. “The worry for Wirtz now is that what he’s given Liverpool is so low. Where we were expecting him was to take Liverpool to another league title, to take Liverpool to a Champions League. The gap he’s got to close to justify what people were expecting I almost think is too big. You can’t get there. Even if he improves a bit, it’s still not what Liverpool thought they were getting. Andoni Iraola’s got a decision to make here. Wirtz would not be in my Liverpool team.”

Carragher derided Wirtz – who has just one assist in six games this season – for his performance in the team’s 1-0 win at Bournemouth, calling it “one of the poorest I’ve ever seen him in a Liverpool shirt”. Iraola was more generous though and accepted that the German had struggled in the first half. “He started the game slowly,” Iraola said. “After that first phase, we improved. Florian has helped us also to improve. Second half he was playing much better, he was finding better spots to receive and turn. I’m much more happy with his second half.”

Wirtz’s numbers from the game were not that bad. He created three chances, the joint-most of any Liverpool player along with Cody Gakpo; he won six of his eight duels; and he won possession four times: only Alexis Mac Allister (seven), Ronald Araújo (six), and Jérémy Jacquet (six) won the ball more often for the visitors.

Perhaps we should not be saying this, being Opta and all, but data does not always tell the whole story. Anyone watching the game could see a player struggling to impose himself, with several passes not finding the target. Only 26 of Wirtz’s 37 attempted passes reached a teammate (70.3%). That is not unusual for a creative midfielder but there were too many simple balls sloppily overhit or played too close to Bournemouth defenders.

Wirtz received a lot of criticism for giving the ball away; he lost possession 15 times before leaving the pitch in the 71st minute. Only Araújo (24) and Gakpo (16) did so more often, though they both played the whole game. That said, “possession lost” is a tricky statistic to hang your hat on, as creative players who play risky passes in the busiest areas of the pitch often find themselves losing the ball the most.

He also made a near-post run in the second half that led to the ball dropping kindly for Isak to score the winner. It did not go down as an assist as it touched a defender on the way to Isak but, without Wirtz’s run, the goal would not have happened. He also showed some nice moments, even in the first half. He drifted through defenders before winning a free-kick on the edge of the Bournemouth penalty area early on, while a classy one-touch layoff to Isak could have been a nice assist if the striker hadn’t sent his shot high and wide.

Expectations were greater for Wirtz, though. He was meant to take games by the scruff of the neck and decide them with moments of brilliance like he did at Leverkusen. Suggestions that Wirtz maybe just isn’t good enough to be the player he was expected to be in the Premier League seem harsh, though. There was hype around his arrival for very good reason.

After joining Leverkusen from FC Köln at the age of 16, he recorded 18 goals and 21 assists in 69 games in his first two full seasons. Wirtz tore the anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee in March 2022, though, and missed 10 months of action.

He showed no ill effects on his return, playing a central role in one of the most incredible campaigns by a team in recent years. Leverkusen won their first Bundesliga title, becoming the first team to go unbeaten over a league season in the German top flight. They also won the DFB-Pokal, and reached the Europa League final, where a defeat to Atalanta was their only loss in any competition across the entire campaign.

Wirtz recorded 18 goals and 19 assists in 47 games that season; the only player from Europe’s top five leagues to record at least 16 goals and 16 assists in all competitions. He produced 16 goals and 14 assists in his final season before heading to England, with only Mohamed Salah (18) and Lamine Yamal (13) getting more than his 12 assists from open play among players from Europe’s top five leagues.

However, he recorded only seven goals and eight assists in 49 games in his first season at Liverpool, and it took until late December to register his first league goal as the champions struggled, ultimately limping home in fifth place and ending the campaign without a trophy. To be fair, it was a hard environment to come into. The death of Diogo Jota cast a dark cloud over the club and Arne Slot struggled to get his team playing anywhere near as coherently as they had the previous year.

Wirtz was far from terrible, though. He was by some considerable distance Liverpool’s most creative outlet in open play, which helped after the loss of Trent Alexander-Arnold. He created 95 chances from open play in all competitions, at least 27 more than any other Liverpool player. But there was no denying that it was a disappointing debut season for him.

The World Cup was a chance to show he could do it on the big stage and he managed three assists in four games for Germany before they were eliminated on penalties by Paraguay in the last 32. Only two players at the tournament had more assists at the end of that round, and only five players created more chances from open play than his nine. Despite that, he still bore the brunt of criticism from many in Germany for their underwhelming showing, such are the standards expected of him.

With a pre-season under Iraola, though, there was hope that a new system and a fresh start would help. You could argue he has played pretty well in at least two of his six appearances so far this season. Liverpool were not great in the 2-2 home draw with Nottingham Forest, but Wirtz was their main threat, denied what would have been a well-taken goal by an offside call against Jeremie Frimpong, and playing a neat pass into Víctor Muñoz for their second equaliser.

He was also impressive in the 2-1 home win over Atlético Madrid in the Champions League, and would have had another assist had Bradley Barcola not dragged his shot wide when sent through on goal by some sharp play by Wirtz.

While he struggled to make much of an impact in games against Newcastle, Ipswich Town and Fulham, those “what if” moments have been a theme. Wirtz was not great in the 2-0 win at Ipswich, but he did produce a fine turn and cross for Isak to score what would have been his hat-trick goal, only for the flag to deny him by the narrowest of margins.

Wirtz has at least been trying to make a difference in possession. He has made 19 progressive passes in the league this season (joint 16th), level with Martin Ødegaard and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall. He has also made 43 line-breaking passes at a rate of 9.6 per 90, almost double his 5.2 per 90 in the Premier League last season.

Another area where there has been an increase, numbers-wise, from Wirtz this season is off the ball. He has won possession in the opposition’s final third six times in the Premier League; only five players have done so more often, while only five have applied more pressures than him (419) and only six have received more pressures (260), showing that he is doing his work out of possession and is occupying defenders in possession. He ranked joint 12th, 21st and 27th in the Premier League for each metric, respectively, last season.

Wirtz has also covered the most distance of Liverpool players in three of his five Premier League games, but it is his lack of impact on the ball that seems to have most people taking aim. He has been underwhelming, but six appearances into a new season seems early to be making damning conclusions. Things have barely got going under Iraola, and Liverpool as a team are clearly still several rungs below their potential.

Wirtz is a 23-year-old trying to find his feet in the strongest league in the world, and while there is no denying that he’s far from his best, that doesn’t mean improvement is impossible, or even unlikely.

The eye-watering fee is undoubtedly a factor for the critics. Whether fair or not, players are judged against how much they cost. Paul Pogba was hardly a success story at Manchester United, but the criticism often felt over the top, mostly because of his £93m fee and the hype that followed his return to Old Trafford in 2016.

The big question is can Wirtz ever show more in England? Undeniably world-class players have failed to do so in the past, including another highly rated former Bayer Leverkusen midfielder in Michael Ballack, who never really found his best form in a Chelsea shirt after his move from Bayern Munich in 2006. Patience has been shown, and more is required for now. It still feels too soon for sweeping statements and loud conclusions.

This is an article by Opta Analyst

Sports.title: Chelsea have entered the realm of late-stage American sports capitalism | Leander Schaerlaeckens
Sports.content:
Here follows a list of the things accomplished at Chelsea Football Club during a time that historians may choose to grandly term the First Clearlake Era, or perhaps the Boehly Bungle.

Since the May 2022 purchase of the club from the sanctioned Russian oligarch Roman Abramovich, when Todd Boehly took over the club’s daily operations, Chelsea – Premier League champions as recently as 2017 and 2015, and Champions League winners in 2021 – have placed 12th, sixth, fourth and 10th in the league.

After the sacking of Thomas Tuchel, the incumbent upon the takeover, five permanent and four interim managers were installed. They employ five sporting directors.

About $2.37bn (£1.78bn) – with a B! – was spent on 60 new players, per Transfermarkt. The same source values Chelsea’s current first team at just $1.23bn (£920m). And when, to put it in Professional Business Guy speak, your entire trading strategy rests on buying young players you plan to profit from later, it doesn’t seem great when you’ve spent twice as much on your portfolio of assets as it is now worth.

Those signings included at least one of the Premier League’s all-time busts (Mykhailo Mudryk) and one of its worst contracts (Raheem Sterling).

Chelsea set a new Premier League record for the biggest pre-tax loss.

And, infamously, the club sold its women’s team to itself as part of some accounting shenanigans to stay on the right side of financial regulations.

And now let us go through the things that were not achieved:

A credible title challenge.



Qualifying for European competition in two of four seasons, which ought to be the rock-bottom minimum for a club of Chelsea’s means.



Building a new and larger stadium, even though one was mooted.

All the same, Boehly will walk away after four years as chair of Chelsea – although his influence had recently waned – with a profit in his bank account, or wherever it is that money men of his kind stash their cash. So too will his fellow American and minority stakeholder Mark Walter, after both men sold their 12.8% shares to Clearlake Capital last week.

Welcome to the final stage of the American ownership model, which has now enveloped most of the Premier League. At this stage, members of the billionaire class just pass stakes in teams around among themselves, always for at least a bit more than they paid. They are not stewards of their clubs and don’t see themselves as such. They feel no obvious alliance or allegiance to the fans, acting only as the current holders of the paperwork that confers financial control over a valuable asset.

As part of the Clearlake takeover group, Boehly and Walter each bought their stakes with the club at a $3.3bn (£2.5bn) valuation and have now sold at $6.7bn (£5bn), doubling its supposed value after four chaotic years. The exiting owners made a “modest profit”, per the Financial Times. That would probably be explained by the $2.3bn (£1.75bn) investment that Boehly, Walter and the other new owners committed to when they took over the club.

That they should get to exit with more money than they spent at all is instructive in a way that the exact figures involved here are not.

The dirty little secret of the way American sports functions at the highest levels is that the season-to-season balance sheet is sort of immaterial. So is being competitive (unless you care about fan sentiment). The ownership class makes its money by buying a club and then holding on to it; by possessing a ultra-scarce asset for a spell, until someone else is willing to pay more for it. They may move the furniture around in the name of optimization, but the house largely remains unaltered. If the team makes a bit of money – although nothing like the sort of profit that would justify its valuation – or breaks even, then that’s dandy. If it suffers losses, that’s probably fine, too, as they will be offset, and then some, in profit from the sale.

There is no correlation between price point and how well or poorly these teams have actually been run – all that matters is the premium someone else is willing to pay for an institution that has historically been as safe a bet as any. It is virtually impossible to lose money by parking it in a beloved sports team over the long term. All you have to do is not get relegated (if such a thing is even possible in your league). And so clubs, or chunks of them, are now picked up and dumped as easily as Normals like you and me might grab and ditch a stock in an online brokerage account. And with little more ceremony than an earnest press release.

That’s the game England’s many legacy clubs find themselves in now. The game the Glazer family kicked off when they bought Manchester United mostly with borrowed money in 2005 for $1.47bn (£800m at the time) and then, in 2023, sold Sir Jim Ratcliffe a quarter of the club for about $1.6bn (£1.3bn) in cash and infrastructure investment. Which is to say that the Glazers recouped more or less the entirety of the investment they made with the money of others – even though much of it still sits on the club’s books as debt – and retained three-quarters of one of the planet’s most valuable sporting brands.

This is the game Mark Walter mastered when he bought the Los Angeles Lakers for $10bn and flipped them on for $12.5bn just 14 months later, as he liquidates some of his vast sporting portfolio in the face of a federal investigation into fraud.

This summer, a consortium including Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought 30% of Liverpool for $2.2bn (£1.65bn) from Fenway Sports Group, which had acquired the club outright for $464m (then £300m) in 2010. That represents a 1,580% profit , in case you’re keeping score. In that light, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola really don’t sound all that expensive.

That’s how things have been done stateside for decades. It is now also how things are done in England. It doesn’t drive sporting excellence or foster deeper connections with the fans that bring the club its value in the first place. The clubs now exist to make rich people richer. There’s little anyone can do about it. It sucks.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: US Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Sports.title: Slip sliding away: football season-ticket holders fear falling down pecking order
Sports.content:
The document known as “the oldest football season ticket in the world” promises its bearer access to every Burnley home game of the 1884-85 season. It is a ticket that predates the Football League by four years, with all the fixtures played against east Lancashire neighbours. All the same, the legend on the ticket carries a stern warning: “This card is not transferable. Any member violating this rule will be at once expelled from the club.”

For Burnley 1884 read Manchester United 2026. While the oldest remaining season ticket is preserved safely at Turf Moor, at Old Trafford 685 season tickets were voided this summer after a club investigation found evidence of their having been resold on the secondary market. United said such practices “undermine fair access to tickets for genuine supporters and have no place at Manchester United”. United fan groups again protested against the actions of the club’s ownership, claiming: “The way you treat us is a disgrace.”

Nearly 150 years after fans started paying up front to watch their team, the season ticket remains a key component in the success of English football. It is also an enduring source of conflict between supporters and clubs, with tensions seemingly reaching new heights.

Arsenal, like United, have continued to act against the perceived misuse of tickets, suspending nearly 74,000 club accounts since they began a crackdown in 2024. This summer Chelsea became the latest club to insist on minimum levels of attendance to retain your ticket for the following season. Bournemouth moved 600 season-ticket holders to accommodate new hospitality seats and 14 out of the 20 top-flight sides raised their season-ticket prices.

Season-ticket holders have long felt undervalued. But there is a growing sense, especially among fans of the biggest clubs, that they are falling ever further down the pecking order as economic imperatives change. It is a feeling that intensified after a World Cup that seemed precision-tooled to extract as much money as possible from the most devoted fans. One Liverpool supporter crystallised common fears when he appeared on The Overlap at the start of the season arguing that a big club would soon try to get rid of season tickets altogether. The clip went viral.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal celebrate victory over Atlético Madrid with fans in May. The club have suspended 74,000 fan accounts under a crackdown launched in 2024. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

The Football Supporters’ Association argues that clubs’ present behaviour shows an antagonism towards season-ticket holders. “There’s a sense from supporter groups at the most successful teams that their club executives and owners don’t fully appreciate season ticket holders and would rather have stadiums full of one-off visitors,” an FSA spokesperson said.

“Those who only measure things by the bottom line see season-ticket holders as a group whose matchday spend is lower than the once-a-year fan who will fill their bag at the club shop and pay a bigger premium for their ticket. It’s a shortsighted vision.”

The claim that clubs want to swap longstanding supporters for one-off tourists is at the heart of many fans’ fears over season tickets and, to a certain extent, it bears out. Dominik Schreyer, a professor of sports economics at the WHU Otto Beisheim School of Management in Düsseldorf, says season tickets “come at a cost” for clubs.

“In the Premier League, demand is way higher than seat supply,” Schreyer says. “But season-ticket holders get discounted seats, right? They are also more likely to be no-shows. When they do come they spend less on food, less on merchandise and they come later to the stadium. They also don’t churn, because these tickets are so scarce that nobody in their right mind would give them away. Every year the average age grows by one because there is no one new getting tickets. So for the clubs, there are a lot of economic problems from their season-ticket holders.”

That, however, is only one side of the ledger. “What we should not forget is that, in the end, season‑ticket holders are part of a product that, in the case of the Premier League, is marketed to a global audience,” Schreyer says.

View image in fullscreen Manchester United fans protest against the banning of season-ticket holders, which has worsened an already fractious relationship between club and supporters. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

“They are creating an atmosphere. Season-ticket holders are also used to all the rules and the rituals and the songs, the moments that make this experience very special. So tourists want to come because they want to experience it. If you were to get rid of all the season-ticket holders, you would have all the operational and coordination costs of doing it and the product would not be the same any more.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There are other reasons why season tickets work for clubs, not least because they generate a largely predictable amount of revenue that turns up at the same time each year (at the very end of the season where it can be usefully deployed to help with transfer spending limits).

For most clubs, it would not be feasible to replace season‑ticket holders with one-off fans even if they wanted to. But with the average number of season tickets at any given Premier League fixture running at 75% of all tickets, is there a case that this number should not be set in stone? Could access to matches be broadened without killing off a part of what made them great?

“In theory, you could give all the seats to season-ticket holders and still have a lot of tickets for new fans if you manage it effectively,” Schreyer says. “You just need to change the mechanism in order to get the ticket that is unused on to the secondary market.”

View image in fullscreen A packed Anfield. Bigger clubs have been accused of prioritising tourists over season-ticket holders, who generate the atmosphere that enhances the attraction. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

This is what is happening at a number of clubs, with fans being asked to return their tickets for resale if they are not being used. But these requests have often come with warnings that tickets could be removed should fans not comply. Ultimately some of the tension around season tickets is simply because clubs are not talking clearly or frequently enough with fans. “Clubs don’t communicate that well,” Schreyer says. “I don’t understand why they don’t get fans on board better. You can make things so transparent.”

It is instructive looking across the Premier League at the season‑ticket policies of each club, the way they were announced and the response they received from supporters. Brentford raised prices for the first time in five years, but faced minimal pushback. Brighton’s 3% rise was backed by the fan advisory board. Chelsea and Tottenham froze prices but still found themselves at odds with their fanbase.

The season ticket is a device as old as the game itself but has grown to become a symbol of the connection between fanbases and clubs. Disputes over the importance of season tickets may prove to be a harbinger of their demise, but may equally be better understood as a sign of the dysfunction at the top of our biggest clubs.

Sports.title: Ten of the best-value deals from this summer’s transfer window
Sports.content:
1 Rodrigo Mora: Porto to Roma (£21.4m)

Even in this era of relentless transfer inflation, a fee of more than £20m does not usually represent a bargain. Roma’s move for the Porto playmaker Mora may be an exception, though. Now 19, he has been on the radar of Europe’s elite teams since starring for Porto’s B-team at 15, and Porto were braced for his €70m (£59.5m) release clause to be met in the summer of 2025. That didn’t happen and Mora then fell out of favour under the new head coach, Francesco Farioli. Roma swooped with an offer of €25m (£21.4m), plus a 50% sell-on fee which can be bought out. The potential move also intrigued Mora, who was eager to play under Gian Piero Gasperini. “He played a big part in my decision to come here because he likes players with my qualities, and I’m a fan of the way he wants his teams to play,” Mora said. The early signs are positive, with Mora netting his first Roma goal against Lecce as the Giallorossi made a flying start in Serie A.

2 Elliot Stroud: Mjällby to Hull (£3.5m)

Getting promoted to the Premier League is an expensive business. This summer, Ipswich, Coventry and Hull collectively spent £450m net on players. Amid such frantic investment, Hull’s move for the 24-year-old Sweden international Stroud looks like excellent business. The wide player was a standout for Mjällby as the small-town team won the Swedish title last year, earning a place in Graham Potter’s World Cup squad. Sergej Jakirovic identified him as a key squad addition after Hull’s playoff final success. “He’s a very good player; he’s very versatile,” the Hull manager said. “He can play full-back, wing-back, left-winger, and in the middle. He’s a runner too, so I think he will suit us very well.” The 24-year-old has been a pacy creative outlet for Jakirovic’s hard-working unit.

3 Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang: Marseille to Deportivo (£1.3m)

On the face it of, paying a nominal fee to sign a striker of Aubameyang’s class and experience is a no-brainer. Still, the former Arsenal and Dortmund player is 37 and has endured a nomadic career since leaving Barcelona. An unsuccessful stint with Chelsea has been followed by two seasons with Marseille, sandwiching a year in Saudi Arabia. Aubameyang’s goal return has still been impressive, with 44 across the last three campaigns, and he has reportedly accepted a greatly reduced salary to play regular La Liga football. Dépor’s ambitious project looks the perfect fit, with Aubameyang scoring five goals in seven league games.

View image in fullscreen Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has five goals in seven league games for Deportivo. Photograph: Miguel Riopa/AFP/Getty Images

4 Satoshi Tanaka: Fortuna Düsseldorf to Schalke (£900,000)

The Bundesliga’s trio of promoted clubs, in sharp contrast to their English counterparts, spent a combined £7.2m net on signings. The second-tier champions, Schalke, secured some notable names on loan (including boyhood fan Robin Gosens) but the holding midfielder Tanaka was their most expensive permanent recruit, at €1m. The 24-year-old still represents something of a gamble, his only previous experience of German football coming since January with Fortuna, who were relegated to the third tier. Tanaka still caught the eye of Schalke’s director of football, Youri Mulder, who said: “His work rate and intensity fit our game really well.” On his Bundesliga debut, Tanaka’s battling qualities helped his team hold Bayern Munich to a goalless draw, and he could be key to whether Schalke stay clear of trouble.

5 Nico Elvedi: Mönchengladbach to Leeds (£6.8m)

Leeds have a clear recruitment model: sign reliable, experienced players with strong physical attributes, preferably from the Bundesliga. The Swiss centre-back Elvedi fits that mould perfectly. Daniel Farke might have anticipated an adjustment period for a player who had spent 11 years at Borussia Mönchengladbach. Instead, Elvedi has settled quickly alongside his fellow newcomer Tarik Muharemovic, mostly playing on the left of Farke’s back three. It’s a welcome reunion for the 29-year-old with his former Gladbach coach. “It was just one year but I loved him as a manager,” Elvedi has said of Farke. “I learned a lot from him and I will learn a lot now.” He is learning fast already.

Quick Guide How last year's picks have fared Show Robin Roefs (NEC to Sunderland, £9.1m; pictured) The Dutch keeper’s commanding presence was key as Sunderland secured European football. Kept 10 clean sheets in 35 league games, with only three teams conceding fewer goals than the promoted Black Cats. Ferran Jutglà (Club Brugge to Celta, £4.7m) Made a solid start at Celta with nine La Liga goals, but struggled to make an impact in Europe. Hit a purple patch in March and is now playing more regularly as a No 9 rather than out wide. Ernest Poku (AZ to Leverkusen, £8.7m) Featured regularly in his first season at Leverkusen, but was allowed to join Besiktas on a loan-to-buy deal this summer. The winger has made a slow start in Turkey but scored in their Europa League win over Marseille. Adrian Truffert (Rennes to Bournemouth, £11.4m) The left-back settled quickly in Bournemouth’s rebuilt defence, helping his side qualify for Europe. Called up by Zinedine Zidane for the Nations League and could win his second France cap, four years after making his debut. Santiago Hidalgo (Independiente to Toulouse, £2.5m) Enjoyed a promising first season in France with nine goal involvements in Ligue 1. May need to find another goalscoring gear this term with Toulouse struggling early on. Borna Sosa (Ajax to Crystal Palace, £3m) Played in 18 games for Palace last season but managed just 99 minutes in the Premier League as he struggled for consistency. Now on loan at Cologne, and looks unlikely to have a future at Selhurst Park. Berke Ozer (Eyupspor to Lille, £3.9m) Kept a league-best 13 clean sheets in his first season, helping Lille finish third. Ozer has retained the No 1 spot despite the arrival of Paraguay World Cup hero Orlando Gill, and was voted fans’ player of the month in August. Christian Ordoñéz (Vélez Sarsfield to Parma, £6.7m) One of six Argentinian players in the current Parma squad, Ordonez has admitted to being “surprised” at the step up in quality, but has featured regularly in a solid first season in Serie A. Carlos Soler (PSG to Real Sociedad, £6.9m) Midfielder has enjoyed a much more pivotal role at Real Sociedad, scoring in the Copa del Rey final shootout victory over Atletico to help deliver a trophy. Nikola Stulic (Charleroi to Lecce, £4.3m) Signed to replace namesake Nikola Krstovic at Lecce, the centre-forward had a middling first season, scoring four of his side’s 28 league goals. • Read last year's list here Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

6 Gabriel Vidovic: Dinamo Zagreb to Paderborn (£2.6m)

Paderborn have returned to the Bundesliga with a bang after shocking Wolfsburg in the promotion/relegation playoff, smashing their transfer record (which, admittedly, was only £700,000) to sign Vidovic and the striker Marvin Pieringer for €3m each. Vidovic is a former Bayern Munich academy talent and his return to Germany’s top flight is an intriguing prospect. He was brought through at Bayern by Julian Nagelsmann but the Croatian playmaker could not become a regular there. A successful loan in Zagreb led to another chance to impress with Mainz but Vidovic barely featured and Bayern cut the loan short. After moving back to Dinamo permanently, the Bundesliga looked a distant prospect until Paderborn pounced. “His sporting CV speaks for itself,” their sporting director, Sebastian Lange, said. The 22-year-old’s arrival is a risk for a club with limited means, but the potential ceiling spotted by Nagelsmann makes it one worth taking.

View image in fullscreen Gabriel Vidovic came through at Bayern Munich under Julian Nagelsmann. Photograph: Leon Kuegeler/AFP/Getty Images

7 Giovanni Reyna: Mönchengladbach to Strasbourg (£2.6m)

As the self-styled “league of talents”, Ligue 1 functions as a development pool for young players who are sold on for hefty fees. Strasbourg, a “partner club” to Chelsea, are closely tied to this model: four of their summer signings were drawn from the vast stock of spare players at Cobham, while Valentín Barco and Emmanuel Emegha went in the other direction. Reyna, despite being 23, feels like a different prospect. He was once a heavily hyped youngster who thrived with Jude Bellingham and Erling Haaland at Dortmund, but injuries and inconsistency have stalled his career. Reyna made only four league starts in his solitary season at Gladbach but has begun promisingly in France. He scored his first Strasbourg goal in the 6-2 rout of Troyes in early September; if he can stay fit and capitalise on this new start, it may not be long before he is linked with a move across the Channel.

8 Flávio Nazinho: Cercle Brugge to Monaco (£4.3m)

An attacking left-back once touted as the next Nuno Mendes, Nazinho was called up to Sporting’s first team by Ruben Amorim but made only 11 appearances before drifting back into the reserves. An initial loan to Cercle Brugge in 2023 became permanent for €2m the following summer, and regular game time began to breed results. After recording four goals and eight assists last season, Nazinho was snapped up by Cercle’s partner club, Monaco. He has made an immediate impact, striking up a left-flank partnership with Stanis Idumbo as Filipe Luís’s side sit top of Ligue 1. Their Conference League campaign will offer Nazinho further chances to trust his attacking instincts, and potentially earn a first Portugal call-up.

View image in fullscreen Flávio Nazinho, battling here with Achraf Hakimi of PSG, joined Monaco from one of their partner clubs. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

9 Fran García: Real Madrid to Real Betis (£3.2m)

Real Betis stole a march on several Premier League clubs with a move for the prolific forward Troy Parrott, who quickly showed his worth with a winner against Real Madrid. The Ireland international cost Betis €20m, though, and the fee would doubtless have been higher if Parrott were heading back to Spurs, rather than to Seville. García, a left-back, may be this summer’s real steal, sold for £3.2m plus 50% of any future sale as Madrid cleared out fringe players. At 27, he is approaching his prime and has plenty of big-match experience, featuring more than 100 times for Madrid and playing two full top-flight campaigns on loan at Rayo Vallecano. García was, perhaps unsurprisingly, linked with Fulham this summer; Álvaro Arbeloa may come to regret allowing Betis to swoop.

View image in fullscreen Fran García faced Real Madrid this season after playing for the club more than 100 times. Photograph: Diego Souto/Getty Images

10 Ainsley Maitland-Niles: Lyon to Everton (£4.3m)

Everton experienced a traumatic transfer deadline day that left David Moyes with one senior striker and a squad desperately short of depth. They did at least wrap up a late deal for Maitland-Niles, a versatile addition at a decent price. The former Arsenal full-back’s arrival may not have soothed fans’ frustrations, but his late equaliser against Manchester United may already have repaid a decent chunk of his fee.

Sports.title: Ireland manager gets prime minister Martin’s backing in row with Israel over ‘genocide’
Sports.content:
Ireland’s prime minister, Micheál Martin, backed his country’s football manager, Heimir Hallgrímsson, after Israel’s football federation accused Hallgrimsson of “stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy” over comments about the war in Gaza.

“I think those are unacceptable remarks; they should be withdrawn,” Martin told reporters in New York, where he is attending the UN general assembly. “Israel can’t keep denying what the world knows, and what the world understands.”

Hallgrímsson sparked the row after saying before two Nations League fixtures against Israel: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide. We’re playing against Israel, we’re not playing with Israel.”

Quick Guide How do I 

Martin said Hallgrímsson’s comments reflected concerns about the scale of death and destruction in Gaza, also citing remarks by the UN secretary general, António Guterres.

On Wednesday Hallgrímsson, preparing for Thursday’s game in Kosovo, expressed gratitude for Martin’s backing. “What I said at the last press meeting has taken the attention away from maybe what’s most important; we are playing an important game against Kosovo,” Hallgrimsson said.

“Maybe, from a ‌leadership point of view, not clever for me to take the attention like this. But to answer the question, we are thankful for all the support we get. It’s a tricky time for ​us.“

The dispute comes amid mounting controversy in the Republic over the fixtures, scheduled for 27 September and 4 October. More than 160 Irish sportspeople have signed an open letter calling on the national team to boycott the matches, and protesters gathered outside the team’s Dublin hotel on Monday. Further protests are planned around the country in the run-up to the games.

The Football Association of Ireland (FAI) passed a motion last November requesting that European football governing body, Uefa, suspend Israel from international competition. The FAI has said it has little choice but to fulfil the fixtures or risk sporting and financial sanctions.

Ireland’s designated home match on 4 October was moved from Dublin’s Aviva Stadium to Backa Topola, Serbia, after concerns over disruption and security. The 27 September match, officially Israel’s home fixture, will also be played at a neutral venue, in Debrecen, Hungary.

Israel strongly rejects allegations that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide. Hamas led the deadliest attack against Israel on 7 October 2023 when militants killed 1,221 people and dragged into Gaza 251 hostages, 44 of them already dead, according to Israeli official figures.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Sport in Focus Our picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown in Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Israel launched a massive retaliatory offensive that has displaced virtually the entire population at least once and has killed 73,919 people, according to the Gaza health ministry, which operates under Hamas and whose figures are generally considered reliable.

Ireland has long been a strong supporter of the Palestinian cause, with sympathy for Palestinians often linked to the country’s history of British rule. Dublin formally recognised a Palestinian state in 2024 alongside Spain and Norway and has repeatedly criticised Israel’s conduct of the war in Gaza.

Reuters contributed to this report

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo says he’s happy to sit on the bench as he makes retirement admission
Sports.content:
Cristiano Ronaldo says he’s happy to sit on the bench as he makes retirement admission

Cristiano Ronaldo has admitted that he considered stepping away from international football after the World Cup.

The Portuguese superstar endured yet more World Cup heartbreak in the summer as his nation were dumped out by Spain.

3 The World Cup has remained out of reach for Ronaldo Credit: Getty

Ronaldo led the line throughout, but they were no match for eventual champions La Roja, who saw them off in the round of 16.

Mikel Merino scored the only goal of the game, and Roberto Martinez departed.

Martinez had already announced that he wouldn't be staying on as manager of the Portuguese national team, but it was another failure for Ronaldo and co.

But new gaffer Jorge Jesus has called up the 41-year-old for this extended international break.

Portugal are in action four times over the three weeks, starting off against Wales in the Nations League.

And ahead of that contest at the Estadio Jose Alvalade, Ronaldo was asked if he'd considered calling it a day.

His response was very honest as he said: "Yes. I considered stepping away. I am always thinking about my future. I'm a thinker. This is why you see me here.

"I had a conversation with our president and our coach. I believe I can still help the national team reach to where they want. Also outside of football. This is a new generation, a young generation."

He added: "The critics will always be there... the most important thing is I know who I am. I know why the young kids especially love Ronaldo.

"I will continue to do that. I will continue to do that when I retire in ten years... I'm a happy person".

3 Ronaldo's legacy with the national team won't ever be surpassed but some feel he should call it a day

He also made it clear that he'll do whatever Jesus requires of him, even if it means he's not on the pitch.

Ronaldo said: “Whatever the coach needs from me with the national team, whether that means playing, coming off, coming on, coming off again, or even not playing at all... I am available.

"The pride I feel in representing Portugal is greater than that of any other international player”.

And for Ronaldo, there are two things left he'd like to achieve; winning the Nations League and reaching 1000 career goals.

On that, he said: “The missions now are two: winning the Nations League and reaching 1000 career goals”.

Continuation of an era

As it stands, the Al Nassr striker has appeared an incredible 233 times for Portugal and has scored 146 goals.

3 Ronaldo grabbed three goals at the World Cup to extend his record of scoring in every one Credit: Getty

This makes him the highest goalscorer at national level in men's professional football.

In terms of honours, he has the European Championship and Nations League to his name.

But the World Cup has more than likely evaded him, given he'll be 45 by the time the next one rolls around.

He has scored 11 times across the six World Cups that he's played in.

But Ronaldo refuses to deny that he could go on and on, saying: “Will this be my final chapter? Maybe, I don’t know. This could be my final season. But I don’t know.

“If my body allows me to, and if my mind does too, and if I’m still in good shape, then I don’t know. I don’t know what will happen”.

The race to 1,000 goals

That 1,000 career goal mark is getting closer and closer for Ronaldo.

The forward is on 979 career goals for club and country, and he has three for Ange Postecoglou's Al Nassr this season so far.

But if you look at his previous scoring rate in Saudi Arabia, Ronaldo has scored over 30 in each of his years there.

So, if he sticks to that rate, the 1,000 goals target will fall at some point this season.

And he can get there a bit quicker with a solid opening to the Nations League.

Portugal take on Wales, Norway on two occasions as well as Denmark with their first match against Wales on Thursday night, kick-off 7:45pm.

Sports.title: Idrissa Gana Gueye invests in top flight club with ex-Liverpool star in surprise announcement
Sports.content:
Idrissa Gana Gueye invests in top flight club with ex-Liverpool star in surprise announcement

Former Premier League midfielders Idrissa Gana Gueye and Lucas Leiva have become the latest athletes to invest in Le Mans FC.

It follows the club's return to the French top-flight earlier this year following a 17-year thanks to two successive promotions.



3 Former Everton and Aston Villa star Gueye has invested in Le Mans FC alongside ex-Liverpool man Lucas Credit: Getty

Le Mans had dropped as low as the sixth-tier after they were liquidated in 2013.

However, they now find themselves rubbing shoulders with the likes of Paris Saint-Germain and Marseille once again.

Gueye and Lucas invest in Le Mans FC

There are also notable names within the club's group of investors, who have now been joined by Gueye and Lucas.



Real Madrid goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic are already shareholders.

Meanwhile, former Formula 1 drivers Felipe Massa and Kevin Magnussen have both invested.



Brazilian businessman Georgios Frangulis, who is engaged to world No.2 tennis ace Aryna Sabalenka, is also an investor.

Ex-Everton and Aston Villa man Gueye has now joined the club to help strengthen Le Mans' ties with African football.



The 36-year-old is Senegal's all-time leading appearance maker with 135 caps to his name.

Having left the Toffees in the summer, Gueye joined Saudi Pro League side Al Diriyah last month.

3 Le Mans were promoted to Ligue 1 after a 17-year absence last season Credit: AFP

Gueye and Lucas statements

In a statement, Gueye explained: "I am proud to join the Le Mans FC project as an investor.



"The club has a strong identity, genuine ambition, and a clear commitment to talent development.

"I look forward to putting my experience in French, English, international, and African football to work for the project and helping to strengthen its ties with Senegal and West Africa, particularly through the For Hope Campus."

Meanwhile, Lucas will work within player recruitment and development at the Stade Marie-Marvingt.

The Brazilian added: "I am very proud to join Le Mans FC alongside OutField and to be part of this new chapter for the club.



"Football has shaped my life and given me the opportunity to experience the sport at the highest level. Today, I want to put everything I've learned throughout my career to use in ambitious projects with a clear vision for the future.

"I deeply believe in what Le Mans FC is building. There is a history, an identity and real potential here, but above all, a shared ambition to build something sustainable and successful in the long term.

3 Leiva is set to work within recruitment and player development at Le Mans Credit: Getty

"For me, becoming a partner in this project means believing in its vision, contributing to its future, and helping Le Mans FC take the next steps in its history."



Lucas had spells with Brazilian club Gremio, Liverpool and Lazio before retiring in 2023.

The 39-year-old also won 24 senior caps for Brazil during his playing career.

Le Mans are currently ninth in Ligue 1 after claiming their first win of the season against Lorient on Saturday.

Patrick Videira's side face PSG at the Parc des Princes on October 10 in their first game after the international break.

Sports.title: Arsenal teenager joins Premier League rival just a year after poaching him from EFL club
Sports.content:
Arsenal teenager joins Premier League rival just a year after poaching him from EFL club

Academy star Mishel Nduka has left Arsenal after just one year to join Manchester City.

The 16-year-old joined the Gunners in the summer of 2025 on a scholarship deal from Championship club Charlton Athletic.



2 Nduka is a very highly rated teenage star Credit: Getty

The midfielder had the option to stay in north London with the offer of a deal from Arsenal.

But he turned it down to accept a scholarship contract from Man City instead.

Nduka is seen as a hot prospect for the future and has represented England at youth level and is currently away with their under-17 squad.



Arsenal offered a competitive salary to Nduka, but he has picked the Etihad over the Emirates. He will sign a professional deal with City once he turns 17 in April.

Nduka impressed enough to play for the Under-18s plenty of times last year and made the step up to Premier League 2.



He is expected to mainly play for Man City's Under-18s having come off the bench at the weekend for his new club.

The Citizens won 6-0 and have made a fantastic start to the season, sitting top of the table with a maximum 18 points from their first six matches.



Another starlet slips past Arsenal

Nduka is another talented player who has picked Man City over Arsenal this year.

The most obvious example is Jeremy Monga, who left Leicester City to join City over Arsenal.

The talented forward had looked set to join the Gunners in the summer with the two clubs agreeing a fee for the winger.

2 Monga has headed out to join Swansea City for some valuable first-team football Credit: Manchester City



But Arsenal felt it was too high, and they wanted to re-negotiate.

That allowed City to swoop in for Monga, and they agreed to pay the League One side an initial £10million with an additional £2.5m in add-ons.

That made Monga the most expensive 16-year-old in Premier League history.

And in the end, Monga decided that the pathway at City to the first team was clearer.

Speaking after his Man City debut during pre-season, he said: "It [Arsenal interest] was very strong because it was very close to me going there, very close.



"The main decision was probably the pathway and the club itself. They've been so successful that it was a no-brainer when City call. It's every child's dream to win trophies and be at the top with the best.

"Once I get the opportunity I just need to show myself, and once I do that, everything will take care of itself. I feel like, to me personally, I see myself at City more. I see myself in blue."

Sports.title: Jim White corrects Arsenal fans who made Fabian Hurzeler clip go viral
Sports.content:
Jim White has made it clear that Fabian Hurzeler didn't just go into the talkSPORT studio because Brighton beat Arsenal.

The German joined White and Simon Jordan on Tuesday morning and reflected on Brighton's start to the season and their 3-0 win over the Gunners.



3 Brighton have claimed some massive scalps since the German arrived at the Amex Credit: Getty

The Seagulls ended Arsenal's 100 per cent start to their Premier League title defence in emphatic fashion.

However, due to the proximity to the win over Arsenal, many Gunners fans accused Hurzeler of embarking on a media tour.

But that has been dismissed by White.

Speaking on White and Jordan, he said: "I noticed that a clip of Fabian talking about how Brighton went about in attempting to beat Arsenal...



"And they were successful in doing so, winning 3-0, and I noticed there was a pile-on from Arsenal fans saying that Hurzeler was on tour, suggesting he was doing a media tour because they had beaten Arsenal.

"But just for all of you out there who did jump on that, you totally wasted your time posting these comments because the interview yesterday was organised way before that match was played at the weekend.



"So, he was always coming in during this international break, so if Arsenal had won at the weekend, Fabian Hurzeler would have still been sat in that seat."

Jordan added: "The timing happened to work out as a very apt time for us."



3 Brighton are unbeaten in all competitions this season Credit: Getty

How did Brighton beat Arsenal?

The champions arrived at the Amex expecting a hard game, but it proved to be way beyond that.

Pascal Gross opened the scoring with a drilled right-footed effort from the edge of the area.

That lead was doubled just before half time as Charalampos Kostoulas was given time to pick his spot from distance.



And in the second half, Chema Andres headed home from a corner.

In the interview with talkSPORT, Hurzeler made it clear how they got the win.

He said: "We focused on us, really. We wanted to win the small battles first, what I mean is win the first header, win the first tackle, win the first throw-in, win the first corner.

"It sounds a little bit old school but it really was our approach because when you win these small battles, then you grow into the game.

"Then you can maybe create a bigger chance, then you can create a bigger win of scoring a goal. But first of all, it's getting into this game, having this commitment to our style of play, to our principles, and then winning the small battles.



"When you win the small battles, the players gain confidence, the players create self-belief, the players really trust each other. We grew into this game, and we also had the right moments on our side."

3 Brighton turned in one of the most complete performances of the season Credit: Getty

Good but not perfect

As much as Hurlezer was happy with his side's win and performance, he wants more.

"Our philosophy is we want to play intense football, having a good balance between defensive ability and controlling the game in possession.



"Therefore, if you want to control the game in possession, you need to have this intensity to win the ball back as quickly as possible.

"You need players who have this commitment to our pressing and I think that was definitely key - they played, we scored, and that was our commitment from the first second.

"Was it a perfect game? I'm a perfectionist, I wouldn't say it was a perfect game.

"There's still things to improve. But, overall, our challenge now will be to make these kind of exceptional performances normal. This is the challenge we have now.



"We have this phrase, 'We want to challenge the establishment'. Challenging the establishment doesn't mean to challenge them in one-to-one games, you have to challenge them when you're not playing against them.

"So, we have to be consistent in performances and these kind of performances, they have to get normal for us and that, I think, is the biggest challenge we can set ourselves."

Sports.title: Christian Eriksen has contract torn up three months after collapsing on pitch
Sports.content:
Christian Eriksen has contract torn up three months after collapsing on pitch

Wolfsburg have terminated Christian Eriksen's contract by mutual consent, the club have announced.

The decision comes three months after the midfielder collapsed on the pitch while playing for Denmark.

3 Wolfsburg have terminated Eriksen's contract by mutual consent Credit: Getty

Eriksen later reassured fans after their friendly against Ukraine was abandoned in June.

The 34-year-old has not played since, with Wolfsburg already six matches into the new 2. Bundesliga season.

They have now announced Eriksen has left the club in order to be closer to his family in Denmark.

Eriksen statement

In a statement, Eriksen said: "Right now, it’s important for me to be close to my family in Denmark.

"I’m happy that we were able to find a solution together. My time in Wolfsburg was marked by many highs and lows.

"I know that the club is now in good hands to make the journey back to the Bundesliga, and I’m convinced that VfL has a successful future ahead of it.

"I would like to sincerely thank everyone who supported me at VfL and in Wolfsburg.

"It was a great pleasure to play for you, and I will fondly remember this time."

Eriksen joined Wolfsburg in September 2025 on an initial two-year deal following his release by Manchester United.

He went on to make 34 appearances for the club last season, scoring three goals and providing 10 assists.

3 Eriksen joined Wolfsburg on a two-year deal in September 2025 Credit: Getty

However, he was unable to help the club avoid relegation from the Bundesliga.

Wolfsburg dropped out of the top-flight after an aggregate defeat to Paderborn in the play-off, ending their 29-year stay in the division.

Will Eriksen retire?

Despite leaving the club, Eriksen has not retired from professional football.

Following his collapse in June, Wolfsburg had revealed he was on a pathway to return to the pitch.

The incident marked the second time Eriksen had collapsed whilst playing for Denmark.

He suffered a cardiac arrest during their match against Finland at Euro 2020 five years ago.

3 Eriksen collapsed on the pitch whilst playing for Denmark against Ukraine in June Credit: Getty

Eriksen was subsequently fitted with an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) before returning to football with Brentford in January 2022.

The ICD's intervention was what caused him to regain consciousness after his collapse earlier this year.

After receiving medical treatment, Eriksen was able to walk off the pitch.

He has since been completing a rehabilitation programme in his native Denmark.

Sports.title: Man United saved millions after Ruben Amorim was hired by AC Milan – as cost of sacking revealed
Sports.content:
Man United saved millions after Ruben Amorim was hired by AC Milan – as cost of sacking revealed

Ruben Amorim's appointment as AC Milan boss saved Manchester United £8.5million in severance pay.

The Red Devils had looked set to lose £16.7million as a result of sacking the Portuguese in their third-quarter financial results in May.



3 United saved millions after Amorim was appointed Milan manager in June Credit: Getty

Amorim was dismissed in January following 14 months in charge at Old Trafford.

United were due to pay him and his staff until the conclusion of his contract in June 2027.

Amorim appointment saves United millions

However, Amorim was subsequently appointed by Milan in the summer.

The release of United's end of year financial results on Wednesday have now revealed how much the club saved as a result.



In total, £8.2million was paid out in 'exceptional items', largely consisting of payments to Amorim and his backroom team.

Corporate restructuring fees were also included in this figure.

Overall, United saved £8.5million from their previous forecast due to Amorim's return to the dugout.



Clubs generally do not pay out a manager's full remaining salary in one lump sum when they are sacked.

Instead, they will continue to receive their weekly wage until their contract expires or they land a new job.



In Amorim's case, his United deal would not have run out until the end of the current campaign.

3 United had been set to lost £16.7million after sacking Amorim in January Credit: Getty

The Red Devils were able to avoid a repeat of the previous debacle involving Erik ten Hag thanks to Milan's appointment.

Ten Hag was dismissed in October 2024, just three months after the club triggered a one-year extension in his contract through to 2026.



The Dutchman then did not land a new managerial role until the following summer when he took over as Bayer Leverkusen boss.

Amorim at Milan

Having left United at the start of the year, Amorim has enjoyed a strong start at the San Siro.

His side are currently unbeaten after five matches in Serie A, winning three of those.

Their 3-0 home win over Lecce on Sunday leaves Milan fifth in the table ahead of their return following the international break.



3 Amorim is yet to lose a match in Serie A since taking charge of Milan this summer Credit: Getty

However, they did suffer a setback in their opening Europa League fixture last week.

Milan were beaten 2-0 at home by Benfica as they failed to kickstart their league phase campaign.

Sports.title: Jurgen Klopp told one way he can fix major Liverpool issue 28 months after leaving
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp told one way he can fix major Liverpool issue 28 months after leaving

Florian Wirtz has been told how important it is to have Jurgen Klopp as his Germany manager, with the scrutiny surrounding his club form.

The 23-year-old is without a goal and has laid on just one assist in five matches for Liverpool in all competitions for Liverpool this season.



4 Iraola has dismissed £116million man Wirtz’s lack of goals and assists Credit: Getty

New Reds head coach Andoni Iraola has already come out in defence of his No.7 by claiming that he is not 'too focused on numbers'.

However, the reality is that Liverpool fans expected much more since Wirtz made his £116million switch to Liverpool in the summer of 2025.

The German was one of only two players, alongside Mohamed Salah, to both score and assist 10 or more goals in each category in Europe’s big five leagues across the last two seasons (prior to arriving at Anfield).



His run came to an end during his first year in the Premier League, in which he managed nine combined goal contributions in 33 games.

Wirtz, who has at least covered more distance than any Liverpool player in the last four matches, is yet to translate his work off the ball into game-state-altering moments on it.



Jason Cundy not convinced by Florian Wirtz

“Wirtz has been here now, right, this is his second season,” Cundy said on talkSPORT's GameDay Phone-In.

“I am not convinced that Wirtz is going to be a success. I think I might have seen enough of Wirtz.”



Klopp calls out Carragher's criticism of Wirtz

Cundy's sentiments echo those made by Liverpool legend Jamie Carragher, who claimed he doesn't see where Wirtz fits into the team.

Klopp said in response: "From a footballing point of view, he is beyond any doubt, for me and for everyone else too.

"But Jamie Carragher, Gary Neville and so on are, of course, always the first ones to get nervous in England."

4 Iraola has said he is very happy with the contribution Wirtz has made to his new-look attack Credit: Getty



It is far from the first time Klopp has hit back at criticism of his compatriot, having previously called him 'a once-in-a-century talent'.

The 59-year-old will now have the chance to run the rule over Wirtz himself, having been appointed Germany's new manager - his first return to the touchline since leaving Liverpool 28 months ago.

Klopp 'really important' to Wirtz

Speaking about the potential impact Klopp's arrival could have on Wirtz's form, European football expert Andy Brassell told talkSPORT.com: "It's really important to him.

"I think it's really important to Germany at the moment as well, because of course there's an element of doubt over Jamal Musiala.



"He's found it hard to come back from that big injury. He's had these neurological issues in recent weeks slash months as well.

"So whether he'll be well enough to be called up for international duty is a big question. So for that reason, I mean, when you go back to the 2024 Euros, Germany looked pretty good with that dual number 10 pairing of Musiala and Wirtz.

4 Cundy admitted he is not convinced that Wirtz is going to be a success Credit: Getty

"That feels like a really long time ago now. If there's only going to be one number 10, it's got to be Wirtz.



"So everything has got to go through him. It feels to me that, in terms of his club, because there's been so much change at Liverpool, his role has been not that clearly defined in a way that's not massively helpful to someone who's trying to settle in English football.

Wirtz will get there with Liverpool

"I still believe he'll get there with Liverpool, but it's proven more difficult, that's for sure. He obviously arrived with a lot of pressure on him and a huge expectation of being a star and all the rest of it.

"But I think we've seen with creative players, they've been given that bit of freedom by Klopp.

" And certainly that's something that he was given by Xabi Alonso as well at Leverkusen, which was a huge part of his platform, a huge part of his ability to excel at Leverkusen.



"So I guess the question is, do you play him with another number 10 type guy? My guess is probably no, but I would think Nadiem Amiri would be a candidate for that of mine.

4 Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak both failed to hit double figures in the Premier League last term Credit: Getty

"Quite a physical midfielder, but again someone who's good at creating his own shot, as you would say in basketball.

"Definitely someone who is a sort of independent creator. I think the two of them next to each other would be quite interesting.



"We know that Klopp is someone who wants to grab the ball by the horns.

"So hopefully that suits Florian Wirtz because it would be good for Liverpool as well as good for him and good for Germany."

Sports.title: England players told it’s impossible to win major trophy unless they follow Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo example
Sports.content:
England players told it’s impossible to win major trophy unless they follow Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo example

Danny Mills wants to see England players follow the South American example and not miss any games for their country.

Players' commitment to the Three Lions has been questioned following a raft of withdrawals ahead of the three-week international break.



3 The call-up marked the first time Tuchel had turned to the Chelsea man since his 2026 World Cup snub Credit: Getty

Thomas Tuchel's side will play UEFA Nations League games against Spain, Czechia (twice) and Croatia over the coming weeks.

Cole Palmer is one of several who have pulled out of the squad, with Declan Rice, Tino Livramento, Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford all not travelling 'due to respective injury issues'.

Morgan Gibbs-White and James Garner have since been drafted in as replacements.



The current international window marks an expanded three-week stint - the longest in modern football history.

It allows national teams to fit four matches into one window and reduces the number of international breaks in the first half of the season from three to two, and limits the total number of weeks that club seasons are put on hold reduced from six to five.



Former England right-back Mills, who played 19 times for the Three Lions, does not want to see players missing games.

He said: "Look at Argentina's team, look how many caps they get, there’s players with over 100 caps.



"Brazil are the same, the South American teams have more qualification games, and they just turn up and they play - they don’t miss games.

"Look at Cristiano Ronaldo, he may be a bit selfish, but he turns up for internationals and he wants to play.

"Until we get back to it being such a proud thing to do and wanting to win everything, then it will be impossible to win and create a culture.

3 Messi holds the most appearances for his country Credit: Getty



"That’s what creates competition for players because they know they might not get back in again. Because we haven’t won anything for so long, the modern day footballer doesn’t understand the importance of what winning a World Cup or Euros is like."

South American calendar

The South American qualifiers for the World Cup allows for six direct slots in the final tournament and one inter-confederation play-off slot.

There was a total of 18 matchdays during the FIFA International Match Calendar, with six competitive clashes played every year in the build-up of the international tournament - including against giants like Brazil, Colombia, Uruguay, and Paraguay.

On the other hand, England only played eight fixtures against Albania, Serbia, Latvia, Andorra to qualify for the World Cup in the USA, Canada and Mexico.



Lionel Messi has accumulated 207 appearances for Argentina over his decorated career.

Ronaldo is another player who represents his country with an immense amount of pride and passion, and has been on record multiple times saying 'nothing compares to winning for Portugal.'

He has played a record 233 times, scoring 146 goals.

Mills added: "When we win something, it will make these players the biggest thing in the country and could inspire a generation.

3 The 41-year-old has yet to officially retire from the Portugal national team



"There’s not many of the England squad left from 1966 and we’ve lost that now which is very sad. But playing for your country, you should want to turn up every single time.

"I look back now and thought it was going to go on forever. People still talk to me about England now though.

"They don’t talk about Charlton vs West Ham or Leeds vs Wimbledon - England is the biggest thing that people talk about, it’s not just about your club, it’s the whole country."

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney hits out at Benjamin Sesko for wearing 'little stupid shinpads' as Man United legend questions striker's shin injury in brutal takedown
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney has questioned why Manchester United striker Benjamin Sesko sat out the club's 1-1 draw away at Fulham with a shin injury.

Rooney took to his podcast Stick to United to voice his displeasure with Sesko's absence from Sunday's game, implying that the Slovenian's shin injury was not serious enough to rule him out.

'Shin? Has he broken it?' said Rooney. 'You can hurt your shin, you can take tackles... I bet he's wearing them little stupid shinpads as well.'

The former United skipper did not stop there, later going on to say, 'If you're trying to play No9 [for Man United] and you've got a must-win game and you've got a sore shin and you're not playing... that's a big part of the problem.'

Later on in the show he reflected on his time at United, saying: 'Unless you physically can't play, you play when you're injured. I remember before games we used to get injections and the doctor used to put them in your arse.'

Wayne Rooney did not mince his words when criticising the Slovenian international

Sesko has enjoyed purple patches in his short time at Old Trafford but has been unable to pick up consistent form

Two more former United players, Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt, also voiced their concern over the striker's omission from Sunday's squad.

On their podcast, The Good, The Bad & The Football with Paddy McGuinness, Scholes aligned with his ex-teammate's view, saying: 'If it isn't broken, just wear your shinpads.' Butt then added: 'You're a player - you either break your shin or you don't play!'

Paul Scholes (left) and Nicky Butt (right) agreed with Rooney that Sesko should have played through the injury

As Daily Mail Sport reported yesterday, the comments by Butt and Scholes did not go down well in Slovenia, with Leeds defender Jaka Bijol backing Sesko to rise above it.

‘I hope and believe that Beni knows how to distance himself from this kind of pressure,’ he said. ‘When things aren't going your best on the pitch and you have certain doubts, reading things like this can make your confidence even worse.

‘He shouldn't pay too much attention to it, since we all know what quality he has. He himself knows what kind of footballer he is, and I think he always shows it with incredible things on the pitch.’

Another of Sesko's compatriots, Zan Vipotnik of Swansea, also spoke out in defence of the forward as he said: 'It's not easy for him. Recurring physical problems are bad, and to add to that it messes with your head... I really hope and believe his absence from the pitch will be as short as possible and that things will turn for the best very soon.'

Sports.title: Man United reveal how much money they've SAVED with sacked boss Ruben Amorim taking over at AC Milan - as they try to rake in more cash by selling bits of the pitch for £125!
Sports.content:
Manchester United saved £8.5million when Ruben Amorim took over as head coach of AC Milan, the club’s latest financial results have revealed. United reported in May that the total compensation due to Amorim and his staff could rise to a maximum of £16.7m. But his appointment as Milan boss in June meant United have paid £8.2m, less than half that figure. Wednesday’s results also revealed that the cost of financing United’s debt has now rocketed past the £1billion mark since the Glazer family’s leveraged takeover. The club’s annual figures show that United paid £69.6m – an increase of £48.4m or 228.3 per cent from the previous year – in interest and other finance costs. The overall debt itself still stands at more than £1bn despite the cost-cutting measures imposed by minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and Ineos which contributed to United turning a £18.4m operating loss into a £22.6m over the last year. It consists of £577.6m of historic debt from the Glazer takeover in 2005, £111.4m owing on the club’s revolving credit facility and outstanding transfer fees. Ineos co-owned Man United have announced record revenue of £677.6m for the 2025-26 season The Americans’ £790m buyout has been the biggest factor in United bleeding over £1bn in the last two decades, and that infuriates fans who are fiercely opposed to the Glazers’ ownership and increasingly disillusioned with the Ratcliffe regime. After spending just £163m in the transfer market this summer – substantially less than many of their rivals – United are 12th in the Premier League table after one win in five games. The club are also at odds with large sections of the fanbase over their attempts to increase revenue and, more recently, crack down on ticket touts. It has also emerged that emails have been sent out to members and season ticket holders offering them the chance to buy miniature squares of the Old Trafford turf – which was re-laid in the summer for the first time in 14 years – for £125. United laid a new playing surface at the 'Theatre of Dreams' for the first time in 14 years over the summer, and the old pitch has been cut into 7cm x 7cm squares. Those squares have been packaged in acrylic cubes and are being sent out to supporters who want them in a smart black casing. The United website reads: 'Take home a piece of Old Trafford with this official turf cube, perfect for fans who want a keepsake from one of the most famous pitches in the world. 'Carefully preserved, this piece of turf makes a priceless memento of iconic games played at home and keeps the memories of match days alive. The sacking of Ruben Amorim in January cost the club £8.5million in compensation 'Perfect for gifting to passionate Reds, this turf cube makes a great addition to desks or can be displayed in a cabinet with other Manchester United collectibles.' The club have described the purchasable turf as a 'one-of-a-kind collector’s item' to club members and season-ticket holders in an email offering them 'exclusive' early access. Despite the huge debt and costs of servicing it, United are still committed to building a new £2bn stadium. The latest financial results revealed that the club spent £63.5m in June on a 25-acre triangle of land located 350 metres away from Old Trafford. While United were able to announce record revenues of £677.6m despite not playing in Europe last season, they reported an overall net loss of £43m – up from £33m last year – which sources say demonstrates the importance of maintaining financial discipline. Chief executive Omar Berrada said: ‘We are pleased to have secured record revenues which demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football. United are selling small cubes of last season's Old Trafford turf to fans for £125 ‘This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years. It also proves Manchester United’s enduring popularity and commercial strength. ‘While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.’ Commercial revenue for the year was down £16m and sponsorship revenue by £27.9m, partly due to United having no training kit sponsor following the end of their partnership with Tezos. The club have since signed a record £20m-a-year deal with Betway, as well as replacing sleeve sponsor DXC Technology with SumUp. Retail & merchandising revenue for the year was up £11.9m, and broadcasting revenue by £33.9m due to United finishing third in the Premier League after Michael Carrick replaced Amorim in January. Matchday revenue was down £6.8m due to the club’s shortest season since the First World War. Not playing in Europe and going out of both domestic cup competitions at the first hurdle meant that United played just 40 games.
