Sports.title: Revealed: Jurgen Klopp's list of four rules for Germany's stars in his first managerial job since leaving Liverpool - with WAGs told to stay away, barbers BANNED and new professional standards
Sports.content:
Jurgen Klopp has reportedly introduced four rules for Germany stars as the former Liverpool boss seeks to turn around the fortunes of their national team. Klopp will take charge of Germany for the first time on Thursday when they face the Netherlands in the Nations League, after being unveiled as the new national team boss back in July. The 59-year-old, who took the job after a two-year break from the dugout, will hope to restore Germany’s standing after a decade of underperformance at international tournaments. Klopp succeeded Julian Nagelsmann after Germany crashed out of the World Cup to Paraguay in the last-32, with the presence of players’ WAGs and families placed under the spotlight in the aftermath. Nagelsmann's partner also made headlines, with German media reporting that his girlfriend, Lena Wurzenberger, was an almost constant presence in the camp. According to German newspaper Bild, Klopp has sought to significantly restrict their presence as one of four rules for his squad to follow in Germany’s new era. Jurgen Klopp has introduced four rules for his Germany squad as part of their new era Players' wives and girlfriends will have limited access during training camps and tournaments The presence of players' families around the camp was a major talking point during Germany's underwhelming World Cup campaign The Germany head coach will no longer permit ‘team outings’ during tournaments, which had enabled players’ entire families to visit the team’s headquarters throughout the last World Cup. Instead, Klopp will reportedly allow families to visit on a limited basis, with the intention that players are able to fully focus on their common goal during training camps and at Euro 2028. Players have also been banned from being visited by hairdressers at Germany’s team accommodation, with stars instead having to have their hair cut prior to the camp as part of an aim to introduce new professional standards. Klopp is also reported to have stressed that players must be present for dinner promptly at 7pm or 8pm, rather than arriving gradually, in a move aimed at giving players more time to socialise and connect with each other. A focus has been placed on encouraging conversations between players in an attempt to grow team unity, including during gym sessions and massages. As part of the drive, Klopp has banned the use of mobile phones at these times, as well as on matchdays, ensuring his side are focused on essentials in the build-up to their matches. The rules aimed at improving team culture come with Germany seeking to transform their performances at major tournaments. Germany have made three consecutive early exits since winning the World Cup in 2014, with group stage eliminations in 2018 and 2022 before a last-32 exit this year. Klopp has reportedly banned mobile phones at certain times and is encouraging players to socialise more together in an attempt to build team spirit The national team were also eliminated in the last-16 and quarter-finals of the past two European Championships, with their last semi-final coming back in 2016. Klopp will assess a 44-man split squad in the first matches of his reign, with the players used across four Nations League fixtures. The unusually large squad is being separated into two to handle an extended three-week international break, as they face Netherlands, Greece and Serbia. Klopp has already clashed with German media after his squad selection was leaked earlier this month, while in his first press conference he threatened to resign if his family faces any scrutiny. After his first game as Germany boss on Thursday, Klopp's side will then take on Greece for the first of two clashes just three days later. The former Liverpool boss will then switch to his second squad for a clash with Serbia on October 1 before they play Greece again on October 4.

Sports.title: These pitches made Ollie Robinson look like Curtly Ambrose! England legend DARREN GOUGH delivers his verdict on the Test summer, the Ashes ticket-price controversy... and what Yorkshire's next generation must do to become international stars
Sports.content:
Even though Darren Gough has no reservations about Ollie Robinson’s ability with the new ball, the former England pacer feels that the Sussex seamer has been made to look like an all-time great by bowler-friendly pitches.

Armed with the new ball, Robinson kickstarted England’s Test summer by running through New Zealand’s top order at Lord’s in June. Capping off an incredible home season against Pakistan at Edgbaston, Robinson finished with 21 wickets as Joe Root’s England recorded a comfortable 3-0 series win this month.

Despite the rain gods making their presence felt, only two of England’s six home Tests reached day five this season. Only on four occasions did a team manage to breach the 400-run barrier in a single innings on English pitches.

‘You only have to look around Test cricket, and a lot of the games are finishing in three days. The pitches have become very bowler-friendly, which is a shame. You go back to Test cricket 10-15 years ago when the pitches were hard and flat, and you had to really bowl out the opposition,’ Gough tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘I made a joke of it, but James Anderson and Stuart Broad - it has cost them (retiring), probably 100 wickets each on their totals. These last two years, so many Test matches have finished in three days or just after. It's ridiculous.’

Robinson, who admitted he was ‘nowhere near ready for the Ashes’, recorded the fifth-best bowling average in a series of three Tests or more against Pakistan. The 32-year-old also became only the third English seamer to reach 100 Test wickets at an average under 20 this season.

Ollie Robinson averages just 19.25 after a stellar summer which saw him torment Pakistan

Having gone past the likes of Jasprit Bumrah and Pat Cummins, Robinson now boasts the best bowling average (19.25) of any bowler with 100 or more Test wickets in the last 100 years. ‘Robinson's been made to look like Curtly Ambrose,' Gough adds. 'And he's a good bowler, but he's been made to look like he is one of the best bowlers of all time on these pitches that we've had this year so far in the Pakistan Tests. And the one at Lord's earlier (against New Zealand) in the year as well.'

England’s fifth-highest wicket-taker across formats, Gough also voiced his dismay at Headingley being overlooked for next year’s Ashes. ‘I played alongside a lot of great players for England,' he says. 'They would all say: Lord's, Edgbaston, and Headingley. So those three Test venues are favourites to the players. Nothing's changed from my day, from the people I know. We always play good cricket on these pitches. And it's a real shame’.

After Warwickshire sparked a fierce backlash by raising the price of Ashes tickets from £115 to £165 in Edgbaston's Hollies Stand, Gough warned that cricket is in danger of following football down an expensive path. ‘I think my problem with cricket - I experienced it when I was growing up, in under-14s and 15s. I think it is an elitist sport, and it still does have that, and it carries that on with the pricing for some of the matches,’ Gough says.

‘Is it affordable? No. £170 for a day of cricket is a lot of money. And it's not affordable, is it? If you were to go in there with a few mates, it makes it a very expensive day on top of drinking, food while you're in there, and travel; you're looking at a £250 day,’ he added.

‘So, this is expensive, not affordable. Football's gone that way, and cricket's going exactly the same route. You would think, with them just making millions and millions of pounds after selling the Hundred. The prices would remain the same, but naah - not to be...It's an Ashes year, and it's the strongest series England have, and that's where they make all the money.’

England are entering another World Cup cycle, with Kevin Pietersen installed as specialist batting mentor, and captain Harry Brook has already propelled Brendon McCullum’s men to No. 1 position in the T20I rankings.

Darren Gough took 229 wickets in 58 Test matches for England

Attention this week turns to the ODI series against Sri Lanka, where Brook’s side will look to dominate again. Having finished the Test summer without a century, Brook blasted an unbeaten 114 from 49 balls in the T20I opener. Gough, who welcomed Pietersen’s return to the England camp, has rallied behind Brook to keep playing his current brand of cricket.

‘Brook is an enormous talent, and when you get talking about the brand of cricket England play, I have no problem with Brook playing that way. But he's the only one who should be playing that way in all formats,’ Gough said.

‘The rest have to play their natural game, wherever that may be; Brook can carry on playing like that for me. He averages 50-odd in Test and ODI cricket; he looks the real deal. So, I've no problem with Harry Brook being Harry Brook.’

As Brook has been joined by Yorkshire teammates Joe Root and Adil Rashid in the ODI squad for the Sri Lanka series, Gough is quick to observe that Yorkshire are no longer flooding the England team.

‘It's not as many as it used to be. We've always had a strong outing in the England side, but I think it's where we are as a county, isn't it? Yorkshire has struggled in the last few years, and the players are just not coming through now,’ Gough says.

‘We had that golden period in my era where we had myself, Craig White, Richard Blakey, Martyn Moxon, Ryan Sidebottom and Matthew Hoggard, and all these players that play for England. And then you had the Ballance, Root, Bairstow era. And then all those guys like Michael Vaughan, but we seem to be not having as big an effect on the England team as we used to.’

Gough feels all-rounders George Hill and Matt Revis have potential, but both still have plenty of improving to do as Yorkshire hunt for their next big Tyke. ‘One player I have always liked as a cricketer is George Hill. But in the current mould of England, it probably doesn't fit the bill they're after. England are after bowlers that bowl at 84 miles an hour. George is a very skilful bowler,’ Gough explained.

Gough thinks Harry Brook deserves licence to play ultra-attacking cricket

‘He would be a fourth seamer for England, not in the top three seamers, but he only bowls in the late 70s. I would like to see him get a few more runs. I have kind of been disappointed with the lack of runs the last few years. He's a terrific player,’ adds Gough, who also captained Yorkshire for two seasons.

‘And Revis, he's the opposite. I think his batting's really, really good. His bowling just needs to improve; it's been the same question for Revis the last few years. He just needs to step up his bowling, and he's another top-quality cricketer.’

Beyond the two familiar all-rounders, Gough also said young Will Bennison may soon be knocking on the selectors’ door. ‘Will's a good player. he was a lot younger when I was there. Always been highly thought of as a cricketer,’ Gough recalls.

‘England U-19s now. He is doing well for the under-19s; he got his chance for Yorkshire in the Metro Bank. And yeah, he did well. There aren't many players in our 1st team in Yorkshire getting runs. So, he's got to be knocking down the door. He must be pretty close,’ he concluded.

Sports.title: Liverpool Confidential: Inside the 'aggressive' recruitment team helping Reds beat rivals to the brightest prospects in world football, how they poached Lucca Brughmans from under Real Madrid's nose - and the untapped markets they will target in future
Sports.content:
Liverpool Confidential: Inside the 'aggressive' recruitment team helping Reds beat rivals to the brightest prospects in world football, how they poached Lucca Brughmans from under Real Madrid's nose - and the untapped markets they will target in future

From the outside looking in, Matt Newberry is a low-key figure. A Google search returns little information other than a job title, and he does not have a profile on Liverpool’s official website.

Yet despite the unassuming digital footprint, Newberry and his team have an incredibly important role in moulding the club's future.

Newberry's role since 2024 has been ‘director of global talent’, where he leads a youth recruitment drive that has seen the arrival of what Liverpool believe are some of the best youngsters in the game.

In 2026 alone, the Reds have signed Mor Talla Ndiaye from Senegalese club Amitie FC, Ifeanyi Ndukwe from Austria Vienna, Samuel Martinez from Atletico Nacional in Colombia, Lucca Brughmans from Genk and Djylian N'Guessan from Saint-Etienne.

Hungarian Armin Pecsi, who has one cap and is represented by the same agency as Liverpool vice-captain Dominik Szoboszlai, was also signed in a similar move which club staffers describe as an aggressive desire to recruit the very best emerging young talent.

Internally, the club believe Brughmans is the best young goalkeeper in the world. They feel the same about Ndukwe at centre half – and his talents were already evident in pre-season before he went on loan to La Liga side Levante.

Defender Mor Talla Ndiaye (centre) is one of a host of talented youngsters Liverpool have signed in 2026 alone

Despite his unassuming digital footprint, Matt Newberry and his team have an incredibly important role in moulding the future of Liverpool

Not all of the above names will make it in Liverpool’s first team. But Liverpool believe that if even just a couple do, Newberry’s team have succeeded. Others can be sold on and the club can benefit in alternative ways.

The process of Newberry and his team goes well beyond just scouting young players.

Insiders point to the fact all of these kids will have been known by every top club in the game. One of the global talent team's key responsibilities is nurturing relationships with clubs around the world and selling Liverpool to players.

Newberry, for example, recently travelled to Colombia to work with Martinez, who will join Liverpool’s academy from next season – or when he turns 18, due to Brexit rules prohibiting British clubs signing foreign talent before they are an adult.

Young keeper Brughmans had been taken to Real Madrid and was expected to follow in the footsteps of his idol Thibaut Courtois, until Newberry and Co intervened and sold him the pathway at Liverpool.

The club moved quickly and made their offer to Genk on the Sunday morning before transfer deadline day. By Monday morning, he was on a jet to Merseyside.

So who is Newberry himself, the man at the helm of this operation?

Born in County Down, Northern Ireland, Newberry’s first role in football was at Birmingham City as an academy scout and he was soon a recruitment officer for young talent. He joined Liverpool just under 15 years ago and has held multiple roles in youth scouting and recruitment.

When working as a scout, Newberry is credited with being the man who first watched Ryan Gravenberch playing for Ajax Under 16s as a 13-year-old. Liverpool signed him several years later and Gravenberch was named Premier League Young Player of the Year when Liverpool won the title in 2024-25.

Young goalkeeper Lucca Brughmans was expected to move to Real Madrid but Liverpool got their man

Anfield insiders regard Ifeanyi Ndukwe (left), on loan at Levante, as one of the best young defenders in world football

Newberry was influential in bringing fellow Northern Irishman Conor Bradley to the club, too. His local team Dungannon Swifts welcomed two Liverpool staffers, who checked out their facilities. Bradley remained attached to the club and would fly back and forth to Merseyside to train. Coaches at Dungannon are still looked after and flown over to Liverpool games.

James McConnell, who played for Liverpool's first team last week, had a similar story. The Newcastle fan was signed from Sunderland at 14 and placed in a school just down the road from some family friends who housed him.

Newberry also spent a year working as pathways manager, essentially sorting out loans for youngsters – making sure the new club is the right one, their playing style fits and that the player's personal needs and development are looked after.

Liverpool were one of the first adopters of this role and Julian Ward, who is to take over from Richard Hughes as sporting director, previously occupied the position. Ward’s successor was David Woodfine, now assistant sporting director and a key cog in the operation.

One of the reasons the club has turned to foreign talent is Brexit and rules that prohibit British clubs signing Europeans before the age of 18. This might sound like a contradiction, but British talent now costs a premium.

Academy director Alex Inglethorpe said earlier this year: ‘The market is more competitive now around the age of 16 than it’s ever been. There’s no question that since Brexit, the landscape has changed and it’s driven up the price of young English talent.’

There is something of an arms race developing in the youth game. Teenagers (and sometimes pre-teens) are being offered flash cars, big houses, promises of first-team debuts within certain time frames, eye-watering bonuses to get around salary caps, and all sorts.

Liverpool poached Rio Ngumoha from Chelsea two years ago and the Blues tried to retaliate by targeting several youngsters in Liverpool's academy. Ngumoha could have earned more at Stamford Bridge but was instead sold on the pathway at Anfield.

He is now a fully-fledged member of the first team and in line for a bumper new contract soon. Last term, he was paid a nominal salary – for a footballer, anyway! – but remunerated with healthy bonuses and performance-related add-ons.

Rio Ngumoha, 18, is already a fully-fledged member of the first team and in line for a bumper new contract soon

Rival clubs were willing to pay 16-year-old winger Joshua Abe nearly £50,000 a week to sign for them

Some clubs were willing to pay 16-year-old winger Joshua Abe nearly £50,000 a week to sign for them, with Chelsea, Arsenal, Manchester City and Real Madrid all keen. It shows the success of Liverpool’s youth policy is about more than finances.

Several academy stars have already played for the first team this season, with boss Andoni Iraola in regular contact with youth staffers. Captain Virgil van Dijk is also a regular at youth games and not just because his young son Jacey has trained at the club.

Newberry’s team is not designed to cut across any domestic scouting operations or loan pathways. They work closely with the other departments and Gary Probert, brought in from Ipswich as loan manager, has won many fans inside the club.

Everyone is keen to stress that all recruitment at Liverpool is a team game and no individual should take all the credit. Recently departed head of academy recruitment Chris Dowling, who was influential in bringing Ngumoha to the club, was also a key player.

Think of Newberry’s team then, as an extension of the sporting director with a particular focus on the emerging talents in the game. Remember, the club have recently invested £20million in the redevelopment of the academy and its facilities, with a full-size indoor pitch under a dome.

Part of their remit has also been to extend Liverpool’s tentacles into less traditional markets. Before the signing of Martinez, for example, the Reds had not previously done much shopping for South American youngsters. Before Ndiaye, the African market was largely untapped.

The president of Gambian side BST Galaxy was invited to the AXA Training Centre to meet club staff and two players were given trials at Liverpool. Again, this drive is as much about nurturing relationships as it is finding the players in the first place.

The Reds employ many regional scouts, such as Dassler Marques and Gonzalo Siegrist in South America. In February, they recruited former Mechelen left back Laurens Paulussen to focus on Belgium and the Netherlands.

Jasper Vallmark has covered Scandinavia for a year, Tika Musonda moved from Spurs to be a global talent scout. These are just some examples of their global operation, but they still have plenty of domestic employees – such as former winger Stewart Downing.

That is why they are keen to spread their wings, but the arrivals of current first-teamers Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni from fellow English clubs show the global drive is not coming at the expense of domestic recruitment.

Liverpool still have plenty of employees scouting the domestic market – such as former winger Stewart Downing

Another player Liverpool have watched is striker Michael Mulholland from Northern Irish side Crusaders. The Belfast-born forward supposedly once scored 256 in a single season. He already has several caps for the Northern Ireland youth team and an adidas deal.

In two other moves first revealed in Confidential, Liverpool also signed Zach Trinder from Wolves, rated as one of the best young goalkeepers in the country, and defender Dara Jikiemi from Celtic.

Any of those could be the next cab off the rank for Liverpool, whose reach stretches further than ever before. Newberry and Co are just as crucial to shaping the future as anyone at Anfield – and they are confident some of their recruits will strike gold.

Sports.title: How Premier League clubs are exploiting their most loyal fans - the season ticket tricks used by Chelsea and Man United, the subtle ways 'old-school' supporters are being swapped out for tourists, 'hospitality' rip-offs and why the worst is yet to come
Sports.content:
The railing that once hoisted the Holmesdale Fanatics flag at Selhurst Park has gone. The distinctive and raucous Crystal Palace ultras group? Disbanded.

The flagpole remained in place for the first home game of the season, just 24 hours after the group announced their dissolution, but had vanished by the following match.

Selhurst has felt a little lifeless ever since. The ceaseless noise from the 400-man section behind the goal in the Holmesdale Road End is no more.

When Daily Mail Sport asked the Holmesdale Fanatics for an explanation, they declined and redirected us to their initial statement, where they criticise the ‘draconian restrictions’ imposed on supporters.

Those restrictions extend well beyond Selhurst Park. Across the country, the football fan experience is changing, replaced by a game that is increasingly commercialised and gentrified.

Daily Mail Sport has spoken to insiders across the Premier League and beyond, industry experts and, most importantly, loyal supporters themselves to uncover just how the modern-day fan is being exploited – and why the worst may yet be to come...

Crystal Palace's distinctive and raucous Holmesdale Fanatics group has disbanded, leaving Selhurst Park a little lifeless

It is a sign of the wider exploitation and disenfrachisement of old-school, matchgoing supporters

Times are tough for football fans of all stripes, but season-ticket holders are feeling the pinch more than anyone. Premier League regulations now restrict those fans from sharing their season tickets with fellow supporters, family and friends.

At the start of the season, digital tickets became mandatory, supposedly to improve stadium security, prevent ticket touting and streamline entry into stadiums.

Manchester United have used digital ticket enforcement to identify what they describe as ‘suspicious activity’ and curb ticket touting, banning 685 season ticket holders as a result. However, fears remain that innocent fans using the ticket sharing system have been caught up in the clean-up operation.

A cynic would argue the new policy presented a fresh opportunity for clubs to squeeze supporters and monetise them sharing their season ticket.

Rather than the trusty plastic card which supporters could hand over to friends if they were not attending a match or wanted to split the cost of a season ticket, fans must now resell their tickets through official club channels – which clubs can make a profit from – or share them using the club’s ticketing platform, with access often commanding a membership fee.

At Chelsea, for example, to share a ticket the recipient must be a member, with prices beginning at £45. Meanwhile, Crystal Palace allow season-ticket holders to share their match ticket with non-members but charge a one-off £50 fee for the privilege.

Manchester United offer a ‘ticket sharing’ membership which allows supporters to receive forwarded tickets from season-ticket holders – charging £30 per person.

There are, in fairness, valid safety concerns behind this development. The Premier League partly introduced the scheme to ensure match attendees can be identified, which helps the enforcement of banning orders and detection of high-risk supporters.

But the self-serving, avaricious clubs have opportunistically commercialised supporters' autonomy over their own tickets.

At Manchester City, season tickets must be used for 16 Premier League home games, ten of which must be attended by the named individual, or the ticket will be cancelled

Across town, United have used digital ticket enforcement to identify what they describe as ‘suspicious activity’ but fears remain that innocent fans have been caught up in the clean-up

Things are unlikely to get better anytime soon. One senior football executive told Daily Mail Sport that clubs view season tickets as a ‘discounted rate’, blocking a conveyor belt of high-spending corporate and tourist spectators attending one-off games that would generate more revenue. They added that clubs could look to reduce the number of their season tickets.

That perspective was echoed by football finance expert and host of The Price of Football Podcast Kieran Maguire, who told Daily Mail Sport: ‘The bigger brands see season-ticket holders as bed blockers because tickets can be sold at a higher price to international fans and those desperate to see their club but who can only manage it once a year due to logistical challenges.

‘If we take the case of Liverpool, Anfield has gone from 44,000 to 61,000 capacity, but there was hardly any increase in season-ticket sales. It is far more lucrative to target the corporate market or the day-fan market as opposed to someone who is a local Red and unlikely to go to the megastore and drink in the ground beforehand because they go to the pub with their mates, sit at the same table and have the same chats.

‘These people, of course, are the bedrock of football fans. For political reasons, clubs won’t want to be seen to be reducing season tickets. But I don’t think we will see an increase going forward unless they are for corporate seats.

‘In some of the more desirable areas of the stadium, the clubs might not convert season tickets that haven’t been renewed into new season tickets despite long waiting lists.'

That shift has already begun, with United relocating around 500 fans sat behind the dugout at Old Trafford to the top of the North Stand to increase hospitality tickets in what United describe as a ‘high value area of the stadium’.

At Manchester City, meanwhile, season tickets must be used for 16 Premier League home games, ten of which must be attended by the named individual, or the ticket will be cancelled. Some fans argued the move breaches the Equality Act as pregnant women, mothers or disabled people could struggle to attend for prolonged periods.

To make matters worse, season-ticket waiting lists are becoming increasingly exploitative. Arsenal’s exceeds 110,000 people, meaning the club would need to turn over every season ticket three times before reaching the bottom. With the current wait time estimated at around 20 years and a £50 deposit required to join, it is difficult to envisage many supporters ever securing one.

There is therefore logic in closing the waiting list – as Liverpool have done – rather than asking supporters to part with their hard-earned cash for a ticket they may never receive. However, clubs' passive income would take a hit. Arsenal say they regularly review the waiting list and would consult supporters on any proposed changes.

Liverpool supporters recently successfully protested ticket price hikes of 3 per cent for three consecutive seasons

English football is shifting towards a matchday experience built around tourists rather than hardcore supporters. Americans fans used to taking in entertainment that goes beyond the game itself

Aside from their wallets being raided, the fan experience is also declining as English football culture shifts towards a matchday experience built around tourists rather than hardcore supporters. American fans, in particular, are accustomed to taking in entertainment that goes beyond the game itself.

Tourism dilutes the home support. At Selhurst Park, people were spotted wearing Erling Haaland Norway shirts in the home end during Manchester City’s 4-1 win over Palace in August.

And when Palace travelled to Craven Cottage earlier this month, Daily Mail Sport observed Chicago Fire and Brazil shirts in Fulham's newly redeveloped Riverside Stand, with some spectators even whipping out their phones to record themselves when the visitors scored. A similar picture is painted weekly across Premier League stadiums.

Fan experience has played a significant role in the breakdown in relations between Palace and the Holmesdale Fanatics. The fan group want an organic atmosphere inside the stadium, while the club have veered towards an artificial one.

Before kick-off, the HF had found themselves competing with Natasha Bedingfield’s Unwritten - among other pop songs - blared over the recently upgraded PA system.

There is an internal directive to ensure the stadium looks attractive on television; hence the introduction of fireworks and pyrotechnics when the players enter the pitch. But manufacturing a look is precisely what the HF stand against.

Perhaps the pomp and circumstance makes football clubs more marketable to international audiences.

The Premier League’s own economic and social impact report from July 2026 boasts that the top flight drew over a million international fans to matches in the 2023-24 season, with a trip-related spend of £903million. Those numbers are projected to rise continuously.

The Premier League say the top flight drew over a million international fans to matches in the 2023-24 season, with a trip-related spend of £903million

Palace's Holmesdale Fanatics want an organic atmosphere inside the stadium, while the club have veered towards an artificial one

Daily Mail Sport spoke to one US-based neutral who regularly flies over to attend Premier League games. Among the thousands he has spent on tickets already this season, he paid £350 for a general admission ticket to watch Ipswich take on Liverpool at Portman Road, purchased through a third-party reseller.

Clubs discourage buying third-party tickets as they do not receive the benefits besides the money spent in the stadium on merchandise, food and drink – although it does indicate the extravagant prices international fans are willing to pay for a £38 ticket, splashing nine times over the odds.

It has not gone unnoticed at Premier League clubs that World Cup stadiums in the United States were 99.7 per cent full despite extortionate general admission prices. That spells danger for domestic supporters.

Sites like Seat Unique and Sportsworld have partnerships with Premier League clubs including Manchester City, Manchester United and Everton and market padded seat packages suitable for tourists. For Manchester City’s Champions League match against Paris Saint-Germain next month, Sportsworld are selling a £279 padded seat package which non-members can purchase – the only requirement is they are not in away colours.

'Westview' at Stamford Bridge is similar. The package ranges from £225 to £625 per game depending on the prestige of the fixture for a padded seat and a market hall style concourse with no food or drink included.

It is barely a hospitality package, besides sitting in a swankier area of the stadium. Simply put, Westview allows Chelsea to sell extortionately priced tickets to non-members, enabling the club to benefit directly from the tourist trade. These visitors are also likely to spend money on food and drink and visit the megastore.

Some Premier League clubs have even been spotted bringing the megastore to fans, with merchandise staff now carrying trays of baseball caps and scarves around the pitch and concourses to cater to the tourist market.

The Premier League needs to captivate an international audience but it should not come at the expense of ordinary fans.

Last year, the Football Supporters' Association said: ‘Football is becoming a luxury good for some, pricing out working-class communities, young supporters and families who represent the future heartbeat of the game. Record broadcast revenues – the 2025-28 deal is worth £12.25billion – and packed corporate hospitality sections tell us that financial sustainability does not depend on pricing out traditional supporters.’

Yet the cheapest ticket for a Category A game in nine of the 20 Premier League grounds exceeds £50, while general admission season tickets range from £380 to £3,192. Newcastle offer the cheapest season ticket, and Fulham’s is the most expensive.

Coventry City are one of the few clubs that have looked out for their supporters in recent years

‘Football is becoming a luxury good for some, pricing out working-class communities, young supporters and families who represent the future heartbeat of the game,' say the FSA

Although the outlook for fans appears bleak, there are rays of positivity to cling on to. Coventry City deserve praise for rewarding loyalty. In 2023, the club committed to giving supporters who bought a season ticket a free one should they reach the Premier League. This season, some 5,000 fans are benefiting from that scheme.

The £30 price cap for away fans has been extended until the end of the 2027-28 season – providing good value for the most loyal supporters.

And despite the widespread rip-off, fans can still fight back. Liverpool supporters had success at the end of last season after the club announced season ticket price hikes of 3 per cent for three consecutive seasons. But a protest at Anfield – where supporters raised yellow cards – prompted the club to reconsider, raising prices for this season and freezing them for 2027-28.

In light of the European Super League debacle, Premier League clubs created fan advisory boards to ensure that supporters' concerns were heard. Now, however, those bodies must stop being symbolic – and ensure English football remembers its most loyal fans represent the heart of the game.

Sports.title: 'Xabi appears not to love him': Inside Estevao's uncertain future at Chelsea, why Brazilian is struggling for minutes under new boss Alonso and the compromise he may be forced to accept
Sports.content:
'Xabi appears not to love him': Inside Estevao's uncertain future at Chelsea, why Brazilian is struggling for minutes under new boss Alonso and the compromise he may be forced to accept

Brazil’s games this international break are in Australia and India, and yet Estevao may not mind travelling to the other side of the world. He knows, at least, that he stands a chance of receiving more minutes for his country than he has for his club so far this season.

Estevao has received a grand total of 23 minutes from Xabi Alonso for Chelsea in the Premier League, a figure that does not include stoppage time.

In their five league fixtures, his contribution can be summarised thusly: 83rd-minute substitute, unused substitute, 81st-minute substitute, 86th-minute substitute, 87th-minute substitute with his team already trailing by two goals to Brentford.

That has led to talk back in his homeland of Estevao feeling frustrated, which would be understandable. Reports in Brazil have even hinted he is considering his future at the club and there would be no shortage of suitors for the 19-year-old, despite Chelsea insisting he is a prospect who very much features in their long-term plans.

Some sources close to the player shot down talk of him being disillusioned to Daily Mail Sport, insisting the season is long and there is confidence he will have fairer opportunities to impress.

Others, however, have said there is surprise at how he has been restricted from finding any rhythm under Alonso. One contact in Brazil said simply: ‘Xabi appears not to love him.’

Estevao has been limited to just 23 minutes of Premier League action by new manager Xabi Alonso so far this season

Reports in Brazil have even hinted Estevao is considering his future at the club - there would be no shortage of suitors for the 19-year-old

Estevao himself showed some understanding when speaking while away with Brazil this week, saying: ‘We have quality players at Chelsea, so what I do is focus on what I can control. I try to give my best in training. When I get an opportunity, I try to give my best. It goes day after day.’

Estevao has recovered from the hamstring tear suffered in April which brought a premature end to last season and saw his World Cup dream dashed. That was a tough blow for the teenager to take.

Any hopes of going on a run with Chelsea have been restricted with Cole Palmer and new signing Morgan Rogers forming a formidable front three with Joao Pedro. Pedro Neto has largely impressed as a right wing-back in Alonso's 3-4-2-1 set-up, a position where Estevao may also have to share some of the responsibility himself.

Away at Arsenal, the Brazilian came close to scoring a late equaliser after coming on while Chelsea trailed 2-1, denied brilliantly by David Raya.

It won him a starting place in their Carabao Cup clash with Leeds a few days later. However, he struggled and was hooked at half-time alongside three others as Chelsea came back from 1-0 down at the break to win 6-3.

A lack of European football means impressing in cup competitions is crucial if Estevao wants to play more in the Premier League. Yet he is not alone in his predicament. Indeed, he may not be the only winger concerned by his lack of opportunities under Alonso at Chelsea.

Jamie Gittens – a £52million signing from Borussia Dortmund in 2025 – has been an unused substitute in all five of Chelsea’s Premier League games this season. He too started against Leeds in the Carabao Cup, and he too was hooked at half-time.

Roma were interested in Gittens in the summer. Chelsea insisted he was not for sale because he was an important part of their own plans. We have not seen the evidence to back up those words as of yet.

Estevao's minutes have been limited by the arrival of Morgan Rogers, who has formed a formidable front three with Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer

The international breaks offers an opportunity for Estevao - who missed the World Cup through injury - to stake a claim for more chances back at Chelsea

Geovany Quenda – a £44m arrival from Sporting this summer – has likewise had limited opportunities. He has not started in any competition this season, appearing just twice as a substitute.

When players return from injury – Joao Pedro, Moises Caicedo, Reece James and Marco Palestra all missed Chelsea’s last trip to Brentford – some of these wide men may miss out on Alonso’s match-day squad altogether.

They would then risk falling out of sight and out of mind, much like Emmanuel Emegha and Aaron Anselmino, both of whom have only made one matchday squad all season, each acting as unused substitutes in the Carabao Cup against Luton Town. Anselmino was missing when the Chelsea squad posed for their picture, released last week.

Yet Estevao has attracted more attention than most because his potential is so obvious. Signed for a total package worth £51m from Brazilian club Palmeiras on a pre-agreement for when he turned 18, he showed his worth at times in Enzo Maresca’s 4-2-3-1.

Alonso’s 3-4-2-1 is leaving little room for his inclusion, but this international break could be good for him, as a way to try to take the opportunities that Carlo Ancelotti will allow him.

Sports.title: BBC begin 'systematic dismantling of TV sports news' in brutal new cost-slashing with top journalists told their jobs are at risk and furious staff considering strikes
Sports.content:
BBC Sport staff have been told that 41 jobs have been scrapped as part of a cost-cutting drive across the corporation. Daily Mail Sport understands that figure includes the job of seven journalists - including four senior roles. Sports bulletins on the 24-hour BBC News channel will also be lost as part of the drive to save money, staff were told on Wednesday morning. The impending cuts - as reported by Daily Mail Sport on Sunday - are likely to mean some staff have to reapply for their jobs, with some considering strike action. Ski Sunday, fronted by Chemmy Alcott, has already fallen victim to BBC Sport cost-cutting Earlier today, a group of producers from the team responsible for sourcing sports stories were told their numbers were being cut from 15 to 11. Sources have confirmed that employees were told in their afternoon summit at BBC Sport’s HQ at Media City in Salford that 41 roles will be removed. Five new positions will also be created. That leaves a loss of 36 jobs in total. While that could lead to compulsory exits, Beeb insiders pointed out that a second voluntary redundancy window is now open, and they will be seeking to make up as many of those losses via that avenue. It is said that some staff members were emotional at the summit. One insider said: ‘This is the systematic dismantling of TV sports news at the BBC as we know it.’ Daily Mail Sport understands the staff were also told that they will not be able to work four-day weeks and will instead all be expected to work across five days. The prevailing view among staff is that they already work 40 hours across those four days and that the demand is evidence that chiefs do not understand how television operates. There is also understood to be some upset within the department that decisions are being made now amid a belief that discussions with BBC director general Matt Brittin, who started in the role in May, are due in the next fortnight. The news of cuts and programme losses come with director of sport Alex Kay-Jelski having already overseen a programme of change, with dozens of redundancies made last year. Earlier this month, the BBC announced it was to axe Ski Sunday while it came in for criticism for not building a studio in North America for the summer’s World Cup. A series of events have been dropped, including the Commonwealth Games, the Boat Race and the Rugby League World Cup. Football Focus was also canned at the end of last season.

Sports.title: Sarah Glenn issues Ashes target as England cricket star banishes demons
Sports.content:
Sarah Glenn issues Ashes target as England cricket star banishes demons

The leg-spinner missed a significant part of the season after picking up the injury on her bowling hand when she had a ball hit back at her during an England training camp in the winter

View Image Glenn was speaking at Metro Bank’s Girls in Cricket Fund networking event held at Hampshire’s Utilita Bowl on 19 September (Image: imagecomms)

Sarah Glenn has set her sights on an England return for next summer’s Ashes after overcoming a broken finger and rediscovering her rhythm with Yorkshire.

‌



The leg-spinner missed a significant part of the season after picking up the injury on her bowling hand when she had a ball hit back at her during an England training camp in the winter.

‌



However, Glenn made her comeback for her new county in June before taking seven wickets in nine matches for Southern Brave during this year’s The Hundred. The 27-year-old has taken 112 wickets across 92 England appearances across both ODI and T20 formats but has not featured for her county since October 2025.

‌



Now back fully fit, and with the visit of Australia on the horizon, Glenn, who has played in three previous Ashes series, including the 8-8 draw on home soil in 2023, is determined to force her way into head coach Charlotte Edwards’ plans.

“Regaining my England place is my ambition and doing that sooner rather than later would be awesome, but I also know that I’ve missed a lot of cricket this year and I need to get a lot of performances under my belt again,” said Glenn, speaking at Metro Bank’s Girls in Cricket Fund networking event held at Hampshire’s Utilita Bowl on 19 September.

“It would be really special [to make the Ashes squad]. I’ve been a part of the home Ashes before, and I remember it being really cool. So, to be a part of that again would be amazing.”

‌



The Women’s Ashes gets underway on 24 June with the sole Test taking place at Headingley, before a trio of T20Is is followed by three ODIs.

And with England having not won the contest with the old enemy since 2014, and having also lost the recent Women’s T20 World Cup final to Shelley Nitschke’s outfit, Glenn knows that everyone involved within the international set-up is chomping at the bit to end 12 years of pain against the Southern Stars.

“The ambition is to win the Ashes and get them back. You saw the strides the team made during the T20 World Cup. They’re getting out of difficult situations and dealing with pressure better now. For them, it’s just self-belief when it comes to playing the world ’s best.”

‌



Glenn has also backed fellow spinner Charlie Dean, praising her leadership qualities after assuming the captaincy in the absence of Nat Sciver-Brunt at various points across the summer, including during the Women’s T20 World Cup.

“I was really proud of her,” Glenn added of Dean, who most recently led the ODI squad to a 3-0 win over Ireland earlier this month. “I wasn’t surprised with how well she did. She’s a great teammate, a great friend, and I’ve built that friendship off the field as well.

“How she is on the field and off the field is just completely the same. And that’s really key as a captain, and I was very proud of how she did."

Article continues below

By helping more girls access welcoming clubs, supportive coaches and visible role models, the Metro Bank Girls in Cricket Fund gives them more than a chance to play, it helps build confidence, belonging and ambition. Because when girls feel supported in sport, they carry that belief into their lives.

Sports.title: Bruno Guimaraes sent warning by Newcastle star ahead of reunion after Arsenal move
Sports.content:
Bruno Guimaraes sent warning by Newcastle star ahead of reunion after Arsenal move

Bruno Guimaraes left Newcastle in the summer and will return with Arsenal for the first time in November - with his close pal and compatriot warning him about what to expect

View 2 Images Bruno Guimaraes swapped Newcastle for Arsenal in the summer

Arsenal star Bruno Guimaraes has been warned to expect a lot of stick on his return to Newcastle - from his own 'brother'.

‌



Guimaraes quit the Magpies in controversial circumstances this summer, eventually joining the Gunners in a £75million move. The Brazilian told the club he wanted to leave in a pursuit of Champions League glory and more titles, having been the captain who ended Newcastle's 70-year wait for a domestic trophy when he lifted the Carabao Cup in 2025.

‌



Alongside him in that success was fellow Brazilian Joelinton, who once admitted that Bruno was "like a brother" to him. The two stars were inseparable at the club's training ground, on the pitch and were each other's best men at their respective weddings.

‌



Joelinton says he holds no grudges against Guimaraes for leaving Newcastle, and the pair remain close friends, with the Arsenal man staying over at his pal's house after scoring for the Gunners against their old North East foes Sunderland earlier this month.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



However he has fired a stark warning to his old pal that he won't show him any friendship on the pitch when Arsenal visit St James' Park on November 21.

Joelinton said: "As a footballer, you have to make decisions, and he made his. Of course, he was sad to leave because he loved the city and club; he also had a great relationship with the fans, so it was not that easy for him. Now it's done, we wish him all the best.

"Just when he comes here now, he can't have a good time! We will be waiting for him here and give him some things! But he did great for him, and I wish him the best because he is one of my best friends in life. I wish him all the best for him and his family."

‌



View 2 Images Bruno Guimaraes and Joelinton became close friends and remain as such despite now playing for different clubs

Guimaraes' exit followed swiftly after Eddie Howe dramatically resigned from Newcastle after five years in charge. The double blow rocked Newcastle's summer, following on from the previous summer's transfer saga involving Alexander Isak.

Joelinton - who has stepped into a leadership role after his friend's departure, being named vice captain to new skipper Dan Burn - says he won't be shedding any tears after the departures of both men.

‌



Joelinton told Chronicle Live: "It's never time to cry, because football always moves forward. Like I say about Eddie, Bruno is the same, a great person for Newcastle United who has left the club.

"What Bruno did here was amazing, and we have to remember that. He always gave his best for the club and respected everybody. We have to remember him as a great player - because he was.

"We wish him all the best, but football doesn't stop, players come and go, coaches come and go, the only thing that is permanent is the fans and the club. We always move forward, we have had good players, and we have signed good players that we now hope can deliver great things for the club in the years ahead."

Sports.title: Teenager denies sending racist message to Lioness star Jess Carter during Euros
Sports.content:
Teenager denies sending racist message to Lioness star Jess Carter during Euros

Aaryan Aggarwal, 19, denied sending a racist message to England footballer Jess Carter during last year's Women's European Championship

View Image Footballer Jess Carter allegedly received a racist message on Instagram (Image: PA)

A teenager has denied sending a racist message to England footballer Jess Carter on Instagram.

Aaryan Aggarwal, 19, appeared at Chelmsford Magistrates' Court on Wednesday charged with sending a message over a public network that was offensive, indecent, obscene or menacing.

Prosecutor Grace Court told the hearing that Carter received the message on July 17, 2025 - the day on which England beat Sweden in their quarter-final at the UEFA Women's European Championship.

Court said the message read "well done, stupid ugly" - before using a racial slur.

The defendant, of Chigwell in Essex, pleaded not guilty to the offence during Wednesday’s hearing.

A trial date was fixed for October 3 next year at Cambridge Magistrates' Court.

Sports.title: Six Arsenal stars set for extra training with Mikel Arteta during international break
Sports.content:
Six Arsenal stars set for extra training with Mikel Arteta during international break

Mikel Arteta is set to be without an array of his Arsenal stars, with the international break having brought Premier League action to a halt but the Gunners’ boss is still keen to get out on the training pitch

View 2 Images Mikel Arteta is set to get back on the training pitch (Image: Getty Images)

Mikel Arteta will be putting Arsenal’s non-internationals to work over the next few weeks as he aims to make the most of the enforced break.

‌



Premier League action has been brought to a pause due to the first international break of the campaign. And it might have come at the best possible time for Mikel Arteta and his staff following the 3-0 defeat to Brighton in their most recent outing.

‌



In an ideal world, Arteta would have all of his players available to find out exactly what went wrong at the Amex. Unfortunately, a whole array of stars have flown away to all corners of the globe after getting call-ups from their national teams.

‌



But that does not mean that Arteta will not be on the training pitch over the coming weeks. Ben White is set to remain with Arsenal for the international break after an intriguing turn of events.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



He was not originally called into the England squad, albeit Thomas Tuchel did confirm that he wanted to work with the defender. White was then forced out through injury and will now rest but could potentially train under Arteta.

Fellow defender Piero Hincapie has also been nursing a small groin issue and has been left out of the Ecuador squad as a consequence. After being named on the bench against Brighton, he could complete an individual training plan over the coming weeks.

Arteta could also have a couple of goalkeepers to call upon throughout the international break. Illan Meslier is set to be available, while Kepa has not been called up by Spain - albeit he was spotted leaving the Amex alongside David Raya, Mikel Merino and Martin Zubimendi so could opt for a return to his homeland over the break.

‌



The final player who Arteta could look to work with is Noni Madueke. Despite having gone to the World Cup, the wideman was not selected for Tuchel in his latest camp so will be aiming to sharpen up over the coming weeks.

View 2 Images Ben White and Noni Madueke are set to stay in North London (Image: Getty Images)

There is a question mark over the availability of Kai Havertz. The forward was named in Jurgen Klopp’s first Germany squad but the ex-Liverpool boss has been somewhat unconventional and named two separate selections.

‌



Havertz is one of those who will drop out for the second round of fixtures, albeit it remains to be seen whether he opts to return to North London or not. If he does, Havertz would be another first-team star available for training.

Speaking about the international break before the defeat at Brighton, Mikel Arteta said: “Let's see, it's something that we'll have to experience. As you've seen, different national teams, different managers have taken different approaches in terms of the numbers that they have put in the squad.

“So it's going to be really important to have good communication with them so they understand where our players are, what we expect, what they expect as well. And work together, that's the best way always.”

Sports.title: Micah Richards doubles down on plans to quit punditry as he names successor
Sports.content:
Micah Richards doubles down on plans to quit punditry as he names successor

Micah Richards has reinforced his plans to give up punditry but the Sky Sports and BBC favourite has now named his heir apparent

View 3 Images Micah Richards has doubled down on his plan to quit being a pundit (Image: Getty)

Micah Richards is standing firm on giving up punditry in 2034. And the 38-year-old believes current Tottenham star James Maddison could be the one to fill his chair.

‌



After hanging up his boots in 2019, following a 14-year playing career which featured spells with Manchester City, Fiorentina and Aston Villa, Richards picked up the microphone.

‌



The 13-cap England star became an instant hit, making his broadcasting debut for Sky Sports and becoming a staple on the BBC, providing analysis on Match of the Day, Final Score and Radio 5 Live.

‌



He was front and centre at the World Cup in the summer for the Beeb, analysing the final alongside former team-mates Wayne Rooney and Joe Hart. Richards also makes up one-quarter of the revered CBS Sports Golazo team, covering European football with host Kate Scott, Jamie Carragher and Thierry Henry.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Micah Richards opens up about dad's death and tough decision to carry on with live BBC punditry READ MORE :

Roy Keane refuses to apologise as Andy Robertson tells Man Utd icon he went too far READ MORE :

Yet for all his popularity, Richards does not envisage himself staying in the punditry game for long. In July, he put a specific timeframe on when he'll step away. Now, he's dug his heels in and has even gone so far as to name Maddison and Everton star Jack Grealish as two who could step in to succeed him after they call it quits.

‌



View 3 Images Richards thinks Maddison could be the next in line once he retires (Image: Getty)

Speaking to The Telegraph two months ago, Richards said that he would be out of mainstream media by the time he is 46. He announced that he would not work beyond the 2034 World Cup and has informed Sky Sports, the BBC and CBS of this.

In an interview with The Times this week, Richards was resolute, confirming that this is still very much the case and explaining his decision. He said: "By then I'll have been 15 years a player and 15 years a pundit and what more could I ask for?

‌



"So it'll be, 'What can I give back to the game?' I don't want to work past my sell-by date. Fifteen years, whether you like me or hate me, that's enough time to get across my point. There'll be someone else on the sofa by then. [Jack] Grealish . . . or [James] Maddison. Definitely Maddison. He's a natural on TV. He's the next one."

Spurs midfielder Maddison has frequently appeared on Sky Sports, including a player-guest appearance on Monday Night Football in 2025. He has been hailed as charismatic and honest in these instances, much like the authentic Grealish.

Continuing about his punditry journey, Richards recalled how co-star and Arsenal legend Henry helped him analyse games at a new level. He said: "I remember having a chat with Thierry Henry.

‌



View 3 Images The ex-Man City defender credits Henry with helping him grow as an analyst (Image: Getty)

"He said, 'You've got a good football brain, but all my friends text me about is how much of a great personality you are.' Thierry said at some point there's got to be a switch, because when you talk about football, it was, 'I like what you're talking about, but we don't hear it enough.'

"I was taken aback. So I went to his house and we started watching games and he just tapped me like that [on the shoulder]. It was so patronising!

Article continues below

"'What do you see there?' 'Well, I see the defender.' He said, 'Yeah, but what are they trying to do? What is the plan? What is this tactic against that tactic?'

"It opened my eyes. I knew the stuff. But this was him unlocking it. I just look at the game completely different now."

Sports.title: Man Utd announce record revenues but debt rises as Old Trafford grass goes on sale for £125!
Sports.content:
Man Utd announce record revenues but debt rises as Old Trafford grass goes on sale for £125!

Manchester United have announced their fourth quarter and full year fiscal 2026 results with the Reds recording record revenues after Sir Jim Ratcliffe's cost-cutting measures

View 3 Images Manchester United have announced their latest financial results (Image: Bo Amstrup/EPA/Shutterstock)

Manchester United recorded record revenues in their latest financial results. United say that the club continue to benefit from Sir Jim Ratcliffe's operating cost and headcount reductions, alongside the improved third-place Premier League finish during the 2025/26 season.

‌



Despite recording a full year operating profit of £22.6million, United once again posted an overall loss for the year of £43m, compared to £33m the year before.

‌



United's revenue, however, rose by 1.7 per cent compared to 2024/25, which the club believe shows they are on the right track given they had no European football and no training kit sponsor in place. In total, United posted record revenues of £677.6m, up from £666.5m in the previous full year.

‌



The club feel that more "financial discipline" is needed to stabilise the business after they recorded a loss. United have said that the sacking of Ruben Amorim earlier this year contributed to losses. However, the latest results reveal that the departure of Amorim and his staff cost just £8.2m, which is significantly less than the £36.6m United forked out after firing staff, including his predecessor Erik ten Hag, last season.

Roy Keane points finger after JJ Gabriel quit bombshell with reminder about Man United starlet READ MORE :

Debt levels at United, meanwhile, are also still rising, though it is part down to the change in interest rates and the refinancing of some bonds in June of this year.

United believe "non-current borrowings" now stand at £577.6m, up from £471.9m last year. The Reds also have a revolving credit facility, which is similar to a credit card, and that stood at £100m at the end of June 2026.

‌



Meanwhile, United's matchday income dropped by £6.8m, which is no surprise given the Reds had 10 fewer games at Old Trafford last season, due to no European football and being knocked out of the FA Cup and Carabao Cup at the first hurdle.

Once more, United's wage bill fell, down to £302m, and United said that was "primarily due to changes in the make-up of the men’s first team squad, combined with savings associated with headcount reduction programs implemented over the previous two fiscal years."

View 3 Images Manchester United CEO Omar Berrada revelaed record revenues (Image: Getty)

‌



United Chief Executive Officer Omar Berrada said: "We are pleased to have secured record revenues and adjusted EBITDA which demonstrates the underlying strength of our business, particularly in a season without European football. This shows the direct impact of the work we have been doing over the past two years.

"It also proves Manchester United's enduring popularity and commercial strength. While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable.

"With that financial sustainability in mind, we have strengthened both our men’s and women’s teams during the summer window and our men’s team has seen the return of Champions League football to Old Trafford.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

"We have also strengthened commercially and have welcomed Betway as our new Training Kit partner and SumUp as our new Sleeve partner; two excellent organisations which we are delighted to be working with, alongside our kit supplier, adidas and front of shirt partner, Snapdragon.

"Our other main area of focus is our plan to develop a new 100,000-seater stadium. We have now completed the major milestone of securing the land which will form part of the proposed location of the new stadium."

‌



Alongside this, United laid a new pitch at Old Trafford for the first time in 14 years in the summer, and the old surface has been cut into 7cm x 7cm squares. Those have been put in acrylic cubes and sent out to supporters who want them in a smart black casing for £125 each.

View 3 Images Manchester United are selling chunks of the Old Trafford grass (Image: UtdDistrict/X)

"Take home a piece of Old Trafford with this official turf cube, perfect for fans who want a keepsake from one of the most famous pitches in the world. Carefully preserved, this piece of turf makes a priceless memento of iconic games played at home and keeps the memories of match days alive.

‌



"Perfect for gifting to passionate Reds, this turf cube makes a great addition to desks or can be displayed in a cabinet with other Manchester United collectables."

United believe the purchasable turf is a 'one-in-a-lifetime' item for fans, with club members and season ticket holders offered access before others in an email.

The Red Devils have made a disappointing start to the 2026/27 season. They have won just one of their opening five Premier League matches, drawing two and losing two. United made a winning start to life back in the Champions League by thrashing Sabah 4-0 but they were dumped out of the Carabao Cup by Brighton.

Sports.title: Wayne Rooney takes aim at Man Utd board for 'weak' decision and reveals manager hope
Sports.content:
Wayne Rooney takes aim at Man Utd board for 'weak' decision and reveals manager hope

Wayne Rooney hopes Michael Carrick can turn Manchester United's fortunes around but says the squad is 'a bit weak' following the transfer window

View 2 Images Wayne Rooney speaks on Stick to United (Image: Stick to United)

Wayne Rooney believes recruitment figures have let down Michael Carrick and played a role in Manchester United's difficult start to the season. However, the iconic former Red Devils striker is confident that his former teammate can turn things around.

‌



They sit in the bottom half of the table at the first international break of the season after one win in their opening five Premier League matches. They are winless in their last four and Matheus Cunha's deflected effort spared increased scrutiny as United picked up a point at Fulham on Sunday.

‌



Pressure has begun to mount on the United head coach, despite only being handed the reins on a permanent basis in the summer. Rooney has expressed his desire to see Carrick spark an improvement after the break.

‌



He told talkSPORT: "He [Carrick] knows what's in for there and listen, you always want more as a manager, I'm sure he would have wanted more from the transfer window, but he's left with what he's left with.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



"I think the Premier League has got better, there's better teams in there. But if you don't win at Man United, or at any club, at the minute it's very tough, so I hope he turns it around."

United strengthened their squad during the summer transfer window, channelling the bulk of their expenditure into midfield reinforcements. Andrey Santos joined for £48million, potentially rising to £50m, from Premier League rivals Chelsea, while Youri Tielemans came in after his £35m release clause was activated.

Despite this, many felt that other areas of the United squad were left short, particularly in attack and defence. Rooney believes the recruitment team failed to adequately support the manager.

‌



He said: "There's always going to be pressure, Michael knows that. If you're not winning football games at Man United, then that pressure is there if you don't win one game.

View 2 Images Cunha was one of the additions to the United squad in the summer (Image: Getty Images)

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



"So, it hasn't been the ideal start to the season... there are certain things which I felt the club had to do before the window shut, in bringing players in... the squad is a bit weak.

"He's got to find a way to get more and the best out of these players to get up the table after this international break... I think the break has come at the right time.

"He's shown that he can get results out of this group of players. They have to get their head down and work and hopefully get some better results."

‌



Following the draw in West London, Carrick came out defiantly to rubbish reports of pressure mounting on his position in charge, after winning 12 of his 17 games last season. "I think that'll be a lot longer than one or two games of results," he said.

"In terms of future and ownership and how long I've got in the job, I'm not thinking 'how long have I got?' It's ridiculous to think that way in a position that I'm in.

"That's just not on the radar. It's two or three games that we haven't had certain results, and two or three games too many because I really hate losing. But that doesn't mean that the world caves in."

Sports.title: The best manager in international football? Have your say ahead of Jurgen Klopp debut
Sports.content:
The best manager in international football? Have your say ahead of Jurgen Klopp debut

Jurgen Klopp and Zinedine Zidane will begin their spells in international management with Germany and France respectively as the quality of bosses continues to rise

View 5 Images Jurgen Klopp is back in management and will lead Germany (Image: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto/Allstar via Getty Images)

It takes a unique kind of boss to excel on the international stage, and very often the best managers in the world have chosen the club game as their traditional home.

‌



But with the first international break upon us we've got some landmark moments coming up, notably Jurgen Klopp's debut as Germany boss. It could be a match made in heaven and the former Liverpool boss is among the biggest names to enter the international arena in recent years.

‌



He'll encounter new challenges, the obvious one being it tests individuals and demands that they work with what they've got. There's no transfer window to fill holes. Time to get pragmatic.

‌



But often the countries who have managed to lure the biggest names into the dugout have prospered as a result. Spain are the only side in the modern era to win three international tournaments on the trot, largely overseen by a Champions League winner in Vicente Del Bosque.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



England felt for a long time that they had one of the best in the business in Thomas Tuchel, but that's been called into question over recent months.

The domestic game has paused for the first time this season with England facing world champions Spain this weekend at Wembley. The Spanish have excelled with their man, Luis de la Fuente, who would've been in no one's conversation as the world's best manager, and yet look what he's done.

So with that in mind, who really is the best manager in the international game? Is it the manager who's done it and won trophies? Or those who've conquered Europe with a heavyweight club. Have your say as we eye up the runners and riders.

‌



Thomas Tuchel

England's messiah, seen as the difference maker, and at times at the World Cup you definitely though "yeah this is why we hired him". The win over Mexico was a sensational backs against the wall job, an all-time great success, but then the Argentina game saw Tuchel come in for huge criticism.

View 5 Images Thomas Tuchel led England to the last four of the World Cup (Image: Michael Regan - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

His club exploits mark him out as one of the best around, winning the Champions League with Chelsea in 2021, and his defensive system does lend itself to the international game. Tuchel doesn't lack for charisma and whilst his CV is better than most, he does have to again prove himself in light of England's semi-final exit.

‌



Jurgen Klopp

Those in his homeland have wanted the former Borussia Dortmund boss to take charge of Germany for years. This is his first managerial gig post Liverpool, where he showed himself to be one of the world's elite managers as he battled it out with Pep Guardiola.

Of course, as mentioned earlier, Klopp cannot go into the market and land the players that suit the style of play that has served him well previously. But as the German showed at Liverpool, he didn't need long and was able to secure statement results within weeks of arriving, when he had to work with what he inherited. Germany don't lack quality, even if they aren't the heavyweights they once were.

View 5 Images Luis de la Fuente is a World Cup winner (Image: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images)

‌



Luis de la Fuente

Going by the fact that only three men in history have won the World Cup and the Euros back-to-back, its clearly a tough task. De la Fuente joined greats Vicente Del Bosque and Helmut Schon by winning the two tournaments in the space of two years, knocking over some serious teams and managers along the way.

By no means a man in demand before his Spanish exploits, he comes across as the perfect manager for international football. His progression through the age grades in Spain has made him the perfect man to lean into their possession-based DNA. He's brilliantly managed the emergence of Lamine Yamal and always looks like a man in total control.

Carlo Ancelotti

Don Carlo decided to throw himself into international management for the first time recently. His club legacy is secured and he's taken on a glamour job with Brazil, even if the South Americans aren't perhaps the force of old. Their wait for a World Cup is now up to 24 years and Ancelotti is the best manager they've had since that success in 2002.

‌



View 5 Images Carlo Ancelotti will have been disappointed with his first effort at an international tournament (Image: Europa Press Sports/Europa Press via Getty Images)

However a last 16 exit at the hands of Norway suggests its not as easy as it may sometimes look, even for Ancelotti, who was ultimately undone by Erling Haaland and Stale Solbakken, a man who lasted 30 games at Wolves.

Ancelotti's greatest assets have always been working with what he's got, creating the right environment and a system that lends itself to the players he has at his disposal. He's no clear managerial DNA, but whatever he's done has worked for two plus decades.

‌



Lionel Scaloni

Another man, like De la Fuente, who would have had no major clubs chasing his signature before his Argentina exploits, and yet he won three international tournaments on the trot, reaching four finals. Now without Lionel Messi, we may well see what he is actually made of.

But plenty of managers have had the greatest player of all time, but been unable to create the perfect environment for him. Scaloni did exactly that, and has certainly leant into those South American dark arts, all while sprinkling it with that Argentine quality.

View 5 Images Roberto Mancini led Italy to Euro 2020 glory (Image: UEFA via Getty Images)

‌



Roberto Mancini

Maybe not considered among the top bracket post his Manchester City stint, but the manner in which he took Italy to the Euro 2020 title underlined his quality. He ultimately proved he was a level, at least, above Gareth Southgate as he turned that final on its head to secure glory for the Azzurri.

That was also an Italy team far from lacking in individual quality, none of their outfield players at least would go near winning individual accolades, bar perhaps Jorginho at the time. Mancini's ability to rally the collective and create a team was truly outstanding, and now he'll have another bite at the cherry.

Zinedine Zidane

New to the fray like Klopp, but only Ancelotti has more Champions League crowns than the Frenchman, who has been desperate to get his hands on the Les Blues gig for years. His gravitas and stature has always made commanding a dressing room his greatest asset. When you're arguably the don in a Real Madrid changing room, you know you're a big deal.

‌



That aura will continue to stand him in good stead when he takes charge of France, who with one major honour in a decade-long golden generation, may feel slightly shortchanged. The question against Zizou is he's always had elite Real starts to work with, out of that environment, how will he go? It must be said, he's still got his fair share of elite players.
