World.title: Liberia: Government, LSEZA Discuss Investment and Job Creation Agenda
World.content:
Monrovia – The government is seeking closer collaboration with the Liberia Special Economic Zones Authority (LSEZA) as it continues efforts to attract investment, promote industrial development, and create jobs through special economic zones.

The focus emerged during a meeting between Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Samuel Stevquoah and the leadership of LSEZA, followed by a tour of the Authority’s facilities.

The engagement provided an opportunity for the minister to receive an update on LSEZA’s ongoing activities and developments and to discuss the Authority’s role in supporting the government’s broader economic transformation agenda.

LSEZA Executive Chairman Prince Wreh, members of the Board and senior management briefed Stevquoah on the Authority’s work and efforts to create an environment that can support investment and business growth.

The discussions also highlighted the need for continued coordination between the government and LSEZA as the Authority works to develop and promote special economic zones as platforms for investment, industrial activity and employment.

Members of the LSEZA Board expressed appreciation for the engagement and welcomed continued government support as they provide strategic oversight and work with management to advance the Authority’s mandate.

Stevquoah subsequently toured the facility, where he was briefed on ongoing developments and activities.

At the close of the engagement, LSEZA Director of Administration Hattie Wureh Hunder presented the minister with customized LSEZA paraphernalia and a commemorative lapel.

The engagement comes as the government continues to emphasize investment, industrialization and job creation as key components of its economic transformation agenda.

World.title: Liberia: Agriculture Ministry Disputes Its Budget Line as Cattle Deaths Mount
World.content:
Monrovia – Grand Kru County has not had a working cattle herd in a generation. Its old county ranch is mostly memory now — cleared pasture reclaiming itself, pens that haven’t held an animal in years. So, when the Ministry of Agriculture said 200 Muturu cows were coming, and that this southeastern county would be first in line, it read to many there as more than a delivery of livestock. It read as a promise that the ranch, and the income it once supported, might come back to life.

Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]@frontpageafricaonline.com

That promise is now tangled in a dispute over money — one playing out not between the ministry and its critics on the ground, but between the Ministry of Agriculture and the national government’s own budget book.

The ministry’s explanation

Reached for comment, the Ministry of Agriculture pushed back, point by point, against the budget figures FrontPageAfrica had put to it.

In a written response, the ministry said the $3 million line item widely cited from Annex 7 of the National Budget’s ArcelorMittal Liberia Signature Bonus Allocation does not appear anywhere in its approved books.

According to the ministry, its full FY2026 appropriation totals $10,495,326 — $3,477,083 in basic salaries, $1,812,159 in goods and services, and $5,150,500 in government-funded Public Sector Investment Program (PSIP) spending. That PSIP allocation splits into two sub-projects: $3.2 million for Food and Cash Crop Production Value Chain, and $1.95 million for Livestock and Poultry Value Chain Production.

The ministry said the supplemental appropriation it actually received from the $200 million ArcelorMittal signature bonus, after the FY2026 budget recast, was just $358,078 — far short of the $4.5 million ($3 million for livestock, $1.5 million for general agriculture value chain) recorded against its name in Annex 7. “There was never $3 million allocated for ‘Support for livestock and Poultry value chain Production’ in the supplemental budget for MOA from the ArcelorMittal Liberia Signature Bonus,” the ministry wrote. The $200,000 spent on the 200 Muturu cattle, it said, came out of the ministry’s approved core PSIP budget — not the signature bonus at all.

The road to Grand Kru

Twenty-four of the thirty-five cows that set out for Grand Kru never made it. They went down along the way — worn out, the ministry says, by a long haul without enough food, the kind of overland journey that is hard on cattle even in the best conditions.

The supplier has admitted fault and promised replacements at no cost to the government. But no cost to the government is not the same as no cost at all: those were animals meant to found herds, calve, and carry families through lean seasons, and more than two out of every three in the first batch never got the chance.

That toll is far starker than the public was first told. The ministry’s own July 29 announcement, and a Facebook post cheering the program along, both mentioned the deaths only in passing — “some of the cows,” with no count attached. Behind that soft phrase were twenty-four animals a Grand Kru farmer will never see arrive.

What was announced

On July 29, 2026, the Ministry of Agriculture announced the arrival of the first 200 Muturu cattle, a purchase it said was budgeted at $200,000 — $1,000 per cow. Agriculture Minister Dr. J. Alexander Nuetah said the cattle would be distributed to farmers in Grand Kru County, alongside a government-funded rehabilitation of the county ranch under the Public Sector Investment Program (PSIP).

A Facebook page, Jallah TV, later ran a post defending the purchase against unnamed critics — “trashing the lies,” as its headline put it — confirming that of the first 47 cows to land, 12 went to the Central Agricultural Research Institute, and 35 were trucked toward Grand Kru, with some dying en route.

The post framed the losses as routine, noting the transporters had agreed to replace the dead animals, and closed by thanking the minister.

Two documents, two totals

The FY2026 National Budget itself is unambiguous on paper. Annex 7, titled “ArcelorMittal Liberia Signature Bonus Allocation,” lists under “Support to Agriculture Sector”: $1.5 million to the Ministry of Agriculture for “additional support to enhance Agriculture value chain,” and $3 million for “Support for Livestock and Poultry Value Chain Production” — a sector sub-total of $4.7 million once the Liberia Agricultural Commodity Regulatory Authority’s $200,000 line is added.

The ministry says that document does not match what it actually received: $358,078 in supplemental funding from the signature bonus, and nothing more. Neither the newspaper’s review of the published budget nor the ministry’s written response explains why a page of the national budget and the ministry charged with spending it describe two different sums for the same purpose. That discrepancy — not the price of a cow — is now the central open question.

The wider context

Independent reporting on the FY2026 budget adds useful background. The $200 million ArcelorMittal signature bonus — tied to the renewal of the company’s mineral development agreement — accounts for nearly 17 percent of total budget revenue and was described as fully allocated to development projects.

Economists quoted in that coverage warned that a significant share of the budget increase rests on this one-time payment, raising sustainability concerns, with one warning that Liberia will only move forward once it stops the money that is silently flowing backward. Separate analysis of the same budget found the Legislature’s allocation running nearly four times the national agriculture budget, even as hospitals report medicine shortages and schools remain dilapidated.

What still needs answering

The ministry has offered to share the FY2026 PSIP project document, procurement updates, cash plans, and related implementation records, an offer FrontPageAfrica intends to take up. Two questions remain unresolved: why the printed National Budget records $4.5 million in agriculture supplemental funding that the ministry says never existed, and what portion of the $1.95 million core PSIP livestock line — along with the $3.2 million food and cash-crop line — has actually been disbursed as of September 2026, a question the ministry’s response did not directly address.

Why it matters

A government ministry publicly contradicting its own national budget document is, on its own, a story worth Liberians’ attention — whichever account turns out to be accurate, one official record is wrong. Add to that a cattle-import program whose first shipment lost nearly seven in ten animals before reaching the farmers it was meant to help, and the story stops being only about arithmetic. It becomes a question of whether a flagship livestock program was adequately planned, funded, and executed — regardless of which line item paid for it.

The ministry’s response, in full

The Ministry of Agriculture responded in writing to every question FrontPageAfrica put to it, and its full letter — including its rejection of the Annex 7 figures and its account of the cattle deaths — is also being published today.

The ministry says the FY2026 PSIP Livestock Production Project remains under implementation and that no completed audit yet covers it, but it has offered supporting project documentation to this newspaper ahead of further reporting.

For now, the arithmetic sits unresolved in Monrovia, argued over in letters between a newsroom and a ministry. In Grand Kru, the question is simpler and more immediate: how many of the promised 200 cows will actually arrive, healthy, and put to work on pastures that have waited years for them.

World.title: Liberia: How a Failed Harvest Locked an Entire Generation Out of School in Bong County
World.content:
There is a bitter symmetry to this image that is hard to ignore. The very resource being mobilized to save the school is, in the meantime, occupying and potentially damaging the space that school needs to function. Residents watching this unfold are left with a daily, physical reminder of the gap between their aspirations for their children and the economic reality constraining them — a school building slowly becoming indistinguishable from a warehouse, its educational purpose paused indefinitely while it earns its keep as storage space instead.

Kpolokplah Public School relied entirely on volunteer teachers since the government never assigned staff, leaving the PTA to fund salaries through farming and charcoal sales. A failed harvest cut this income, teachers went unpaid for six months, and struck—closing the school. Government response has focused elsewhere, leaving the crisis unresolved.

DISTRICT TWO, BONG COUNTY – In Kpolokplah Town, deep in Bong County District Two, mornings no longer begin with the shuffle of small feet down dirt paths toward a schoolhouse. There is no morning assembly, no recitation of lessons drifting from open windows, no chalk dust settling on wooden desks. Instead, an entire generation of children sits at home, their school year suspended not by war, not by disaster, but by a debt of a few thousand Liberian dollars that a struggling farming community simply cannot pay.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Nearly a month after schools reopened across Liberia for the 2026/2027 academic year, Kpolokplah Public School remains locked in limbo — a casualty not of policy failure alone, but of a bad harvest, a broken funding model, and a government that, by the community’s own account, has left it to fend for itself.

When Volunteers Become the Whole System

To understand how one poor farming season could shutter an entire school, one must first understand what kept that school running in the first place. Kpolokplah Public School, principal Jeremiah D. Yarkpawolo revealed, has no government-assigned teachers at all. Every single instructor who has ever stood before its students in recent memory has been a volunteer — recruited, retained, and paid not by the Ministry of Education, but by the community’s own Parent-Teacher Association.

This is a detail easy to skim past but impossible to overstate. In towns with even a partial complement of government teachers, a dispute with volunteer staff might cause disruption, but rarely total closure.

In Kpolokplah, there was no fallback plan, because there was no government presence to fall back on. The PTA was not merely supplementing the school’s teaching staff — it was the entire staffing infrastructure, quietly substituting for a state responsibility that never arrived. When that substitute system broke down, there was nothing behind it to catch the fall.

The Arithmetic of Desperation

The economics behind the crisis are almost painfully modest. According to David Gorlormator, head of the Parent-Teacher Association, each of the four volunteer teachers is owed just LD$5,000 a month for six months — a sum that would draw little notice in a national budget but has proven beyond the reach of a community whose income depends entirely on unpredictable harvests and the sale of charcoal burned from their own forests.

Gorlormator’s account is one of a community trying, and failing, to outrun its own poverty. Parents and PTA members turned to farming, charcoal-making, and whatever small trade they could manage, funneling proceeds toward teacher salaries in what amounted to a grassroots, informal payroll system. It worked, imperfectly, for a time. But this year’s farming season faltered, yields dropped, and the trickle of income the PTA depended on dried up along with it. What emerges is not a story of mismanagement or unwillingness to pay, but one of a community whose entire financial safety net for education was tied to the whims of rainfall and soil — a safety net that has now visibly frayed.

Four Teachers, One Ultimatum

For the four volunteer teachers at the center of this dispute, patience has run out. Principal Yarkpawolo says they have made their position unmistakably clear that no back pay, no classroom. It is a stance that is difficult to fault. These are people who gave their labor, month after month, to a community that could not always guarantee they would be compensated for it — and who now find themselves being asked to continue that arrangement indefinitely, with no resolution in sight.

Their refusal is not simply the withholding of labor; it is the collapse of the only mechanism keeping the lights on, so to speak, at Kpolokplah Public School. And because that mechanism was never backed by any parallel government staffing, its failure has not dented the school’s operations — it has ended them entirely, at least for now.

From Classroom to Charcoal Depot

Nowhere is the toll of this standoff more visible than inside the school itself. With no students and no teachers, the physical building has quietly taken on a new identity, a storage site for charcoal, the same commodity residents are burning and selling in a desperate bid to raise the money needed to reopen the school. The classrooms meant to hold desks, chalkboards, and children now hold sacks of fuel bound for market.

There is a bitter symmetry to this image that is hard to ignore. The very resource being mobilized to save the school is, in the meantime, occupying and potentially damaging the space that school needs to function. Residents watching this unfold are left with a daily, physical reminder of the gap between their aspirations for their children and the economic reality constraining them — a school building slowly becoming indistinguishable from a warehouse, its educational purpose paused indefinitely while it earns its keep as storage space instead

There is a bitter symmetry to this image that is hard to ignore. The very resource being mobilized to save the school is, in the meantime, occupying and potentially damaging the space that school needs to function. Residents watching this unfold are left with a daily, physical reminder of the gap between their aspirations for their children and the economic reality constraining them — a school building slowly becoming indistinguishable from a warehouse, its educational purpose paused indefinitely while it earns its keep as storage space instead.

A Town That Has Already Buried Too Much

Kpolokplah’s current struggles do not exist in isolation from its past. This is a town that carries the weight of Liberia’s civil war within its history, having been the site where several residents were killed during the 1994 massacre — one of many dark chapters etched into Bong County’s collective memory. For a community that has already endured such loss, the slow erosion of its children’s access to education represents not just a present-day crisis, but another entry in a long history of hardship that seems to have outlasted the war itself.

Residents, understandably, see the school closure as part of a broader pattern — one in which promises of post-conflict rebuilding and development have been slow to reach communities like theirs, leaving basic services like education perpetually just out of reach.

A Lawmaker’s Balancing Act

The predicament in Kpolokplah has not gone entirely unnoticed at the political level. Hon. James M. Kolleh, Representative for Bong County Electoral District 2, has publicly acknowledged the education and water challenges facing communities under his watch, responding to reports that span not just Kpolokplah but other struggling schools such as Barsee Kpangbai Public School in Blemeyea, which reportedly operates with just two teachers for its entire student body.

In Kpolokplah, there was no fallback plan, because there was no government presence to fall back on. The PTA was not merely supplementing the school’s teaching staff — it was the entire staffing infrastructure, quietly substituting for a state responsibility that never arrived. When that substitute system broke down, there was nothing behind it to catch the fall.

Rep. Kolleh’s response has focused heavily on Barsee Kpangbai, where he has pledged to work toward deploying two additional teachers, while more broadly promising to assess the needs of other schools across the district — a commitment that, for now, leaves Kpolokplah’s specific staffing vacuum without a direct answer.

He pointed to past efforts, including last year’s distribution of 5,000 armchairs to area schools, and indicated plans to expand on that furniture initiative this year. Whether

such efforts will translate into the one thing Kpolokplah actually needs — salaried government teachers — remains an open question.

On water access, another pressing concern in the district, Rep. Kolleh was more specific about Kpolokplah itself, confirming that the town is slated to benefit from ongoing water projects and promising, in the interim, to repair the community’s existing hand pump. He framed his broader approach as one of continued responsiveness to constituent needs, describing service to the district as central to his mandate as its elected representative.

Waiting for a Callback

What remains missing from this story is an official accounting from the very body responsible for staffing and overseeing public education in the county. FrontPage Africa contacted County Education Officer David Boakai, who answered the call and indicated he would follow up with a fuller response. That callback never came before publication.

In its absence, silence from the Ministry of Education’s local representative stands in stark contrast to the noise Kpolokplah’s crisis has already generated — a community publicly airing its struggle, a lawmaker publicly responding to it, and, at the center of it all, a county education office that has, for now, said nothing at all. For the children of Kpolokplah, still waiting for a return to their classrooms, that silence may prove just as costly as the unpaid wages that emptied them in the first place.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Prepares to Take Cybercrime Law Fight to Supreme Court After Wrato Release
World.content:
Monrovia-The release of political commentator Jerry Nyantee Wrato from police custody has opened a new and potentially consequential legal battle over Liberia’s recently enacted Cybercrime Law, with the Congress for Democratic Change(CDC) announcing plans to ask the Supreme Court to determine whether portions of the law are consistent with the Constitution.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Lenn Eugene Nagbe, Chief of Office Staff to former President George Manneh Weah said Tuesday, September 22 that the CDC’s Executive Committee had instructed its lawyers to institute proceedings before the Supreme Court challenging the constitutionality of the law.

Nagbe said the party’s decision goes beyond Wrato’s individual case, arguing that the controversy raises broader questions about the limits of political expression, criticism of public officials and the government’s authority to prosecute speech disseminated through digital platforms.

“It is not just about Jerry Wrato; it is about a threat to our democracy,” Nagbe said, announcing the party’s intention to challenge the law.

He said the CDC’s legal team would seek to have the Cybercrime Law declared unconstitutional, describing it as legislation that, in the party’s view, could be used to suppress political expression.

The announcement came hours after Criminal Court “B” of the First Judicial Circuit ordered Wrato released from police custody following a habeas corpus petition filed by his lawyer, Cllr. Garrison Doldeh Yealue Jr.

Judge Pape Suah issued the writ Tuesday, September 22, directing that Wrato be released from further police custody and turned over to the Sheriff of the court.

The order followed a challenge to Wrato’s continued detention after police announced that they had completed their investigation and intended to prosecute him on four alleged violations of Liberia’s Cybercrime Act of 2025.

Wrato’s detention followed the circulation of artificial intelligence-generated images and videos appearing to portray Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung in a derogatory manner.

The material surfaced amid controversy over reports concerning Koung’s security screening at Brussels Airport, reports the Vice President has denied. Police subsequently investigated the circulation of the manipulated content under the Cybercrime Act.

But the case took a different turn after Koung publicly appealed for Wrato’s release, indicating that he did not wish to pursue criminal action against him over the material. Police Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman nevertheless maintained that the matter could not be resolved solely based on the Vice President’s wishes.

In a September 21 communication to Vice President Koung, Coleman said the Liberia National Police had a statutory obligation to investigate suspected criminal conduct and had resolved to proceed against Wrato.

Police identified four alleged offenses, misuse of devices, cyberstalking, distribution of data messages that incite damage to property or violence, and distribution of harmful data messages.

The offenses were cited under Sections 10.1, 15.1, 18.1 and 19.1 of the Cybercrime Act. Coleman stressed that forwarding Wrato to court would not amount to a finding of guilt and that the accused would retain the presumption of innocence and other constitutional protections.

CDC Challenges the Law

Nagbe, however, said the CDC considers the detention a violation of Wrato’s constitutional rights. He said the party assembled a team of lawyers to defend what it described as the right to political expression and fair treatment under the law.

“The CDC hired a team of lawyers that advocate for fair play, for freedom of political expression,” Nagbe said. According to him, the lawyers viewed Wrato’s detention from Thursday, September 17, through Tuesday, September 22, as unlawful and moved quickly to challenge it through habeas corpus proceedings. The petition relied on Article 21(f) of the 1986 Constitution and provisions of Liberia’s Civil Procedure Law governing habeas corpus.

The court subsequently ordered Wrato’s release. The case is expected to return to court on Thursday, September 24, when further proceedings are scheduled.

Where Does Political Speech End, and Cybercrime Begin?

At the heart of the emerging legal dispute is a difficult concern on how far the state can go in regulating political expression when that expression is delivered through digital platforms. Nagbe argued that Liberians have a constitutional right to criticize and even make fun of politicians, particularly those who voluntarily enter public life.

“If you do not want anyone to talk about you, don’t get in the political space,” he said.

But the police position presents a different legal question as to whether digital material that allegedly crosses into cyberstalking, incitement, harmful communications or other conduct specifically prohibited by law can be treated simply as political speech.

That question has not been finally determined in Wrato’s case. The police have maintained that their investigation is based on alleged criminal conduct rather than the political identity of the person involved. Wrato, meanwhile, remains presumed innocent unless and until a court of competent jurisdiction determines otherwise.

The habeas corpus ruling itself addresses Wrato’s detention; it does not, on its face, constitute a final judicial determination that the Cybercrime Act is unconstitutional or that the underlying allegations against him are without legal merit.

A Bigger Legal Test Ahead

The CDC’s planned Supreme Court action could therefore move the controversy beyond Wrato’s individual detention and into a broader constitutional examination of Liberia’s cybercrime framework.

Such proceedings could require the Supreme Court to examine the relationship between statutory restrictions on digital communications and constitutional guarantees relating to freedom of speech, expression and political participation.

For the CDC, Nagbe said, the objective is clear, to challenge what the party considers an unconstitutional restriction on political expression.

“We will render the Cyber Crime Law unconstitutional,” he declared. Whether the Supreme Court ultimately accepts that argument, and, if so, how it interprets the contested provisions, will depend on the legal challenge, the provisions placed before the Court and the constitutional questions the justices are asked to determine.

For now, Wrato is out of police custody, the police say prosecution remains warranted, and the CDC is preparing to take the broader constitutional fight to Liberia’s highest court. The next courtroom appearance on September 24 could provide the first indication of how the dispute over Wrato’s detention will proceed, even as a separate constitutional battle over Liberia’s Cybercrime Law begins to take shape.

World.title: Liberia: Chinese Nationals “Brutalize” Liberian Employee as Victim Alarms Over Selective Justice, Illegal Dismissal
World.content:
The accused and the victim

MONROVIA – The Ministry of Labour has launched a probe into reports of an alleged assault on a Liberian worker by two Chinese nationals in Congo Town, outside Monrovia.

By Obediah Johnson

Victim Francis Flomo was allegedly assaulted by his bosses, one Mr. Liu and another unidentified Chinese national at a local Chinese restaurant O’Cake located adjacent the Giant Gym in Congo Town, outside Monrovia.

In a detailed report submitted to the Ministry of Labour, a copy which is in the possession of Frontpage Africa, victim Francis was physically attacked and assaulted by his bosses for allegedly playing with his phone during working hours.

The report claimed that the alleged perpetrators used steel and stick to physically assault defenseless victim Francis.

Police Intervention

Following the alleged assault, police officers riding a motorbike while on their regular patrol were requested by other aggrieved employees to arrest the situation. According to the report, the LNP officers later took the victim and the accused to the Palace Police Station in Swankamore Community, Oldest Congo Town, around the SKD Boulevard Junction, outside Monrovia.

It added that while at the police station, several unidentified Chinese nationals stormed the area with another police officer. “Shortly after, the officer at the Charge of Quarters who was investigating the case allegedly changed his approach. Instead of treating Francis Flomo as a victim of assault, he charged all three persons — the two Chinese nationals AND the young Liberian Francis Flomo — for “Disorderly Conduct” and effectively threw the case out.”

The report maintained that victim Francis suffered a swollened hand as a result of the assault. It disclosed that the victim was immediately sacked by his Chinese bosses immediately after the case was threw out by the police.

It noted that the victim bosses also refused to pay his one month salary. “The central question this incident leaves is: How can two men jump on a defenseless young boy, beat him with objects, and then the victim himself is charged for disorderly conduct by the police?,” it stated.

The report divulged that the incident points to the abuse and exploitation of a Liberian employee by his foreign bosses in Liberia

It added that the situation also denies the victim the payment of his fair wage and a compromised justice system in the Liberian society.

Meanwhile, the victim is calling on government to investigate the alleged use of influence at the police station to turn a clear assault case into a disorderly conduct charge, thereby denying the victim justice.

“The family and community are now calling for a proper investigation into the matter by the Liberia National Police Professional Standards Division and the Ministry of Labour.”

Labour Inspector General Mr. John O. F. Kangbah reportedly led a team of LNP officers at the restaurant late Tuesday afternoon and requested the management to produce the accused Chinese nationals.

But the management reportedly failed to produce the accused. However, the Labour Inspector promised to shutdown the Chinese restaurant if management fails to produce the accused today Wednesday, September 23.

World.title: Head Of Female Lawmakers Craves Pathway For Cordial Relations With Legislative Reporters As Chambers Near Return
World.content:
Capitol Building, Monrovia, September 22, 2026 – Liberian lawmakers are on the verge of returning from their regular annual constituency break, hence; female lawmakers under the banner Women’s Legislative Caucus of Liberia (WLCL) are chatting a new course for cooperation and collaboration with as with assigned legislative reporters.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

A Partnership That Respects All Parties

This relationship, the Chairperson, Women Legislative Caucus of Liberia (WLCL)Ellen Attoh-Wreh reckoned, would be void of compromise or influence of their professional duties as journalists, a one that promotes improve public outreach.

Speaking recently at a one-day National Media Roundtable held at the Capitol Building – seat of the Liberian Legislature, Rep. Attoh-Wreh, who represents the people of Margibi County Electoral District #3, emphasized that collaborating with the media is essential for effectively communicating their legislative efforts to citizens both locally and abroad.

The meeting was part of efforts to strengthen collaboration and build stronger working relationships between women legislators and media institutions across Liberia.

It was intended to create a platform for open dialogue between women legislators and media practitioners, improve media understanding of the mandate and work of the WLCL, and promote regular, accurate, balanced, and gender-sensitive reporting on women’s legislative leadership and contributions to national development.

This initiative is part of a broader $1 million project designed to empower women in government and enhance their visibility. Funding for these activities is provided by the IBSA partnership, which consists of India, Brazil, and South Africa, alongside support from UN Women.

Importance of Collaboration

The Women’s lawmaking group head stressed importance of strong collaboration between them and the media, especially journalists who follow their activities on Capitol Hill and in their respective constituencies.

This meeting, according to her, will foster a productive partnership with journalists to ensure that information regarding their work is shared accurately and widely.

“So, we count on the media a whole lot. We realize that it is about time we have this roundtable discussion so that we can understand ourselves – how you work, how we should work to strengthen this relationship. So, for and on behalf of the women lawmakers, I, as Chairperson, want to say thanks to all of you for honoring our invitation to be here, and thanks to our partners as well, UN Women,” added Rep. Attoh-Wreh.

Media Role in Growth

In remarks, the President of the Press Union of Liberia, Mr. Julius Kullie Kanubah, outlined the critical role of the media in promoting societal growth and ,as such, called on the women lawmakers to see the media as a strategic partner.

He told the gathering that the media is not just a messenger; rather, it is a powerful partner in shaping narratives, influencing public opinion, and holding institutions accountable.

To amplify women’s legislative leadership, Kanubah called for media partnerships to place key focus on three critical areas: creating visibility and representation, advocacy and agenda setting, and capacity building and collaboration.

“Ensure women legislators are consistently covered in news stories, debates, and policy discussions. Highlight their achievements, policy initiatives, and leadership roles, rather than reducing coverage to stereotypes or tokenism. Use editorial platforms to spotlight issues championed by women legislators – such as education, health, gender equality, and community development.

Position women’s legislative priorities as national priorities, shaping the public agenda. Strengthen partnerships between media councils, women’s caucus, and civil society to provide training in media engagement, storytelling, and digital advocacy,” the PUL President stated.

The Challenges

While suggesting the best solutions forward, Kanubah also recognizes the major challenges that journalists are confronted with, that leads to persistent gender bias in media coverage.

One of the challenges named is limited resources for women legislators to engage effectively with the media, the rise of disinformation and online harassment, which disproportionately targets women leaders.

The Way Forward

To overcome these challenges, the media community head proposed the establishment of joint media-legislative forums where women leaders and journalists engage directly on policy issues.

He also called for the creation of media monitoring mechanisms to track coverage of women legislators and hold media outlets accountable for bias.

“Investing in digital platforms and campaigns that amplify women’s voices and connect them with citizens, especially youth and rural communities.”

World.title: Liberian Contractors Urge Boakai to Expand Access to Public Works
World.content:
PAYNESVILLE— The Association of Liberian Construction Contractors is calling on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to intervene in what it describes as the growing exclusion of qualified Liberian-owned construction firms from public infrastructure projects.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

In an open letter dated September 21 and signed by its President, Kimberly K. Toure, the Association said Liberian contractors continue to face difficulties securing government contracts, despite investing heavily in registration, certification, equipment, personnel, and other requirements to remain eligible.

The Association expressed concern that public infrastructure opportunities are frequently awarded to foreign-owned companies, leaving qualified local firms with limited access to projects they have the experience and capacity to execute.

“Our members have raised concerns that opportunities are frequently awarded to foreign-owned companies, leaving capable Liberian firms with limited access to the public investment that should also contribute to the growth of domestic enterprises,” the letter stated.

The ALCC clarified that it does not oppose foreign contractors, acknowledging their capital and expertise. However, it argued that Liberia’s infrastructure development agenda should also provide meaningful opportunities for domestic companies to grow, create jobs and retain wealth within the local economy.

US$2,202.50 Just to Stay Compliant

The ALCC highlighted the financial burden Liberian contractors face to maintain legal and regulatory compliance, even when they have no active government contracts.

Citing documentation dated September 18, 2026, from a locally owned construction firm, the Association said a company must spend at least US$2,202.50 in direct registration and certification fees alone.

The breakdown includes US$50 for a Liberia Business Registry business certificate, US$150 for Articles of Incorporation, US$1,400 for Ministry of Public Works CCCS certificates, US$102.50 for a NASSCORP certificate, and US$500 for Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) vendor registration.

The Association noted that these expenses exclude transportation, office maintenance, staff salaries, equipment acquisition and maintenance, bid preparation, and site visits.

Such costs, it said, place a significant burden on small and medium-sized Liberian firms that must maintain compliance while waiting for contract opportunities.

“These investments are made by Liberian entrepreneurs before they can benefit from any government contract. Yet compliance alone does not guarantee access to work,” the letter stated.

Wider Economic Impact

The ALCC warned that limiting local contractors’ access to public infrastructure projects could have consequences extending beyond individual businesses.

Construction companies, the Association noted, support a broad network of professionals and workers, including engineers, architects, surveyors, masons, carpenters, electricians, plumbers and equipment operators.

They also generate business for building-material suppliers, transport operators, workshops, food vendors and other small enterprises.

“When local contractors collapse, workers lose income, suppliers lose customers, families struggle to pay school fees and rent, and government loses revenue from reduced formal employment,” the letter warned.

The Association further cautioned that without reasonable access to contracts, experienced local companies could lose skilled employees and equipment, creating a cycle in which they are considered too small for major projects while being denied the opportunities needed to expand.

ALCC Outlines Requests to Boakai

To address the concerns, the Association outlined several measures it wants the Boakai administration to consider, including full implementation of domestic preference and reservation measures when Liberian companies submit competitive bids, transparent review of Liberian firms’ participation and success rates in public procurement, procurement requirements proportionate to project size, including dividing large projects into manageable lots, and greater transparency through accessible procurement plans, evaluation criteria and contract award notices.

The Association called for access to financing and timely payment for certified work, including through engagement with commercial banks, properly structured joint ventures with clearly defined responsibilities and genuine skills transfer to Liberian partners.

The ALCC also requested a high-level meeting involving the Office of the President, the Ministry of Public Works, the Ministry of Finance and Development Planning, the PPCC and the Association to develop a practical action plan.

“The nationality of a company should neither substitute for evidence of competence nor become a barrier to a qualified Liberian company’s participation,” Toure emphasized.

“Our central appeal is that Liberian firms with proven ability should have a fair and meaningful place in building their own country.”

The Association reaffirmed its commitment to high standards, competitive procurement, quality construction and accountability, expressing readiness to work with the government to improve performance and transparency in Liberia’s construction sector.

World.title: Kemayah Warns Politicized Justice, Eroding Trust Could Threaten Hard-Won Peace
World.content:
Monrovia — Former Liberian Foreign Affairs Minister Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah has warned that growing political tensions, declining public confidence in state institutions and concerns over the politicization of justice could undermine Liberia’s hard-won peace, calling for urgent action to prevent political disagreements from escalating into national instability.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Kemayah issued the warning Monday, September 21, while delivering the special keynote address at the First International Peace Summit 2026, held virtually to commemorate the International Day of Peace.

Speaking under the theme “Peace in a Fractured World: Restoring Dialogue, Justice and Confidence in Institutions,” the former minister identified credible diplomacy, justice under the rule of law and public confidence in institutions as essential pillars for achieving sustainable peace.

Drawing on Liberia’s experience following 14 years of civil conflict, Kemayah cautioned that the country’s post-war stability could become vulnerable if political divisions deepen and citizens lose confidence in the impartiality of national institutions.

“Liberia knows the terrible cost of institutional collapse,” he said, noting that the country has spent more than two decades rebuilding a fragile peace.

He expressed concern over what he described as rising political tensions amid highly charged prosecutions of former government officials, saying questions surrounding the administration of justice and the perceived politicization of accountability were deepening mistrust between the government and opposition.

“When political persecution and witch-hunt seem to be the emerging trend, rather than resolve political disputes, and citizens begin to doubt the impartiality of national institutions, with selective justice; the foundations of peace may be dangerously vulnerable,” Kemayah said.

He warned that prolonged mistrust could harden political divisions, make future elections more confrontational and push public grievances from institutional channels onto the streets.

In a post-conflict society such as Liberia, he said, even isolated incidents could become dangerous when they occur in an atmosphere of deep political mistrust.

“Conflict does not begin when a first gun is fired. It begins when trust dies, institutions lose credibility, political opponents become enemies, and citizens cease to believe that justice will protect them equally,” he stated.

Kemayah urged Liberians to recognize the warning signs before political tensions evolve into a broader crisis.

“We have paid too high a price for peace to gamble with it again,” he said. “Liberia must act before political tension becomes political crisis and before political crisis becomes national instability.”

Accountability Must Not Become Political Persecution

A central theme of Kemayah’s address was the need to balance accountability with the protection of constitutional rights, particularly during changes in government.

While affirming that former public officials must remain accountable for their actions, he stressed that prosecutions must be grounded in credible evidence, transparency, impartiality and due process.

“Where credible evidence of wrongdoing exists, the law must take its course. But accountability must be evidence-based, transparent, impartial, and consistent with due process,” he said.

He cautioned that without these safeguards, legitimate accountability efforts could be perceived as political persecution.

“Otherwise, prosecution can be persecution in disguise,” Kemayah warned.

He argued that democratic systems must reject both impunity and politically motivated prosecutions, emphasizing that credible justice—not selective enforcement or political witch-hunts—is necessary to sustain public trust.

According to him, when political actors begin to believe that losing an election could result in imprisonment through politically motivated legal processes, the stakes of political competition become dangerously high.

Kemayah also emphasized that no individual should be above the law, while no one should be denied its protection.

Courts, Diplomacy as Pillars of Peace

The former foreign minister described the judiciary as more than an institution responsible for interpreting and enforcing the law, arguing that courts also serve as mechanisms for preventing conflict.

He said independent courts provide an orderly alternative to confrontation by allowing political, constitutional and electoral disputes to be resolved through established legal processes rather than violence.

“Courts are also institutions of peace,” Kemayah said, calling for greater support for the judiciary as an investment in national stability.

He also underscored the importance of preventive diplomacy, arguing that preventing conflict is less costly than resolving it after violence has erupted.

According to Kemayah, diplomacy should not be treated merely as an emergency response but as a continuous process involving early warning, mediation, confidence-building measures and sustained dialogue.

“Dialogue is not capitulation. Negotiation is not surrender. Diplomacy is not weakness,” he said, describing diplomacy as the disciplined search for alternatives to destruction.

He urged governments and international organizations to strengthen early-warning systems and establish standing mediation teams capable of intervening before disputes escalate into crises.

Calls for Institutional Independence, Political Restraint

Kemayah further called for stronger safeguards to protect the independence of the judiciary, electoral bodies, legislatures and public accountability institutions from political interference.

He recommended transparent, merit-based appointments, clearly defined terms of office, lawful removal procedures and adequate institutional funding.

He also urged political leaders to exercise restraint in using legal and administrative powers against opponents, emphasizing that constitutional democracy requires more than technical compliance with the law.

“The spirit of constitutional democracy requires more than legality. It requires restraint and consideration of expediency,” he said.

On political leadership, Kemayah called for a reduction in inflammatory rhetoric, warning that statements by public officials and political actors could either ease tensions or deepen divisions.

He stressed that political opponents should not automatically be treated as enemies of the state and that governments must tolerate criticism while allowing opposition groups to challenge them within constitutional boundaries.

“The ultimate test of statesmanship is not the ability to defeat every opponent. Sometimes, it is the ability to create sufficient common ground for former adversaries to coexist,” he said.

Challenges International Institutions

Beyond Liberia, Kemayah called on international institutions to demonstrate greater consistency in applying international law, warning that perceived double standards undermine confidence in the international system.

He argued that smaller states, developing countries and vulnerable populations must have confidence that international laws protect them as meaningfully as they protect powerful nations.

“When similar conduct attracts different international responses, depending upon who commits it, confidence diminishes,” he said.

He called for greater transparency, representation, accountability and consistency in multilateral institutions, while urging stronger support for regional organizations that are often better positioned to understand and resolve neighboring countries’ crises.

Proposes Five-Point Peacebuilding Agenda

To translate his recommendations into action, Kemayah outlined five priority areas: strengthening preventive diplomacy, protecting institutional independence, upholding the rule of law consistently, preserving dialogue among adversaries and restoring confidence in multilateralism.

He called for permanent national dialogue mechanisms involving governments, opposition parties, civil society, business leaders, youth, women and traditional authorities.

He also urged political parties to establish internal dispute-resolution mechanisms and commit to nonviolent political competition.

Kemayah highlighted the media’s role in peacebuilding, calling for responsible journalism that provides facts without deliberately intensifying political divisions.

He also urged social media platforms and technology companies to cooperate with governments and civil society in addressing coordinated disinformation and incitement, while protecting legitimate freedom of expression.

In concluding his address, Kemayah said peace must be continuously nurtured through responsible governance, impartial justice, open diplomacy and institutions that command public confidence.

“Lasting peace cannot be imposed by force alone. It must be built through trust, protected by justice, sustained through dialogue, and anchored in institutions that command the confidence of the people they serve,” he said.

He closed by urging world leaders to embrace the summit’s declaration of “One World, One Humanity, One Future,” emphasizing that sustainable peace requires cooperation and a shared commitment to preventing future conflicts.

World.title: ZANACO launches 100m USD bond to support climate projects
World.content:
ZANACO has launched a 100 million United States dollars Medium-Term Note Programme that will support the issuance of sustainability bonds aimed at mobilising long-term capital for green and social projects in Zambia.

British Investment International (BII) offered technical support for the establishment of the bond Framework and has invested USS 15 million on the platform.

The programme will begin with an inaugural US$ 50 million sustainability bond, with further issuances expected over time.

The proceeds will be directed towards eligible projects in areas including renewable energy, climate-resilient agriculture, financial inclusion, affordable housing, healthcare, education and other initiatives with measurable environmental and social benefits.

Speaking at the launch at ZANACO Chief Executive officer Mukwandi Chibesakunda said the bank’s inaugural sustainability bond will go beyond raising capital, with proceeds expected to support climate resilience, economic growth and social development in Zambia.

Dr Chibesakunda said the bond, to be issued under ZANACO’s US$100 million medium-term note programme, has marked a shift from the bank’s earlier commitment to sustainable finance towards execution.

“At ZANACO, our purpose is anchored on our You First philosophy. It is a commitment that places our customers, communities and our country at the centre of every decision we make,” he said.

Dr Chibesakunda said the sustainability bond would create financing opportunities for farmers seeking to strengthen their resilience to climate change, entrepreneurs and small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) looking to expand, as well as communities in need of critical social infrastructure.

She said the initiative was particularly important amid growing climate-related risks facing Zambia and other parts of the world.

Under the sustainability bond programme, ZANACO intends to channel financing towards climate-smart agriculture, renewable energy, energy efficiency, financial inclusion for SMEs and critical social infrastructure.

And British International Investment (BII) Managing Director and Head of Africa Chris Chijiutomi said the transaction was aligned with BII’s new five-year strategy, which places emphasis on strengthening the local financial system.

“One of the priorities of our new strategy that we launched this year is to help strengthen local financial systems and mobilize more private capital,” Mr Chijiutomi said.

Mr Chijiutomi said development finance institutions such as BII could provide investment, but greater mobilisation of private capital was necessary to expand development financing in economies such as Zambia.

He described the sustainability bond as an important milestone for Zambia’s financial sector and said it had the potential to encourage additional local and international investors and contribute to the development of the country’s sustainable finance market.

Africa.

Meanwhile, British High Commissioner to Zambia Rebecca Terzeon said the transaction demonstrated the UK’s shift towards an investment-led approach to development partnerships.

Ms Terzeon said BII’s investment in ZANACO’s sustainability bond showed how UK-supported development finance could be combined with Zambian institutions to support commercially viable investments while delivering development outcomes.

“This is exactly what the UK means when we talk about donor to investor,” Ms Terzeon said, referring to the mobilisation of finance to help businesses grow, create jobs and strengthen Zambia’s economic resilience.

Lusaka Securities Exchange (LuSE) Chief Executive Officer Nicholas Kabaso said the issuance marked a new chapter for Zambia’s capital markets and described it as the first sustainability bond issued by a Zambian bank.

Mr Kabaso said the exchange would work with stakeholders to develop a pipeline of future thematic bond issuances, simplify the issuance process and standardise reporting and verification requirements.

And Securities and Exchange Commission Director of Policy Development and Market Mateyo Lungu said the transaction was consistent with Zambia’s Capital Markets Master Plan, which seeks to develop innovative financial products and deepen the contribution of capital markets to national development.

Green Economy and Environment Minister Gilbert Siame said government supports initiatives that mobilise capital for climate-resilient and sustainable development.

Dr Siame said sustainable finance is important in financing the country’s transition towards a greener and more resilient economy, adding that the government was working to create an enabling policy and regulatory environment for climate finance.

World.title: Kabwe Court puts defilement suspect on defence
World.content:
The Kabwe Magistrates’ Court has found a 24-year-old man with a case to answer in a matter in which he is charged with defilement.

Kabwe Resident Magistrate Sebastian Mwenya has since put Levy Tebulo on his defence after the prosecution closed its case.

This follows testimony from the State’s final key witness, gynecologist Wisdom Banda of Kabwe Central Hospital, who told the court that he examined the complainant and found an injury to the hymen.

Dr Banda testified that the medical findings were consistent with a penetrative vaginal injury.

After considering the evidence presented by the prosecution, Magistrate Mwenya ruled that the accused had a case to answer and directed him to begin his defence.

“I have gone through the evidence presented by the prosecution and find you with a case to answer, therefore, I put you on your defense,” ruled the court.

The court heard that Tebulo is alleged to have had unlawful carnal knowledge of a girl under the age of 16 between February 3rd and February 14th, 2026, in Kabwe District.

After being informed of his rights, Tebulo opted to give sworn evidence in his defence and indicated that he would not call any witnesses.

“I’m going to give you a chance to go and prepare for your defence, and I wish you good luck,” said Magistrate Mwenya.

The matter has been adjourned to October 1st, 2026, for commencement of the defence case whilst Tebulo remains in custody.

World.title: Masebo’s petition case commences in the Lusaka High Court
World.content:
The petition hearing where former Minister of Lands and Natural Resources, Sylvia Masebo, is challenging the election of Annita Kamanga as Chongwe East Member of Parliament has commenced.

Ms Masebo, who stood on the United Party for National Development (UPND) ticket contends in her petition Ms Kamanga’s pre-election campaigns were characterised by conduct that contravened the Electoral Process Act and its Code of Conduct.

Robert Simeza is the lead lawyer for Ms Masebo in the petition case where 20 witnesses have been lined up by the petitioner to testify in court.

Four witnesses have so far testified that they were attacked by suspected supporters of the respondent, who in this case is Ms Kamanga.

One witness testified that he sustained body injuries as a result of the attack and that a medical report was issued at the hospital.

Both, the petitioner Ms Masebo and the respondent, Ms Kamanga, who stoon as an Independent parliamentary candidate, were at Lusaka High Court to follow proceedings.

Ms Masebo polled 6,798 votes against Annita Kamanga’s 16,058 votes in the August 13, 2026 general elections.

Some UPND supporters gathered at the Lusaka High Court grounds to show solidarity to the petitioner.

World.title: Chipangali drug stock stable
World.content:
The Department of Health Services in Chipangali District in Eastern Province has said that clinical services in the district are currently stable with drug availability above 89 percent.

Speaking during a senior management meeting held at the District Administration Office, District Clinical Care Officer Geoffrey Ndhlovu said the 89 percent drug availability in the district reflects adequate essential medicines, essential supplies and vaccines.

Mr Ndhlovu added that three more health facilities have been opened in the district bringing the total number of health facilities to 27.

“We have opened three more health facilities in the district namely Nguluwe, Nyauzi, and Kapatamoyo health facilities which are already providing outpatient health services,” Mr Ndhlovu said.

He however mentioned that the new facilities are not fully operational as they still face challenges relating to inadequate essential equipment and supplies.

“Currently we are not conducting deliveries in these new facilities, because the equipment we have can only support outpatient care,” he said.

He said the department has since requested for equipment through the Constituency Development Fund (CDF), noting that the request was approved and awaits funding.

Meanwhile Mr Ndhlovu disclosed that the department has conducted 297 cesarean section surgeries from October 2025 to date.

He said the surgeries were conducted within the district at Muzeyi Clinic.

Mr Ndhlovu reported that all the surgeries were successful without any complications.

“All women who may require advanced care are referred to Muzeyi, so that they wait to deliver safely. So, the facility sometimes has inadequate space. In view of this, we are also lobbying for construction of a mother’s shelter and ablution block so that our mothers are well kept as they wait to be operated on,” Mr Ndhlovu said.

World.title: Zambia, European Union reaffirm longstanding partnership
World.content:
Zambia and the European Union (EU) have reaffirmed their longstanding partnership, underscoring shared commitments to democracy, rule of law, and economic cooperation.

European Commissioner for International Partnerships, Jozef Síkela, has commended Zambia’s standing as a beacon of democracy and encouraged both sides to maintain respect for the rule of law while advancing a forward-looking partnership.

This is according to a statement issued to the media in Lusaka by First Secretary for Press and Public Relations at Zambia’s Permanent Mission to the United Nations, Namatama Njekwa.

Ms Njekwa revealed that the remarks were made during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81).

She noted that the EU reaffirmed its support for Zambia’s leadership in promoting multilateralism and the rules-based international order, while both parties agreed to deepen cooperation through investment, value addition, and initiatives aligned with the Grow Zambia Agenda.

She added that Mr Síkela highlighted Africa’s critical role in electric-vehicle battery and mineral value chains, with Zambia welcoming the EU’s Global Gateway initiative and development cooperation, including budget support of approximately EUR 110 million.

Ms Njekwa further stated that both sides emphasised that post-election developments should not detract from opportunities to strengthen economic ties.

She indicated that the meeting also reaffirmed collaboration on international peace and security, with both Zambia and the EU pledging to prioritise the consolidation of their partnership.

World.title: Nalolo’s Kaunga Lueti in water blues
World.content:
Nalolo District Commissioner Namatama Mupo has called for an urgent solution to the water crisis that has hit Kaunga Lueti community in Nalolo West Bank.

The media reports that the water reticulation plant at Kaunga Lueti Primary School, which services about 4,000 people, has been non-operational since the first week of September, 2026.

An assessment conducted by Nalolo Town Council after the community reported the matter, established that the pump controller and surge protective device need replacement.

Speaking during an urgent District Disaster Management Committee (DDMC) meeting held at her office, Mrs Mupo said water issues are critical and require urgent attention as they affect the community and public institutions such as Kaunga Lueti Primary School, the health post and the police post.

“Water is life and as such, there is a need to tackle water issues with urgency, as delaying would lead to waterborne diseases and possible closure of the school where the water scheme is located,” said Mrs Mupo.

She has since directed the DDMC to write to the local authority to request for funds under the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) Disaster Management and Mitigation Unit (DMMU) component so that the water plant can be repaired.

And District Disaster Management Officer Annie Phiri assured the District Commissioner that documents requesting for funds will be prepared and once the funds are available, the committee will ensure that the water plant is worked so that the Kaunga Lueti community can have access to clean and safe water again.

Ms Phiri said the water plant is important as it is the only source of clean and safe water in the area, hence the need to find a solution as soon as possible.

Meanwhile, District Education Board Secretary (DEBS) Muyoba Liwakala said there is a need to set up a committee that will be in charge of the water scheme to ensure regular maintenance and avoid future breakdowns.

Mr Liwakala said the water reticulation facility is a huge investment that needs to be maintained at all times so that it can stand the test of time.

The District Commissioner also called on the Department of Agriculture to intensify El Nino sensitisation meetings so that farmers are well prepared and take preventive measures before disasters strike.

Mrs Mupo said following the rains experienced in some parts of the province, some farmers are confused on whether to start farming or wait for the usual planting period.

Responding to the DC, Acting Nalolo District Agricultural Coordinator (DACO) Patience Munalula said El Nino sensitisation meetings are ongoing and Agriculture Camp Officers are currently engaging farmers on venturing into smart agriculture and what to expect in view of climate change effects.

World.title: Silondwa wins Discover golf title
World.content:
Nkana golfer Kedrick Silondwa survived a three-way countback to win the Discover Insurance Golf Championship at Nkana Golf Club.

Silondwa, off handicap 12, carded 42 points to top a tightly contested field and walk away with a K3,500 voucher and the overall winner’s trophy.

“It’s been a great day of golf and I can only thank Discover Insurance for deciding to spend their fourth birthday with us. We hope to see more of you around. To the players, I wish to thank you as well. It was really competitive and you made me work hard for my reward,” he said after receiving the trophy.

In the men’s category, Sam Mpundu also finished with 42 points to claim top prize on countback ahead of Tashbekov Djurabek, with Frank Masaka third on 35 points.

In the women’s category, Gladys Mudenda won outright with 35 points, one better than Emma Makoni, while Elisa Manjolo was third on 33 points.

In the subsidiary prizes, Mpundu won the nearest-to-the-pin award, Wiaan Le Roux won the longest drive in the men’s section, while Manjolo took the women’s award.

Discover Insurance Vice-Board Chairperson Chisuwo Hamwela said the tournament was organised to commemorate the company’s fourth anniversary and support the Grow Zambia Agenda.

“We are happy to celebrate our fourth anniversary with the business community and it’s been great. But on top of that, we are game for the Grow Zambia Agenda and while it is important to grow the economy, it is equally important to expand growth to other areas,” Hamwela said.

“Nkana Golf Club is doing that with its efforts with the junior golf programme and we are more than happy to supplement that with donations to the junior programme. At this tournament, we held a junior event and donated prizes in the form of school bags and more than a hundred golf balls.”

In the junior chipping contest, Peter Kasongo, Blessing Mambwe and Grace Washeni emerged winners.

World.title: Chinese Embassy holds fashion show
World.content:
Government has called for strengthened cooperation between Zambia and China in technology, investment, infrastructure and human capital development to accelerate the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Ministry of Defence, Permanent Secretary Maamba Haamaundu said enhanced collaboration with China will be instrumental in transforming Zambia into a productive, industrialised and export-oriented economy. while creating jobs and improving the quality of life for citizens.

Mr Haamaundu was speaking when he graced the fashion show to commemorate the 77th Anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic of China in Lusaka last night.

Mr Haamaundu said government believes that China’s technological knowledge and investment experience can contribute to achieving the country’s national development goals.

He said Zambia is grateful for the win-win cooperation with China and the numerous benefits arising from the longstanding partnership.

Mr Haamaundu emphasised that President Hakainde Hichilema’s Grow Zambia Agenda is aimed at promoting sustainable economic growth and development, calling on China to continue working with Zambia in investment, technology, infrastructure, value addition and human capital development for the mutual benefit of the two countries.

Speaking at the same event, Chinese Ambassador to Zambia Han Jing says China is committed to deepening practical cooperation with Zambia in agriculture, energy, mining, infrastructure and digital technology.

And Mr Jing said China stands ready to implement the outcomes of the Beijing Summit of the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation (FOCAC) and elevate the China-Zambia Comprehensive Strategic and Cooperative Partnership to greater heights.

He said the two countries are recording tangible progress in key economic sectors, citing the commissioning of the 136-megawatt Itimpi Solar Power Plant, the Zambia Petrochemical Energy Company’s refinery project among other sectors.
