World.title: Colosseum closed after worker dies in 10-metre fall
World.content:
A worker has died after a 10-metre fall at Rome's famed Colosseum, the Italian Ministry of Culture has confirmed.

The 22-year-old technician had been installing a lighting system inside the second level of the ancient amphitheatre at the time of the incident.

"Andrea Moretti, a specialist high-altitude rope access worker … died last night inside the Flavian Amphitheatre following a workplace accident," the ministry said.

Part of the Colosseum, which is one of Rome's main tourist attractions, was closed after the worker's death. (Reuters: Remo Casilli)

Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli said the "tragic event" had shocked the country.

"The few words we can express are dedicated to Andrea, his family, and his loved ones," Mr Giuli said.

"We extend to everyone our deepest, most sorrowful condolences at the senseless death of a young man dedicated to his work."

Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was "deeply shocked and saddened" by the news.

"For a person to die at the age of 22 is unacceptable — and even more so when it happens in the workplace," she said in a statement.

The ministry gave no further details of Mr Moretti's fall, but said police were working to determine the circumstances of the incident.

Up to 20,000 visitors flow through the gates of the Colosseum each day during peak tourism months. (Reuters: Alexandros Avradimis)

The Colosseum Archaeological Park initially said part of the Colosseum near to the area where the accident occurred was closed on Wednesday, local time, as a mark of respect to the worker.

It later said that "once the orderly exit of those currently inside is complete, the Colosseum will be closed to the public".

Built 2,000 years ago, the Colosseum was the biggest amphitheatre in the Roman empire and was used to host gladiator fights, executions and animal hunts for crowds of up to 50,000 spectators.

It remains one of the city's main tourist attractions, with up to 20,000 visitors a day at peak times.

Italy's biggest union, CGIL, took issue with the decision to close only part of the landmark, saying the full site should be closed for the day.

"We expect Minister Giuli to shed light on the incident and to order the full closure of the Colosseum," CGIL Rome general secretary Natale di Cola said.

"Humanity comes before tourists."

Reuters

World.title: Council general manager sacked with $272k payout after hat-draw mayor mix-up
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The general manager of a northern New South Wales council has been sacked a week after she declared the wrong winner of a mayoral ballot.

Clarence Valley councillors held an extraordinary meeting today, calling for general manager, Laura Black, to resign or face having her contract terminated.

In confidential papers accidentally published on the council's website, a breakdown in the relationship between Ms Black and the majority of councillors was cited as the reason for asking her to step down.

Some of the Clarence Valley councillors who voted on the general manager's tenure. (Supplied: Clarence Valley Council.)

The motion said it had led to the council becoming "dysfunctional".

Ms Black did not attend the meeting, but in her absence, councillors voted to terminate her contract.

Councillors noted that Ms Black had not been given notice of any dispute, nor had performance related issues raised previously.

The ABC has attempted to contact Ms Black for comment.

Botched mayoral vote

The contract termination comes a week after Ms Black declared the incorrect winner of a mayoral ballot, leaving the council in disarray.

Incumbent mayor Ray Smith and Cr Peter Johnstone were tied after a council vote.

Their names were put in a hat, and Mr Smith's name was drawn, but instead of calling him the winner as the rules stipulated, Ms Black named Mr Johnstone the new mayor.

When the error was discovered, Mr Johnstone resigned as mayor.

Five-year contract

Ms Black was appointed as the Clarence Valley Council general manager on October 7, 2022, on a five-year performance-based contract.

She had previously held the roles of acting general manager and director corporate governance of Clarence Valley Council.

Ms Black was paid a salary of $372,591 in the 2024/25 financial year.

Her contract includes a clause which entitles her to 38 weeks pay, which is approximately $272,000, plus entitlements.

The councillors thanked Ms Black for her service to the Clarence Valley Council and the community.

The director of Environment and Planning, Adam Cameron was appointed as the acting general manager for four weeks.

The council currently has no mayor, and no general manager. Cr Cristie Yager is the deputy and acting mayor.

Councillors were expected to meet next week to discuss the mayoral role.

World.title: 'Yes dear': Mal and Marge's secret to 75 years
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

As they celebrate three-quarters of a century together, Mal and Marge Grimley, at 95 and 93 respectively, have not forgotten their rainy 1951 Sydney wedding day.

"Marge was 18, and I was 20," Mr Grimley says. "And it wasn't a shotgun wedding," Mrs Grimley interjects.

"It was like winning a lottery that we were so young," Mrs Grimley adds.

Decades later, the couple's romantic-comedy meet-cute at the local cinema is still fresh in their minds.

"You pinched my seat," Mrs Grimley says. "No, you pinched my seat," Mr Grimley says.

"At interval we went out and when I came back in, Marge was sitting in my seat … she wouldn't get out.

"So I sat on her lap," Mr Grimley says.

Marge Grimley says being with husband Mal was like winning the lottery. (ABC News: Ruby McIntosh)

And in what Mrs Grimley describes as a different time, the pair waited nine months for their first kiss.

"One night, we had been to the movies; we sat on the front doorstep … I said, 'If you don't kiss me tonight, I will kiss you,'" she remembers.

" So he kissed me. It wouldn't happen like that these days. "

Diamond anniversary

The couple's diamond anniversary was held at the independent living facility where Mrs Grimley still lives, while Mr Grimley has only recently moved into assisted living.

After 75 years together, it is hard to now face the prospect of living apart.

"It's lonely," he says. "It's hard looking at one toothbrush on the sink," she says.

The couple's three-quarters of a century together was celebrated by everyone, from close family members to their cleaner and personal trainer.

The Grimleys celebrated their diamond anniversary with loved ones. (ABC News: Ruby McIntosh)

Their daughter, Dana Whitty, says her parents' philosophy is:

"Treat your partner as you wish to be treated, listen to what they are saying and look at their point of view. "Embrace Indigenous and multicultural customs and people; they have experienced many things that we have not. "And lastly, in a world where you can be anything, be kind."

'Great wife, big softie'

Moving between Woollahra, the NSW coast and then settling in Canberra for the past 27 years, the couple has volunteered for local charities and cheered for local sporting teams.

Their daughter says they are always the first to roll up their sleeves and help out.

Mal and Marge Grimley at their wedding in 1951. (Supplied)

For their anniversary, the couple was showered in flowers, gifts and cards, even from King Charles III and Queen Camilla and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Their next-door neighbour, who was at the celebration, says: "You get what you give, and they gave a lot."

Mrs Grimley did not want to advise any younger couples hoping to make the distance, but she pointed to Mr Grimley's words, which she said made good advice.

"Two words to make a marriage … yes, and dear," he said.

Tearing up when asked what he loved about his wife of 75 years, Mr Grimley wondered what was not to love about her.

"Couldn't be without her … Marge carried all the weight," he said.

"She's been a great wife and a great nurse and cook and everything else … she's carried all the weight."

And Mrs Grimley? Here's what she said when asked what she loves about Mr Grimley: "He's a big softie; that's what I love about him, big softie."

World.title: 'Terrifies me': Victorian Premier makes One Nation admission
World.content:
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll has declared "One Nation terrifies me" as he escalated the state Labor party's warning about the prospect of the Coalition governing with Pauline Hanson's party after November's state election.

One Nation has recently won seats in by-elections, first in the federal NSW seat of Farrer and in the WA state seat of Secret Harbour.

The rise of Senator Hanson's party has been seen as a warning shot fired across both sides of the political divide as Labor and the Coalition struggle in opinion polls.

Since becoming Victoria's premier in July, Mr Carroll has used the possibility of a Coalition-One Nation government as a central plank of Labor's campaign for re-election, particularly as support for the minor party has surged in the state.

"I will fight every day against the Liberal Party and One Nation coming together, because that is what will happen in November if Labor is not successful," Mr Carroll told 7.30.

" That is why Labor must be successful. Failure is not an option. "

Asked if he was worried about One Nation's rise, Mr Carroll admitted the prospect "terrifies him".

"[The] Liberal Party and One Nation teaming together … they're about attacking working people. I'm about fighting for them."

Pauline Hanson's party has enjoyed a swift rise of late. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Carroll accused of 'fear campaign'

While Mr Carroll was concerned about One Nation, that was not the case for Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson.

"I'm not really interested in the other parties," Ms Wilson told 7.30.

"I am running to win majority government at this election because I know that we have the plan to fix Victoria, and I know the only way to do that is to achieve majority government."

Liberal leader Jess Wilson is not concerned about One Nation's popularity in the polls. (ABC News)

Ms Wilson said she had not spoken to One Nation Victorian leader Warren Pickering and urged voters to "fix this state" by voting for the Coalition.

7.30 approached One Nation for comment, but they did not respond.

The competing pitches have sharpened the battle lines with just over two months until election day.

Redbridge insights adviser Kristy McSweeney — who is a former political advisor and contested the 2022 federal election as the Liberal candidate for the Western Australian seat of Swan — said Mr Carroll was ramping up his One Nation warnings to specifically target disillusioned Labor voters who were considering switching their vote.

"He's going for a fear campaign due to Labor's very low primary vote and Labor trailing those two parties consistently over polls the last six months, including post his leadership change as the third party among Liberal, Labor and One Nation," Ms McSweeney said.

" He's throwing it at the wall to spark the fear of people from switching from Labor. "

Redbridge insights adviser Kristy McSweeney is a former Liberal candidate for the WA seat of Swan. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Recent Redbridge polling shows the scale of One Nation's rise.

Its latest survey of almost 2,400 Victorian voters conducted earlier this month put the Coalition on 29 per cent, One Nation on 25 per cent and Labor on 24 per cent of the primary vote.

Ms McSweeney said Labor's warnings were particularly aimed at voters in Melbourne's west, where the party's traditional support base was frustrated that infrastructure had failed to keep pace with rapid population growth.

"It is a pitch to them to say, 'If you switch from Labor, you will get a One Nation-Liberal Coalition and that represents a lot of things that you don't like in multicultural communities out there on the peri-urban fringe," she said.

Could 'the red wall' fall?

Melbourne's outer west is traditionally a safe Labor area and known as the 'Red Wall'.

The region includes the seat of Melton — the nation's fastest growing local government area — as well as suburbs like Sunbury and Werribee, where Labor has built a strong base among migrant, working-class and first-home-buying communities.

Melton is held by Labor on a 4.6 per cent margin, but the once-safe seat is showing signs of vulnerability after more than three decades in Labor hands.

It was closely watched at the 2022 Victorian election when it was the only seat in the state to swing against Labor, and is now more vulnerable with long-standing Labor member, Stephen McGhie retiring at this election.

Warren Pickering is the leader of One Nation in Victoria. (AAP: Jay Kogler)

There are other concerns too. There have been delays to some infrastructure builds in the area, including the electrification of the Melton train line.

While Ms McSweeney said that Labor faced challenges, she also said voters were starting to have concerns about One Nation policy.

"A lot of people are saying, 'I'm starting to look at One Nation's policies for Victoria and I can't see what they're going to do for Victoria'," she said.

" They're starting to clock that One Nation hasn't come up with specific local policies, or at least not yet. "

World.title: Iranian president vows not to surrender in defiant, historic UN speech
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Iranian president vows not to surrender in defiant, historic UN speech Michael Koziol September 24, 2026 — 3:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian declared his country would not be cowed into surrender in a defiant address to the United Nations that came a day after US President Donald Trump used the same stage to renew his threat to “annihilate” Iran. Pezeshkian’s speech marked the first time in the UN’s 81-year history that a foreign leader at war with the US addressed the body at its New York headquarters. The Iranian president held up pictures of the assassinated supreme leader Ali Khamenei and children killed by missiles in the war that began nearly seven months ago. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday. AP Photo/Heather Khalifa “I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school,” he said. “You see these children? These children perished under bombs, with weapons used by the United States and Israel. They were innocent.” The US has never publicly acknowledged that it was responsible for the missile strike on an Iranian girls’ school on the first day of the war, killing about 120 children and dozens more adults. That is despite multiple reports from US news outlets about the findings of internal investigations which confirmed US responsibility.



Pezeshkian claimed Iran was ready to resume talks and find a diplomatic solution to the war – an outcome that has eluded negotiators so far, despite a short-lived memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June. But his speech projected resistance to any notion that Iran could be bombed into subjugation, as Trump had countenanced from the podium 24 hours earlier. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi watches the Iranian president address the United Nations in New York. Bloomberg “They have learned that Iran cannot be made to surrender,” Pezeshkian said. “He [Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.” A lone American delegate walked out of the UN General Assembly shortly after Pezeshkian’s speech began. An Iranian delegation including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi were authorised by the US to attend, although some members of the proposed delegation were refused visas.



Pezeshkian also argued Iran must be allowed to develop a civilian nuclear program, insisting – as Tehran always has – that the Islamic Republic does not wish to develop nuclear weapons. However, Iran has a long history of building secret nuclear sites and uranium enrichment facilities, and barring weapons inspectors. Pezeshkian said it was Israel that should face scrutiny, not Iran. “Israel targets any neighbourhood in any city in any province – commits assassinations like a true terrorist,” he said. It was the first time a foreign leader whose country is at war with the US has travelled to New York to speak at the UN. AP Photo/Heather Khalifa “They are committing genocide by using the so-called technologies they have at their disposal – then they label others as terrorists. “The nuclear weapon is in Israel, but the inspector is in Iran. Israel kills, but Iran is subject to sanctions. This is a true tragedy.”



Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due to land in New York on Thursday (US time) to address the UN, before immediately flying home. Related Article Donald Trump At UN, Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran but predicts deal after midterms New York mayor Zohran Mamdani has dropped his threat to arrest the Israeli leader based on an outstanding International Criminal Court warrant, saying the city did not have the jurisdiction. On the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial shipping passage between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, Pezeshkian told the UN that Iran would continue to lay a claim over the waterway. “We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us,” he said. “They close access for us to our own waterway … we will not succumb to that.”



While threatening annihilation of Iran – which he has done before – Trump also predicted there would be a deal after the US midterm elections, arguing the Iranians were dragging it out to inflict political pain upon him via higher oil and petrol prices. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have recently targeted Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, another crucial oil shipping route between Yemen and Africa. This has contributed to the latest spike in oil prices, just as the Russia-Ukraine war is causing the price of diesel to rise. The UN General Assembly watching Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Bloomberg But Trump has continued to project that he is in no rush to solve the issue. Helima Croft, managing director and global head of commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, said on Wednesday (US time) there was an “urgency deficit” in the Trump administration because prices were not yet that high. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was trading just above $US100 ($142) a barrel on Wednesday.



“Prices are not $US150,” Croft told an event hosted by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace “If you can keep West Texas International prices below $US100 or below $90, you may think time is on your side, that you can let the blockade do its work. Essentially, let Iran have to deal with a lack of essential goods, soaring inflation, the rial crashing. “I think that’s a theory that many in the administration are now operating under - that they have time on their side.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Gaslighting’: Diana’s brother hits back at palace over his claim about the King
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘Gaslighting’: Diana’s brother hits back at palace over his claim about the King David Crowe September 24, 2026 — 2:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Earl Spencer has accused Buckingham Palace officials of “gaslighting” him over his account of his sister, Princess Diana, when they suggested grief had clouded his memory of the past. Spencer stood by his controversial claim that King Charles – then the Prince of Wales – had said the world would “forget” Diana after she died in a tragic car crash in 1997. Earl Spencer, brother of Princess Diana, on ITV’s Lorraine program. YouTube In his first live television interview about his new book, Spencer also insisted he did not set out to write a “hit piece” on the King and sought instead to celebrate his sister. But his claims are being denounced by palace insiders and defenders of the King across the British media, while broadcaster Piers Morgan threatens to sue him over a glaring error in the book.



The furore centres on Spencer’s account of a private conversation with Charles about plans for Diana’s two sons, Princes William and Harry, to walk behind her coffin in her funeral procession.

Spencer writes that he complained about the plan in a phone call but that Charles insisted it would go ahead. “He unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death,” the earl writes in the new book. “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’.” Related Article Royal family ‘Those are exactly the words he said’: Earl Spencer says he is telling the truth about the King Buckingham Palace issued a statement to the media to dismiss this version of the conversation said to have occurred almost three decades ago. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss,” the palace said in a statement.



Spencer argued that the palace statement tried to cast doubt on his memory but did not deny the words he reported. “If you look at the words, it’s classic gaslighting,” the earl told ITV’s Lorraine program on Wednesday morning (UK time). “So what they do is, ‘Oh, maybe his mind’s not right to remember these things because of the distance of time and grief’. “No one said that the King didn’t say that because he did.” Princess Diana, 36, was killed in a crash in Paris when paparazzi photographers were chasing the car she was in with her partner at the time, Dodi Fayed.



Born Diana Spencer, a member of an aristocratic family dating back centuries in Britain, she was close to her brother, who inherited the title and is now the head of the family. Copies of Earl Spencer’s new book on display in a London bookshop. AP Photo/Kin Cheung Spencer antagonised the royal family at Diana’s funeral by praising her in a eulogy that criticised the way she was treated by them and the media. He said his eulogy had been influenced by the phone conversation with Charles about whether the world would remember Diana. Spencer said this was why he quoted the King’s remark about Diana being forgotten.



“I wasn’t setting out to do a hit piece on the King at all,” he said. Related Article Royal family Earl Spencer’s apology isn’t enough, says Piers Morgan “The bits that have been included in the book are totally in context. So that clip you played of me [on ITV] getting through the end of the eulogy, I end with this thing that the final thought I give is that Diana will never be extinguished from our minds. “That was a direct counter to the King saying, ‘We’ll forget her soon enough’. “So it had to be in because the strand through the book is how did this eulogy come about?”



Spencer joined Charles and Prince Philip in the funeral procession at a time of national mourning for Diana. Extracts from his new book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, appeared in The Daily Mirror last week, setting off a media storm over his claims. Loading Commentators in The Times and the London Telegraph have strongly criticised Spencer and cast doubt on his memory, while also suggesting he has written a salacious book for the money. Spencer has given his critics ammunition with a basic error of fact in the book, when he describes broadcaster Piers Morgan as an editor of The Daily Mirror at a point in time when he was not.



Related Article Review Bashir, royalty and childhood trauma: the revelations from Charles Spencer’s book Morgan has announced he will sue Spencer over the mistake. Spencer admitted he was wrong. “I’m very happy to acknowledge I made a small error, and I’ve apologised, and it will be put right in the in the second edition,” he said. Morgan has called on the publisher, Penguin Random House, to stop selling the book.



“It’s not just a little silly slip-up or mistake,” Morgan said. “He has directly accused me in his book, which is clearly going to sell gazillions of copies around the world, of the most egregious invasion of royal privacy in history.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Australian charged with murder in Syria to be medically assessed after mother’s plea
World.content:
NationalSyrian conflict Australian charged with murder in Syria to be medically assessed after mother’s plea Michael Bachelard September 24, 2026 — 12:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A young Australian man who is facing the death penalty in Syria will be medically assessed for mental impairment after his mother and a lawyer flew to the strife-torn region to advocate for him. Patrick Stevenson, 20, a Muslim convert from the Gold Coast, is accused of murdering another Australian convert, Abdullah Glen Burgess, late last year by shooting him eight times with an AK-47 inside the dead man’s apartment in Idlib province. Patrick Stevenson, a Gold Coast Muslim convert who is now in jail in Syria charged with murdering another Australian convert. Stevenson’s mother Angela Bell and human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan flew to the region last week when it became clear his accuser would not accept “diya”, or blood money, which is allowable under Islamic law, instead of the death sentence. The accuser is Burgess’s widow, who is also Australian, and who this masthead has agreed not to name because she claims it would endanger her. She is a witness in the case and, according to Bell, told the court she would not accept financial compensation because it would not bring her husband back.



Bell and Zaydan say they do not believe Stevenson is guilty of premeditated murder, and insist he does not know what’s going on now because of his ADHD, serious learning disabilities and probably autism, compounded by a fresh head injury and a months-long stay in prison where nobody else speaks English. Related Article Courts ‘Of course I’m frightened’: Australian mother flies to son accused of murder in Syria Bell said she had visited Stevenson three times since arriving in Syria last week. “He is confused. He tells me he does not know why he is here. He has significant problems with his memory… He struggles to concentrate… His thinking appears slowed. There are long pauses. He struggles to process what we are saying to him and has difficulty expressing himself. And he is simply not the same child I knew before this.” She said he had a large wound on the back of his head, and remembers waking up confused in police custody as they were stitching it.



After a court hearing on Wednesday night (Australian time), Zaydan told this masthead she and an Australian government-appointed Syrian lawyer had made a plea of mental impairment, which had been accepted by the court. It ordered that Stevenson should be medically assessed. “His legal team was granted permission to be present at the assessment. Patrick was present, but he didn’t understand what was going on,” Zaydan told this masthead. Another application, to have Stevenson’s electronic devices returned, was rejected with no reasons provided, Zaydan said. Angela Bell is in Syria to help her son. They also negotiated that Bell be able to visit her son daily in the Syrian prison.



Both men involved in the case converted independently to Islam in Australia, then went to live in Idlib province, which is under the control of Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), a group the Australian government considers to be a terrorist organisation. Human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan, who is going to Syria to advocate for her client. Bell and Zaydan travelled to the region last week to query the prosecution’s evidence. Bell argued that her son, a former mobile phone technician, could not have confessed to the crime – as is recorded on the court file – because he speaks no Arabic. Local journalists have confirmed to this masthead that the court hearing the case is a religious court set up as part of the local Islamist administration in Idlib province, and is predominantly focused on punishing foreign fighters. On Bell’s account, the widow told the court through an interpreter on Wednesday night that the dispute between Stevenson and Burgess that led to the killing was over a small debt of about $10.



In court, according to Bell, the widow told Stevenson he could have the money back. Stevenson did not respond to her. After the court was adjourned, Bell told this masthead: “I won’t leave. I won’t leave him here. It’s not right. Who else is going to visit him in jail and speak English?” “He’s not a foreign fighter,” she said. “I do truly believe Patrick decided to come here on his own silly self, on a big lark.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Priced out and staying put: Gen Z Australians are living with their parents in record numbers
World.content:
Half of Australians in their 20s are still living with their parents, while a record share of lower-income families are suffering housing stress as the social and economic cost of the housing affordability crunch mounts. One of the nation’s most important social studies, The Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey, shows the proportion of people aged 18 to 29 years old living in the family home has reached 49.9 per cent, up from 39.4 per cent in 2001. Young men are more likely to live with their parents than young women; 55 per cent of men aged 18-29 still live in the family home compared to 45 per cent of women. However, the gender gap has narrowed – in 2001, young men were 11.9 percentage points more likely than women to live with parents, but that had fallen to 9.6 percentage points by 2024. Ethan Benedicto with his mother, Sheila Benedicto, at home in Melbourne. Picture by JOE ARMAO



Trade journalist Ethan Benedicto, 24, lives with his parents and 18-year-old brother in Clyde North, a south-eastern suburb of Melbourne, and has never lived out of home. “Everything is just expensive in general. Rent’s expensive … but I save over 60 per cent of my fortnightly pay,” he said. “I think it’s kind of cultural as well. A lot of South-East Asian friends, Middle Eastern friends, I know live with their families as well. They have cousins, uncles and aunties at their homes. But I think my other reasoning is that my parents aren’t kicking me out or anything. Like, they still want me to stay at home.” Benedicto does have a cut-off point – he wants his own place with his partner by the time he’s 27 to 30. “I also just think that like my parents want their own space,” he said.



Oliver Mason, 24, lives at home with his parents in Picnic Point. Wolter Peeters Oliver Mason, 24, works part-time at an op shop and feels no pressure to move out of home in Sydney’s Picnic Point. To him, it doesn’t make sense to move out when housing is so expensive and all of his friends live with their parents. “I think there’s a bit of complacency and apathy that’s bred out of the fact that the housing market is hard to access,” he said. “And my parents are middle-class comfortable, so I don’t feel that rush or that push. If your friends are also all moving out, then you might think ‘oh, my friends are having all these new experiences, and I’m at home’. But since a lot of my friends haven’t moved out, I don’t feel like I’m missing out on too much,” he said. Mason said he would only move out if he fell in love.



“If you partner with someone, and you want your own space, I would say that that would be my main driver to move out,” he said. Melbourne University’s Dr Kyle Peyton, a report co-author, said housing costs were a major factor keeping young adults in the family home. “It’s more difficult than it’s ever been in Australia for young people to get out of their parents’ house and find a place to live and start a family,” he said. “Real incomes have been stagnating over the past few years, and so I think for this generation there is a real sense of hopelessness about the future.”



Unhappy and broke renters Most people aged under 30 who live out of home are renters, but the HILDA survey shows many of them are dissatisfied with their accommodation. One in five young people not living with their parents reported their accommodation had “inadequate comfort” versus one in 25 who lived with parents. “The data are showing us that those people who do move out of home are less satisfied with the housing they’re moving into and they are more satisfied if they live with their parents, basically,” said Peyton. “For a lot of young people they’re asking ‘am I going to go live in what may be a mould-infested rental property or do I just stay with my parents until I’m in my late 20s to try to save up for a deposit and try to buy something?’”



The survey also revealed 36 per cent of private renters and 30 per cent of mortgage holders among the bottom 40 per cent of earners in mainland capital cities spent more than 30 per cent of disposable income on housing. Households in the bottom 40 per cent of the income distribution that spend more than 30 per cent on rent or mortgage payments are considered to be in housing stress. “Housing stress reached a record high in 2024,” the report said. “Renters, single parents and older singles have the highest rates of housing stress.” The survey also drew attention to the consequences of a prolonged period of cost-of-living pressure. Nearly 8 per cent reported not being able to pay the mortgage or rent on time, the highest share since 2003. Melbourne University economics professor Roger Wilkins said key measures of financial and housing stress were “heading in the wrong direction” despite a relatively strong jobs market.



“What’s concerning is that this is happening in the context of record high employment rates,” he said. “We’re working more than ever, yet the cost of living is outpacing growth in incomes. The real concern is what if employment starts to turn down? Should the labour market weaken, we could see these measures of economic wellbeing deteriorate even further.” Life is exhausting As Australians struggle with the cost of living, they are also reporting less energy and more fatigue. The survey’s vitality scores – which measure how energetic people feel versus tired and worn out – have fallen steadily across all age groups (for men and women) during the past decade, with the largest decline among women aged 25-34.



There has also been a substantial and persistent decline in self-reported mental health among younger Australians, particularly young women. The HILDA survey has tracked the same 9000 households since 2001; the newly published survey was taken in 2024, tracking almost a quarter-century. World.title: ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval Rob Harris September 23, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese will declare the post-1945 international order “no longer fit for purpose” and warn that Australia must help shape what replaces it as growing strategic competition between the United States and China transforms the Indo-Pacific. In a major foreign policy address in New York, the prime minister will argue that the assumptions underpinning the global system since the end of the Cold War are being tested, forcing middle powers such as Australia to build new partnerships while defending the rules that remain essential. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking to reporters in New York City on Wednesday, AEST. Dominic Lorrimer “Since the end of the Cold War, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security; efficiency mattered more than resilience; and international rules would be observed as a matter of course,” Albanese will tell the Atlantic Council’s Global Citizen Awards dinner on Wednesday night, where he will be honoured alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Formula One chief Stefano Domenicali and actor and singer Cynthia Erivo. “Both those expectations are now being tested. The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.”



His speech carries echoes of the message Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered nine months ago at the World Economic Forum at Davos, Switzerland, where he said the “old order is not coming back” and urged fellow middle powers to unite to find a new way. Albanese will meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday (New York time), where the two countries are expected to sign a bilateral security arrangement. As US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping prepare to meet at the White House on Thursday, Albanese sought several leaders of middle power nations, including Britain’s Andy Burnham, Canada’s Mark Carney and France’s Emmanuel Macron, to help build consensus on several issues, including the rise of artificial intelligence. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations headquarters in New York City. Dominic Lorrimer But efforts appear to have been fruitless, as Trump very publicly rejected the push from more than 20 leading economies several times in his UN address, saying he was interested only in the economic benefits of winning the technology race, and not regulating AI’s capacity.



Albanese was also at loggerheads with the Trump administration, which has condemned Australia’s plans to overhaul social media algorithms and regulate perceived harmful content. In a submission to the Albanese government, the US embassy described the reforms as “facilitating censorship”. “It’s not about giving government control; it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices, which is why it is framed in that way,” Albanese told journalists in New York. The prime minister later met Trump at a UN leaders’ reception, posting a picture of the pair on his social media platforms saying it was “always good to catch up” with the president. There is growing discontent within the group of middle powers at the lack of progress towards peace in the Middle East, Trump’s war against Iran, and Russia’s continued aerial bombardment of Ukraine after nearly five years. Several experts, including former prime minister Kevin Rudd, have also warned about the increased risk of conflict in the Indo-Pacific over Taiwan in the coming years. Albanese will use his speech to set out a vision for Australia to help build a new international order rather than simply respond to the changes under way.



“Australia’s response to this is to actively seek to shape and build the order that replaces the old,” he will say, while preserving “the rules that matter most” and creating new partnerships and relationships. Related Article Social media Albanese defends Australia’s social media crackdown from Trump admin’s ‘censorship’ blast The prime minister will identify the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing as the “most consequential factor” shaping the Indo-Pacific, while rejecting the idea that the region should be viewed solely through the prism of the two superpowers. “Our alliance with the United States is the anchor of Australia’s foreign policy,” Albanese will say. But he will also reaffirm his government’s approach to China, Australia’s largest trading partner, saying the country would engage in the national interest. “How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly,” he will say. “But it cannot be the only lens through which we see the region.”



“The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces. Its countries are not spectators. They are shaping its future and writing their own script.” Albanese will argue that the upheaval of recent years, including war and the pandemic, has exposed the vulnerabilities of supply chains and forced governments to put resilience alongside economic efficiency. “Governments must build the capacity to withstand shocks they did not cause and cannot control,” he will say. That will include strengthening Australia’s sovereign capability while working with partners on economic security, critical supply chains and energy. The Atlantic Council dinner is one of the high-profile events of UN General Assembly week, with more than 700 senior government, business, military, media and civil-society figures expected to attend.



Albanese is being recognised by the Washington-based think tank for his role in strengthening Australia’s alliances and partnerships and promoting security and stability across the Indo-Pacific. Related Article Updated

AI ‘Same sense of urgency’: UN chief compares AI risk to nuclear weapons His speech places particular emphasis on Australia’s expanding network of partnerships across the Indo-Pacific, including its relationship with ASEAN and a growing web of security agreements with Pacific nations. He will describe the Pacific as “both a home and a family to Australia” and say the region’s priorities, sovereignty and culture must be respected. “For our Pacific neighbours, climate change is the most immediate security threat,” Albanese will say.



“Building resilience without abandoning openness,” Albanese will say. “Strengthening regional partnerships without abandoning rules.” And Australia would deepen its alliance with the United States and engage its largest trading partner, China, “without allowing either relationship to define who we are”. “In an uncertain world, leadership means showing up for one another, sharing burdens and giving our neighbours greater power to shape their futures,” he will say. Kool-Aid McKinstry, Amon-Ra St. Brown, Sauce Gardner, Storm Duck, Younghoe Koo, DeMarvion Overshown, Tank Bigsby and Tank Dell. All right, I’ll grant that FuiFui MoiMoi and Steele Sidebottom are pretty good, too.”

The celebrity encounters (C8) continue: “When I was 14, a friend of my father arranged for me to meet Ricky Nelson in the dressing room of the Sydney Stadium,” recalls Janet Scilly of Waterloo. “Of course, my father had to be there. I had a lot to say but was struck dumb on seeing him. My father thought he was a nice young man because he called Dad ‘Sir’ and shook his hand.”

“I’m not sure if I share Alan Phillips’ (C8) view about C8 driving AI mad,” thinks Seppo Ranki of Glenhaven. “As an experiment, I checked out my name and suburb on Google. Part of the AI Overview said: ‘He frequently writes short, witty observations and life stories for The Sydney Morning Herald’s popular Column 8 section. His published items often feature memories of farm life, old vehicles and everyday humorous encounters.’ I suspect AI has a pretty good handle on both C8 and me.”

Mark Berg of Caringbah South writes: “When at high-school German classes (C8) in the late 1970s, we watched German videos and were expected to translate the script. One memorable line was ‘Mit einer Perucke bist du ein anderer Mensch’. It means, ‘with a wig, you are another person’. Very useful indeed.”

“I’m still waiting to inform anyone who’s interested, in my best schoolboy French, that ‘the pen of the gardener’s niece is on the table in the conservatory’,” informs John Clarke (Jean Leclerc to his mates) of Lorn. World.title: ‘Fragmented’ care contributed to Brisbane woman’s death: coroner
World.content:
NationalQueenslandQueensland Health ‘Fragmented’ care contributed to Brisbane woman’s death: coroner Catherine Strohfeldt September 23, 2026 — 8:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The death of a 69-year-old Brisbane woman during medical testing might prompt a rethink of southern Brisbane’s health and hospital system, a coronial report has suggested. Yaqin Han died on October 14, 2022, when she suffered a cardiac arrest during a diagnostic test at the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Hospital. Coroner Ainslie Kierkegaard ruled that while the test – which involved having Han run on a treadmill – triggered the cardiac arrest, her doctors had acted appropriately throughout it. Brisbane woman Yaqin Han was referred to the Princess Alexandra Hospital, but treated at the Queen Elizabeth II Jubilee Hospital (pictured). Courtney Kruk Kierkegaard said cardiologist Reza Reyaldeen stopped the test as soon as the 69-year-old began complaining of symptoms.



By that point, Han’s heartbeat had become erratic before declining into a cardiac arrest, from which she could not be revived. Related Article Mental health Wards were over capacity when patient took her life, inquest told The coroner said it was only “with the benefit of hindsight” that the care team led by Reyaldeen might have stopped the test sooner, as it would have been outside normal practice based on Han’s vital signs, which were being monitored throughout. However, Kierkegaard highlighted that another south Brisbane hospital, the Princess Alexandra, was the area’s “heart valve centre of excellence”. Han was initially referred to the PA Hospital, but was treated through a hub at the QEII Hospital, which was closer to her home.



She had been diagnosed with aortic stenosis – a narrowing of the heart’s aortic valve – having suffered dizziness, lightheadedness, and shortness of breath walking up hills. However, various doctors who treated Han were unclear whether her condition was a moderate or severe case. Experts testifying to the court agreed her symptoms were not enough to determine the severity of her diagnosis. Her care team decided to undertake an exercise stress test, rather than invasive diagnostic procedures, to determine whether she would need surgery. However, Kierkegaard said there were potential warning signs about Han’s condition being more severe than cardiologists at the QEII Hospital suspected, but they were missed because her care was fragmented.



Related Article Healthcare Doctors almost sent Kris home with a migraine. Then her whole face went numb Han was also a Mandarin speaker, requiring a translator for her appointments. The inquest found medical staff, in some instances, had trouble contacting Han, and a period of 10 months had elapsed between the last time she was questioned about her symptoms and the decision to order the stress test. The maximum acceptable limit for the gap between consultation and testing, experts at the inquest testified, was 12 months. In an independent inquiry, which Kierkegaard referenced throughout her inquest, Staff Specialist Interventional Cardiologist Anthony Camuglia provided four reasons for the time lapse.



These included interruption from the COVID-19 pandemic, Han’s multiple GPs, the Metro South Health system, and staff turnover at the QEII Hospital. Kierkegaard agreed COVID-19 restrictions had some effect, but said there was “scope for the health service to re-examine its model of cardiac care”. She pointed to a triage system used in Brisbane’s northern hospital service, where complex cases are referred to the Prince Charles Hospital. World.title: Iranian president vows not to surrender in defiant, historic UN speech
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastMiddle East at war Iranian president vows not to surrender in defiant, historic UN speech Michael Koziol September 24, 2026 — 3:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian declared his country would not be cowed into surrender in a defiant address to the United Nations that came a day after US President Donald Trump used the same stage to renew his threat to “annihilate” Iran. Pezeshkian’s speech marked the first time in the UN’s 81-year history that a foreign leader at war with the US addressed the body at its New York headquarters. The Iranian president held up pictures of the assassinated supreme leader Ali Khamenei and children killed by missiles in the war that began nearly seven months ago. Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian addressed the United Nations General Assembly on Wednesday. AP Photo/Heather Khalifa “I come from an Iran where, in truth, they bombed a school,” he said. “You see these children? These children perished under bombs, with weapons used by the United States and Israel. They were innocent.” The US has never publicly acknowledged that it was responsible for the missile strike on an Iranian girls’ school on the first day of the war, killing about 120 children and dozens more adults. That is despite multiple reports from US news outlets about the findings of internal investigations which confirmed US responsibility.



Pezeshkian claimed Iran was ready to resume talks and find a diplomatic solution to the war – an outcome that has eluded negotiators so far, despite a short-lived memorandum of understanding signed with the US in June. But his speech projected resistance to any notion that Iran could be bombed into subjugation, as Trump had countenanced from the podium 24 hours earlier. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi watches the Iranian president address the United Nations in New York. Bloomberg “They have learned that Iran cannot be made to surrender,” Pezeshkian said. “He [Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only increase in the face of sanctions, increased pressure, increased bullying. We will never bow our head or bend at the knee.” A lone American delegate walked out of the UN General Assembly shortly after Pezeshkian’s speech began. An Iranian delegation including Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi were authorised by the US to attend, although some members of the proposed delegation were refused visas.



Pezeshkian also argued Iran must be allowed to develop a civilian nuclear program, insisting – as Tehran always has – that the Islamic Republic does not wish to develop nuclear weapons. However, Iran has a long history of building secret nuclear sites and uranium enrichment facilities, and barring weapons inspectors. Pezeshkian said it was Israel that should face scrutiny, not Iran. “Israel targets any neighbourhood in any city in any province – commits assassinations like a true terrorist,” he said. It was the first time a foreign leader whose country is at war with the US has travelled to New York to speak at the UN. AP Photo/Heather Khalifa “They are committing genocide by using the so-called technologies they have at their disposal – then they label others as terrorists. “The nuclear weapon is in Israel, but the inspector is in Iran. Israel kills, but Iran is subject to sanctions. This is a true tragedy.”



Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due to land in New York on Thursday (US time) to address the UN, before immediately flying home. Related Article Donald Trump At UN, Trump threatens to ‘annihilate’ Iran but predicts deal after midterms New York mayor Zohran Mamdani has dropped his threat to arrest the Israeli leader based on an outstanding International Criminal Court warrant, saying the city did not have the jurisdiction. On the Strait of Hormuz, the crucial shipping passage between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula, Pezeshkian told the UN that Iran would continue to lay a claim over the waterway. “We cannot let some have free access and gain their interest from a waterway while at the same time using that waterway to impose their aggression upon us,” he said. “They close access for us to our own waterway … we will not succumb to that.”



While threatening annihilation of Iran – which he has done before – Trump also predicted there would be a deal after the US midterm elections, arguing the Iranians were dragging it out to inflict political pain upon him via higher oil and petrol prices. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have recently targeted Saudi Arabian energy infrastructure and the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, another crucial oil shipping route between Yemen and Africa. This has contributed to the latest spike in oil prices, just as the Russia-Ukraine war is causing the price of diesel to rise. The UN General Assembly watching Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Bloomberg But Trump has continued to project that he is in no rush to solve the issue. Helima Croft, managing director and global head of commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, said on Wednesday (US time) there was an “urgency deficit” in the Trump administration because prices were not yet that high. Brent crude, the international oil benchmark, was trading just above $US100 ($142) a barrel on Wednesday.



“Prices are not $US150,” Croft told an event hosted by the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace “If you can keep West Texas International prices below $US100 or below $90, you may think time is on your side, that you can let the blockade do its work. Essentially, let Iran have to deal with a lack of essential goods, soaring inflation, the rial crashing. “I think that’s a theory that many in the administration are now operating under - that they have time on their side.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: ‘Gaslighting’: Diana’s brother hits back at palace over his claim about the King
World.content:
WorldEuropeRoyal family ‘Gaslighting’: Diana’s brother hits back at palace over his claim about the King David Crowe September 24, 2026 — 2:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Earl Spencer has accused Buckingham Palace officials of “gaslighting” him over his account of his sister, Princess Diana, when they suggested grief had clouded his memory of the past. Spencer stood by his controversial claim that King Charles – then the Prince of Wales – had said the world would “forget” Diana after she died in a tragic car crash in 1997. Earl Spencer, brother of Princess Diana, on ITV’s Lorraine program. YouTube In his first live television interview about his new book, Spencer also insisted he did not set out to write a “hit piece” on the King and sought instead to celebrate his sister. But his claims are being denounced by palace insiders and defenders of the King across the British media, while broadcaster Piers Morgan threatens to sue him over a glaring error in the book.



The furore centres on Spencer’s account of a private conversation with Charles about plans for Diana’s two sons, Princes William and Harry, to walk behind her coffin in her funeral procession.

Spencer writes that he complained about the plan in a phone call but that Charles insisted it would go ahead. “He unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death,” the earl writes in the new book. “‘Rest assured,’ he hissed, ‘we’ll forget her soon enough’.” Related Article Royal family ‘Those are exactly the words he said’: Earl Spencer says he is telling the truth about the King Buckingham Palace issued a statement to the media to dismiss this version of the conversation said to have occurred almost three decades ago. “While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss,” the palace said in a statement.



Spencer argued that the palace statement tried to cast doubt on his memory but did not deny the words he reported. “If you look at the words, it’s classic gaslighting,” the earl told ITV’s Lorraine program on Wednesday morning (UK time). “So what they do is, ‘Oh, maybe his mind’s not right to remember these things because of the distance of time and grief’. “No one said that the King didn’t say that because he did.” Princess Diana, 36, was killed in a crash in Paris when paparazzi photographers were chasing the car she was in with her partner at the time, Dodi Fayed.



Born Diana Spencer, a member of an aristocratic family dating back centuries in Britain, she was close to her brother, who inherited the title and is now the head of the family. Copies of Earl Spencer’s new book on display in a London bookshop. AP Photo/Kin Cheung Spencer antagonised the royal family at Diana’s funeral by praising her in a eulogy that criticised the way she was treated by them and the media. He said his eulogy had been influenced by the phone conversation with Charles about whether the world would remember Diana. Spencer said this was why he quoted the King’s remark about Diana being forgotten.



“I wasn’t setting out to do a hit piece on the King at all,” he said. Related Article Royal family Earl Spencer’s apology isn’t enough, says Piers Morgan “The bits that have been included in the book are totally in context. So that clip you played of me [on ITV] getting through the end of the eulogy, I end with this thing that the final thought I give is that Diana will never be extinguished from our minds. “That was a direct counter to the King saying, ‘We’ll forget her soon enough’. “So it had to be in because the strand through the book is how did this eulogy come about?”



Spencer joined Charles and Prince Philip in the funeral procession at a time of national mourning for Diana. Extracts from his new book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, appeared in The Daily Mirror last week, setting off a media storm over his claims. Loading Commentators in The Times and the London Telegraph have strongly criticised Spencer and cast doubt on his memory, while also suggesting he has written a salacious book for the money. Spencer has given his critics ammunition with a basic error of fact in the book, when he describes broadcaster Piers Morgan as an editor of The Daily Mirror at a point in time when he was not.



Related Article Review Bashir, royalty and childhood trauma: the revelations from Charles Spencer’s book Morgan has announced he will sue Spencer over the mistake. Spencer admitted he was wrong. “I’m very happy to acknowledge I made a small error, and I’ve apologised, and it will be put right in the in the second edition,” he said. Morgan has called on the publisher, Penguin Random House, to stop selling the book.



“It’s not just a little silly slip-up or mistake,” Morgan said. “He has directly accused me in his book, which is clearly going to sell gazillions of copies around the world, of the most egregious invasion of royal privacy in history.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Australian charged with murder in Syria to be medically assessed after mother’s plea
World.content:
NationalSyrian conflict Australian charged with murder in Syria to be medically assessed after mother’s plea Michael Bachelard September 24, 2026 — 12:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A young Australian man who is facing the death penalty in Syria will be medically assessed for mental impairment after his mother and a lawyer flew to the strife-torn region to advocate for him. Patrick Stevenson, 20, a Muslim convert from the Gold Coast, is accused of murdering another Australian convert, Abdullah Glen Burgess, late last year by shooting him eight times with an AK-47 inside the dead man’s apartment in Idlib province. Patrick Stevenson, a Gold Coast Muslim convert who is now in jail in Syria charged with murdering another Australian convert. Stevenson’s mother Angela Bell and human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan flew to the region last week when it became clear his accuser would not accept “diya”, or blood money, which is allowable under Islamic law, instead of the death sentence. The accuser is Burgess’s widow, who is also Australian, and who this masthead has agreed not to name because she claims it would endanger her. She is a witness in the case and, according to Bell, told the court she would not accept financial compensation because it would not bring her husband back.



Bell and Zaydan say they do not believe Stevenson is guilty of premeditated murder, and insist he does not know what’s going on now because of his ADHD, serious learning disabilities and probably autism, compounded by a fresh head injury and a months-long stay in prison where nobody else speaks English. Related Article Courts ‘Of course I’m frightened’: Australian mother flies to son accused of murder in Syria Bell said she had visited Stevenson three times since arriving in Syria last week. “He is confused. He tells me he does not know why he is here. He has significant problems with his memory… He struggles to concentrate… His thinking appears slowed. There are long pauses. He struggles to process what we are saying to him and has difficulty expressing himself. And he is simply not the same child I knew before this.” She said he had a large wound on the back of his head, and remembers waking up confused in police custody as they were stitching it.



After a court hearing on Wednesday night (Australian time), Zaydan told this masthead she and an Australian government-appointed Syrian lawyer had made a plea of mental impairment, which had been accepted by the court. It ordered that Stevenson should be medically assessed. “His legal team was granted permission to be present at the assessment. Patrick was present, but he didn’t understand what was going on,” Zaydan told this masthead. Another application, to have Stevenson’s electronic devices returned, was rejected with no reasons provided, Zaydan said. Angela Bell is in Syria to help her son. They also negotiated that Bell be able to visit her son daily in the Syrian prison.



Both men involved in the case converted independently to Islam in Australia, then went to live in Idlib province, which is under the control of Hay’at Tahrir al-Sham (HTS), a group the Australian government considers to be a terrorist organisation. Human rights lawyer Bernadette Zaydan, who is going to Syria to advocate for her client. Bell and Zaydan travelled to the region last week to query the prosecution’s evidence. Bell argued that her son, a former mobile phone technician, could not have confessed to the crime – as is recorded on the court file – because he speaks no Arabic. Local journalists have confirmed to this masthead that the court hearing the case is a religious court set up as part of the local Islamist administration in Idlib province, and is predominantly focused on punishing foreign fighters. On Bell’s account, the widow told the court through an interpreter on Wednesday night that the dispute between Stevenson and Burgess that led to the killing was over a small debt of about $10.



In court, according to Bell, the widow told Stevenson he could have the money back. Stevenson did not respond to her. After the court was adjourned, Bell told this masthead: “I won’t leave. I won’t leave him here. It’s not right. Who else is going to visit him in jail and speak English?” “He’s not a foreign fighter,” she said. “I do truly believe Patrick decided to come here on his own silly self, on a big lark.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Priced out and staying put: Gen Z Australians are living with their parents in record numbers
World.content:
Half of Australians in their 20s are still living with their parents, while a record share of lower-income families are suffering housing stress as the social and economic cost of the housing affordability crunch mounts. One of the nation’s most important social studies, The Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) survey, shows the proportion of people aged 18 to 29 years old living in the family home has reached 49.9 per cent, up from 39.4 per cent in 2001. Young men are more likely to live with their parents than young women; 55 per cent of men aged 18-29 still live in the family home compared to 45 per cent of women. However, the gender gap has narrowed – in 2001, young men were 11.9 percentage points more likely than women to live with parents, but that had fallen to 9.6 percentage points by 2024. Ethan Benedicto with his mother, Sheila Benedicto, at home in Melbourne. Picture by JOE ARMAO



Trade journalist Ethan Benedicto, 24, lives with his parents and 18-year-old brother in Clyde North, a south-eastern suburb of Melbourne, and has never lived out of home. “Everything is just expensive in general. Rent’s expensive … but I save over 60 per cent of my fortnightly pay,” he said. “I think it’s kind of cultural as well. A lot of South-East Asian friends, Middle Eastern friends, I know live with their families as well. They have cousins, uncles and aunties at their homes. But I think my other reasoning is that my parents aren’t kicking me out or anything. Like, they still want me to stay at home.” Benedicto does have a cut-off point – he wants his own place with his partner by the time he’s 27 to 30. “I also just think that like my parents want their own space,” he said.



Oliver Mason, 24, lives at home with his parents in Picnic Point. Wolter Peeters Oliver Mason, 24, works part-time at an op shop and feels no pressure to move out of home in Sydney’s Picnic Point. To him, it doesn’t make sense to move out when housing is so expensive and all of his friends live with their parents. “I think there’s a bit of complacency and apathy that’s bred out of the fact that the housing market is hard to access,” he said. “And my parents are middle-class comfortable, so I don’t feel that rush or that push. If your friends are also all moving out, then you might think ‘oh, my friends are having all these new experiences, and I’m at home’. But since a lot of my friends haven’t moved out, I don’t feel like I’m missing out on too much,” he said. Mason said he would only move out if he fell in love.



“If you partner with someone, and you want your own space, I would say that that would be my main driver to move out,” he said. Melbourne University’s Dr Kyle Peyton, a report co-author, said housing costs were a major factor keeping young adults in the family home. “It’s more difficult than it’s ever been in Australia for young people to get out of their parents’ house and find a place to live and start a family,” he said. “Real incomes have been stagnating over the past few years, and so I think for this generation there is a real sense of hopelessness about the future.”



Unhappy and broke renters Most people aged under 30 who live out of home are renters, but the HILDA survey shows many of them are dissatisfied with their accommodation. One in five young people not living with their parents reported their accommodation had “inadequate comfort” versus one in 25 who lived with parents. “The data are showing us that those people who do move out of home are less satisfied with the housing they’re moving into and they are more satisfied if they live with their parents, basically,” said Peyton. “For a lot of young people they’re asking ‘am I going to go live in what may be a mould-infested rental property or do I just stay with my parents until I’m in my late 20s to try to save up for a deposit and try to buy something?’”



The survey also revealed 36 per cent of private renters and 30 per cent of mortgage holders among the bottom 40 per cent of earners in mainland capital cities spent more than 30 per cent of disposable income on housing. Households in the bottom 40 per cent of the income distribution that spend more than 30 per cent on rent or mortgage payments are considered to be in housing stress. “Housing stress reached a record high in 2024,” the report said. “Renters, single parents and older singles have the highest rates of housing stress.” The survey also drew attention to the consequences of a prolonged period of cost-of-living pressure. Nearly 8 per cent reported not being able to pay the mortgage or rent on time, the highest share since 2003. Melbourne University economics professor Roger Wilkins said key measures of financial and housing stress were “heading in the wrong direction” despite a relatively strong jobs market.



“What’s concerning is that this is happening in the context of record high employment rates,” he said. “We’re working more than ever, yet the cost of living is outpacing growth in incomes. The real concern is what if employment starts to turn down? Should the labour market weaken, we could see these measures of economic wellbeing deteriorate even further.” Life is exhausting As Australians struggle with the cost of living, they are also reporting less energy and more fatigue. The survey’s vitality scores – which measure how energetic people feel versus tired and worn out – have fallen steadily across all age groups (for men and women) during the past decade, with the largest decline among women aged 25-34.



There has also been a substantial and persistent decline in self-reported mental health among younger Australians, particularly young women. The HILDA survey has tracked the same 9000 households since 2001; the newly published survey was taken in 2024, tracking almost a quarter-century. World.title: ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership ‘No longer fit for purpose’: Albanese warns of world order upheaval Rob Harris September 23, 2026 — 10:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Anthony Albanese will declare the post-1945 international order “no longer fit for purpose” and warn that Australia must help shape what replaces it as growing strategic competition between the United States and China transforms the Indo-Pacific. In a major foreign policy address in New York, the prime minister will argue that the assumptions underpinning the global system since the end of the Cold War are being tested, forcing middle powers such as Australia to build new partnerships while defending the rules that remain essential. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaking to reporters in New York City on Wednesday, AEST. Dominic Lorrimer “Since the end of the Cold War, the prevailing assumptions of international affairs were clear: openness was security; efficiency mattered more than resilience; and international rules would be observed as a matter of course,” Albanese will tell the Atlantic Council’s Global Citizen Awards dinner on Wednesday night, where he will be honoured alongside Finnish President Alexander Stubb, Formula One chief Stefano Domenicali and actor and singer Cynthia Erivo. “Both those expectations are now being tested. The post-1945 world order is no longer fit for purpose. Universal institutions that remain necessary are now not always sufficient for the challenges we face.”



His speech carries echoes of the message Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered nine months ago at the World Economic Forum at Davos, Switzerland, where he said the “old order is not coming back” and urged fellow middle powers to unite to find a new way. Albanese will meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Wednesday (New York time), where the two countries are expected to sign a bilateral security arrangement. As US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping prepare to meet at the White House on Thursday, Albanese sought several leaders of middle power nations, including Britain’s Andy Burnham, Canada’s Mark Carney and France’s Emmanuel Macron, to help build consensus on several issues, including the rise of artificial intelligence. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during a meeting with UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham at the United Nations headquarters in New York City. Dominic Lorrimer But efforts appear to have been fruitless, as Trump very publicly rejected the push from more than 20 leading economies several times in his UN address, saying he was interested only in the economic benefits of winning the technology race, and not regulating AI’s capacity.



Albanese was also at loggerheads with the Trump administration, which has condemned Australia’s plans to overhaul social media algorithms and regulate perceived harmful content. In a submission to the Albanese government, the US embassy described the reforms as “facilitating censorship”. “It’s not about giving government control; it’s about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices, which is why it is framed in that way,” Albanese told journalists in New York. The prime minister later met Trump at a UN leaders’ reception, posting a picture of the pair on his social media platforms saying it was “always good to catch up” with the president. There is growing discontent within the group of middle powers at the lack of progress towards peace in the Middle East, Trump’s war against Iran, and Russia’s continued aerial bombardment of Ukraine after nearly five years. Several experts, including former prime minister Kevin Rudd, have also warned about the increased risk of conflict in the Indo-Pacific over Taiwan in the coming years. Albanese will use his speech to set out a vision for Australia to help build a new international order rather than simply respond to the changes under way.



“Australia’s response to this is to actively seek to shape and build the order that replaces the old,” he will say, while preserving “the rules that matter most” and creating new partnerships and relationships. Related Article Social media Albanese defends Australia’s social media crackdown from Trump admin’s ‘censorship’ blast The prime minister will identify the strategic competition between Washington and Beijing as the “most consequential factor” shaping the Indo-Pacific, while rejecting the idea that the region should be viewed solely through the prism of the two superpowers. “Our alliance with the United States is the anchor of Australia’s foreign policy,” Albanese will say. But he will also reaffirm his government’s approach to China, Australia’s largest trading partner, saying the country would engage in the national interest. “How Washington and Beijing manage their relationship matters profoundly,” he will say. “But it cannot be the only lens through which we see the region.”



“The Indo-Pacific is not a chessboard on which superpowers move the pieces. Its countries are not spectators. They are shaping its future and writing their own script.” Albanese will argue that the upheaval of recent years, including war and the pandemic, has exposed the vulnerabilities of supply chains and forced governments to put resilience alongside economic efficiency. “Governments must build the capacity to withstand shocks they did not cause and cannot control,” he will say. That will include strengthening Australia’s sovereign capability while working with partners on economic security, critical supply chains and energy. The Atlantic Council dinner is one of the high-profile events of UN General Assembly week, with more than 700 senior government, business, military, media and civil-society figures expected to attend.



Albanese is being recognised by the Washington-based think tank for his role in strengthening Australia’s alliances and partnerships and promoting security and stability across the Indo-Pacific. Related Article Updated

AI ‘Same sense of urgency’: UN chief compares AI risk to nuclear weapons His speech places particular emphasis on Australia’s expanding network of partnerships across the Indo-Pacific, including its relationship with ASEAN and a growing web of security agreements with Pacific nations. He will describe the Pacific as “both a home and a family to Australia” and say the region’s priorities, sovereignty and culture must be respected. “For our Pacific neighbours, climate change is the most immediate security threat,” Albanese will say.



“Building resilience without abandoning openness,” Albanese will say. “Strengthening regional partnerships without abandoning rules.” And Australia would deepen its alliance with the United States and engage its largest trading partner, China, “without allowing either relationship to define who we are”. “In an uncertain world, leadership means showing up for one another, sharing burdens and giving our neighbours greater power to shape their futures,” he will say.
