Tech.title: YouTube is building AI creator tools that do almost everything for them
Tech.content:
Part of the job of a content creator is to figure out how to get their work in front of the most people. Cracking — or fighting — the algorithm has historically been a frustration for creators, but YouTube is increasingly simply telling creators what they should do.

At the annual creator-focused Made on YouTube event, the company announced updates to the suite of AI-powered creator tools it unveiled in 2025. In its initial iteration, the dashboard of creator tools included things like A/B testing for video thumbnails and a chatbot interface to query how content was performing. This year’s update adds AI tools for more complex tasks.

Perhaps most significantly, YouTube is introducing an AI “agent” that will work in the background to optimize a creator’s channel. For example, the tool will monitor a creator’s back catalog of videos, looking for content that has taken on a new life, is relevant to the news, or has started trending. The agent will offer suggestions for tweaking the thumbnails or titles for older videos to ride the new wave of relevance. The tool can also put together things like pitches for brands by combing through a creator’s YouTube channel and pulling out demographic and audience data to make a case to potential sponsors, says Amjad Hanif, vice president of creator products at YouTube.

Creators can ask YouTube’s built-in AI tools for video feedback. Image: YouTube

The new features iterate on previously existing AI-powered tools. The agent will now generate entire thumbnails and titles based on the content of an uploaded video, and creators can ask the tool for feedback on their own thumbnails. Viewers may also see different content as creators run tests via YouTube Studio: A dynamic thumbnail tool allows creators to upload up to three different images for each video, and YouTube’s system will assign the best one to different audience segments to try to boost watch time. YouTube is taking it a step further, too, by allowing creators to test three different versions of videos — a clip with a different intro and hook, for example, or with a different structure — to see how each performs. The different versions of the same video will be fed to small audience segments to test which results in the highest watch time; creators can go forward with the “winner” to make it the permanent video, or YouTube will automatically do so after seven days. Hanif says the YouTube system ensures the three video versions are not “dramatically different” from one another.

How content creators use AI has been a hot-button issue in some circles. Earlier this summer, Hank Green angered fans when he acknowledged that he had been relying on AI to do research for his videos. (Some observers diagnosed Green’s problem as not one specifically about AI, but rather about overwork and burnout in the creator industry.) It’s not just Green who’s had to defend himself: There are countless stories of brands using or promoting AI — or simply being suspected of doing so — that have spiraled into scandal. For many content creators or public figures, using AI in their work is a reputational risk; is using YouTube’s behind-the-scenes AI tools something they’re worried about? Hanif differentiates between instances where creators are using AI to be more efficient, versus when the tools are doing the actual job of a creator.

“What I’ve heard from creators and what I’ve seen from my own conversations with viewers is that when it feels like it’s not actually from the creator, but the tools have taken over and the tools are producing the content, I think that’s kind of where it crosses the line a bit,” Hanif says. Writing the script, shooting the scenes, wholesale creating the content — these are the types of AI use that might become a problem for creators and viewers, he says.

The real question is what tangible effects this suite of AI tools actually has on creator success. Have views exploded for YouTubers doing A/B testing? Does using the chatbot to plan or tweak content help creators connect more with what their audiences want to see? I asked YouTube and Hanif if they had data that shows the tools actually improving metrics for the creators who use them, but the company declined to share anything. What it does do, per Hanif, is save creators time.

“The time that we’ve saved there is time that goes back into the creativity,” Hanif says.

Tech.title: Discord will now automatically estimate your age
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Let me see some ID: age verification is spreading across the internet

Discord is rolling out a new global age assurance system, seven months after pausing its previous verification measures following backlash from users. Starting today in every country except Australia and the UK, Discord will automatically assign users to an estimated age group based on “multiple account signals,” with account restrictions placed on users believed to be between 13 and 17.

The updates follow Discord slamming the brakes on its earlier age verification rollout in February in response to data privacy concerns. Its previous system required adults to verify themselves via video selfies or ID documentation, and faced criticism after a data breach at a third-party Discord vendor exposed user info and scanned photo IDs.

If Discord is unable to automatically assign you an age group, or places you in the wrong one, you’ll have to head to this setting to provide verification information. Image: Discord

Since then, Discord has now pivoted to a system that shouldn’t require users to take any action themselves. According to the announcement from Discord cofounder Stanislav Vishnevskiy, signals examined by the platform’s age group estimation model include account age and history, activity levels across channels and servers, and connected communities, servers, and games. Vishnevskiy says the system doesn’t look at user “messages, calls, or other content,” and that its age estimation accuracy is on par with “what’s possible with biometrics.” Discord is anticipating that under this system, 90 percent of its users won’t be asked to confirm their age.

Here are all the methods Discord users can now use to manually verify their age. Image: Discord

Users believed to be over 18 will be placed in the Adult age group, with no changes to their account. Users in the Teen age group will have certain safety protections enabled by default, including filters and blurring for sensitive content, and restricted access for +18 servers and messaging features. Discord pledged to introduce additional verification options when it paused the age assurance launch, and these are now rolling out as part of this update. Alongside face and ID scans, users can also choose to confirm their age via credit cards, Apple’s App Store, Google’s Play Store, Google Wallet, and the AgeKey credential system.

If Discord is unable to automatically estimate the user’s age, some settings and features won’t be available until the user provides additional information to confirm their age group in User Settings > Account Status. Adult users can also use this setting to supply additional verification details if they’re misassigned to the teen group.

“We believe meeting age requirements shouldn’t require ID checks or selfies for everyone. We’d prefer to give you more choices, including less intrusive options that don’t require biometrics or sensitive personal data,” said Vishnevskiy. “My hope is that our approach shows we can preserve what makes Discord special while taking seriously the responsibility that comes with it.”

Tech.title: Even Americans who use AI every day are worried about it
Tech.content:
People across the world are increasingly turning to AI for everyday tasks, from looking up recipes and doing their homework to researching work projects or making presentations.

But using AI every day doesn’t necessarily mean people are feeling comfortable with its implications for the world: About 68% of Americans who use AI daily are worried about it, according to a new survey conducted by opinion research firm Gallup, and concern about the tech skews even higher among people who use it less frequently.

Coming at a time of intense debate around the dangers of AI, quick developments around AI safety, the implications of AI going rogue, and accusations of anti-competitive behavior, these findings complicate the notion that adoption can serve as a straightforward measure of public enthusiasm for AI.

Commissioned by Microsoft, the Gallup study currently has results from 37 countries, where researchers polled about 1,000 people in each country between April and July. The project will eventually span 140 countries. Notably, India, a large population of tech users, is not currently part of the reported results, nor is Australia and Malaysia.

The findings appear to put the U.S. at the anxious end of an international chart even as people in other parts of the world expect the technology to improve their lives. According to Gallup, Western countries are most concerned about AI, with the United States leading in anxiety — 74% Americans reported feelings of worry, and only 36% expect AI to mostly help the country.

Other wealthy Western countries showed a similar mix of relatively frequent use and concern. In Canada, for example, 29% of those surveyed reported using AI daily, and of those, more than half expressed concerns about the impact of the technology. Overall, 64% of Canadians aware of AI said it worried them.

They’re likely not imagining it. There’s certainly been a growing wave of discontent around AI, with tech companies laying off hundreds of thousands of employees in order to invest in AI, shrinking entry-level openings, life-ending cases of AI psychosis, and dire warnings from AI leaders like Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, who have warned that the tech will wipe out jobs en masse.

The survey paints a different picture in the rest of the world, however. In Singapore, which had the highest portion of daily users in the study (46%), more than 80% of those aware about AI expect the tech to improve their everyday lives, and 77% think it’ll help the country. China, where 35% of people report using AI daily, most people expect it to help the country. The story is similar in Israel.

Still, optimism about AI doesn’t necessarily appear to translate to trust in the tech’s accuracy. According to Gallup, people who use AI daily were generally more trusting of its results, especially in high-adoption countries like Singapore, Israel and China, while less frequent users remain skeptical across the board. In the U.S., only 45% of daily users expressed that level of confidence. Altogether, only 36% (median) of the people surveyed said they trust AI’s results a lot.

Overall, though, Gallup reports that positivity about AI outweighs negative sentiments: In 34 of the 37 countries surveyed, people mostly reported feeling curious about the tech, with a fewer number saying they felt happy or excited. Only about 32% of those surveyed said they felt worried about AI. Positive emotions seem to be most common in China (90%), Singapore (89%) and Kenya (87%).

It’s not clear how much sentiment in some countries, especially China, might have changed since the survey ended in July, as the pace of AI development has lately burgeoned into a matter of international importance. AI safety is one of the major topics on the table for discussion when U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese Premier Xi Jingping meet on Thursday.

Notably, China’s head of the Ministry of State Security, Chen Yixin, wrote in a recent article that AI will have “a systemic impact on the political and security environment,” and could threaten China’s “political security, institutional security, and ideological security.”

“One of the clearest findings is that attitudes toward AI are multidimensional. People can be curious about AI, expect it to be beneficial and use it frequently while still being worried about it. Similarly, they can see considerable potential in AI while remaining skeptical about whether the information it provides is accurate,” Pablo Diego-Rosell, senior scientist at Gallup, told TechCrunch.

While the report paints a picture of optimism colored by some concern, it’s nevertheless true that AI worries are increasingly becoming part of public discourse. People who rely on AI for day-to-day tasks may end up supporting tougher rules or resisting its use in hiring, healthcare, education or government. And there’s certainly an argument to be made that training and serving AI models can harm the climate, and their unregulated use can disrupt cybersecurity, diminish content ownership, upset the creative arts fields, or harm data privacy.

At the end of the day, the report suggests that greater exposure alone will not resolve the unease around the technology. Still, given the amount of money that’s being invested, AI will likely continue proliferating even as disputes rage around where it belongs and what limits should be placed around it.

Tech.title: YouTube is making comments more fun — and fandom more lucrative for creators
Tech.content:
YouTube’s comments section is getting an upgrade, alongside the rollout of other community-focused features such as exclusive paid memberships, the company announced at its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday. Commenters will now be able to respond with GIFs or leave comments from their TVs, while creators will get new tools to support their fan communities, including features to personalize moderation, invite members into VIP-like areas, and give fans new ways to help them make money from their content.

Comments are still one of the main ways YouTube viewers interact with creators’ content, but they’ve often lagged behind other social networks’ commenting features. For instance, TikTok just announced that commenters can respond to videos with their voice and add polls, photo carousels, and Live Photos to their comments. Spotify lets video podcasters use polls and Q&As to engage their audiences.

Image Credits:YouTube

YouTube is finally catching up a bit by adding support for leaving GIFs in comments and letting users comment while watching YouTube on TV. The latter works by voice, not painfully typing out “LOL” on your remote control, YouTube noted.

One of the more interesting additions is a new comment moderation tool that’s personalized to each creator’s needs. Though YouTube already offers a comment moderation filter, creators may want to tailor it more precisely, particularly on live videos, where it’s harder to keep up. For now, the company is calling this personalized moderation an “experiment” and didn’t provide specific technical details about how it works.

Image Credits:YouTube

Other features are meant to help creators grow their fan communities — and make money from that fandom. These arrive at a time when revenue from advertising is no longer the only way creators monetize their videos.

The company said its Channel Memberships features are evolving, with the addition of paid, members-only communities, where members can share posts and start discussions with other top fans. YouTube will market these communities alongside other memberships on a new “channel memberships” page for viewers, designed to help them discover ones that match their interests.

Hype, a feature that lets fans recommend smaller creators’ videos to others and climb fan leaderboards, will gain new functionality dubbed “Hype with Jewels.” Previously, fans could only “hype” videos three times per week for free. Now they can buy Jewels, a virtual currency of sorts, to hype videos even more, helping to support creators and grow their audience. Fans motivated by clout may also appreciate that their handles will be permanently added to the video’s description.

YouTube said viewers have so far hyped more than 75 million unique videos over 1 billion times.

Image Credits:YouTube

The company’s direct messaging feature for sharing videos with family and friends will also support group chats in the next few months. Users will be able to record quick, raw videos and share them in these conversations, too.

These community-focused features arrived alongside other creator tools, including those for A/B testing, live dubbing, AI-assisted video editing, and more.

Tech.title: YouTube’s conversational video editing tool lets creators make edits in natural language
Tech.content:
YouTube announced a bunch of new creator tools at Wednesday’s Made On YouTube event, including a conversational editing tool that uses natural language to refine both long- and short-form footage.

“A one-hour shoot can be 10 hours or more in the edit. So, what if we could speed that process along without sacrificing any of our creative control?” YouTuber Happy Kelli shared onstage.

In a chat interface, creators give the AI instructions on how to help them put a video together. In Happy Kelli’s example, she shares footage of her dancing in different outfits and asks the AI to select the best take for each outfit. Then, she adds music and transitions that go along with the dance.

Image Credits:YouTube

“If at any point I want even more control, I can jump back into the editing timeline and manually adjust things myself,” she said. “Overall, conversational editing turns the process of editing into a literal conversation with an infinitely patient helper. It’s a collaborative partner that edits with you, not for you.”

This feature can also add text overlays, remove pauses in speech, and more. It can also make suggestions to the creator based on the context of the conversation.

While some creators may find that this tool saves them time and speeds up the often tedious process of video editing, others may feel that their individual editing style sets their videos apart and be reluctant to relinquish control to an AI.

Conversational editing will be available for both YouTube Shorts and the YouTube Create app in early 2027.

Tech.title: YouTube Music gets more conversational with new AI features
Tech.content:
YouTube is adding new AI-powered features to YouTube Music that aim to make it easier for listeners to discover music, explore artists, and find podcasts they may otherwise miss.

Announced at this year’s Made On YouTube event, the updates include “Ask Music,” a conversational tool for music and podcasts, and “Your Podcast Lineup,” a personalized audio guide designed to help listeners discover new shows.

Built directly into the YouTube Music app, Ask Music lets users describe what they want to hear in everyday language rather than searching for individual songs or artists. The feature works across YouTube Music’s catalog of more than 300 million songs, including official recordings, remixes, live performances, covers, and DJ sets. Users can use it to build custom listening queues, explore an artist’s motivations, or dig deeper into music history.

Image Credits:YouTube

YouTube explains that, instead of manually searching, the user simply types the request as if they were asking a friend. For instance, someone could ask Ask Music to create a mix based on the tracks that inspired a particular song. Users can also ask other questions, such as who played bass on a particular song or other details about its creation.

Image Credits:YouTube

YouTube Music is also introducing Your Podcast Lineup, a personalized AI-generated audio guide for podcast discovery.

The feature is designed for a familiar problem: There are more podcasts than most people have time to listen to. Even listeners who already have a list of favorite shows can struggle to keep up with new episodes, let alone find new ones.

Your Podcast Lineup will appear on the podcast page in the YouTube Music app. Each week, it will provide a short spoken preview of recommended shows and explain why they might appeal to the listener. It can then move directly into suggested episodes.

Spotify recently introduced an AI-powered feature that follows a similar direction. Its personal podcasts feature uses AI to generate podcast episodes based on their interests and prompts.

The new features are part of YouTube’s broader push to use AI throughout its services. Last year, YouTube Music experimented with AI-powered music hosts that provide stories, fan trivia, and commentary related to what users are listening to.

Both updates are coming soon to YouTube Music and YouTube Premium subscribers worldwide.

Tech.title: Eight Sleep’s new Pod 6 comes in smaller and solo sizes, starting at $1,999
Tech.content:
Sleep tech company Eight Sleep on Wednesday launched its new Pod 6 device in a smaller size than previous editions to fit more bed frames, along with solo sizes for one-person use. The company said that the device can be used to adjust the temperature on either side 20% faster than the previous-generation gadget.

Because the new pod has a 50% smaller footprint, it can fit most bed frames. The company claims the device has 9x more sensors, enabling it to understand granular temperature controls for each user even if they are sleeping close together. Plus, it can ignore data from a pet or a kid sleeping on the bed with two users.

The Pod 6 is available starting today in over 37 countries, starting at $1,999 for solo sizes and $2,699 for standard sizes. Solo sizes can fit a twin bed and one side of queen, king, and California King beds. Standard sizes will be available in queen, king, and California King. Plus, it can work with existing add-ons like a blanket, pillow cover, and base.

Image Credits:Eight Sleep

Beyond new sleep products, the company is pursuing Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval to transition its Eight Sleep Pod into a regulated medical device for sleep apnea in the U.S.

Earlier this year, the company raised $50 million from Tether at a $1.5 billion valuation. Eight Sleep also took steps to expand its international footprint by launching its product in China, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and Singapore in the last year, with China becoming one of the fastest-growing regions.

The company’s CEO Matteo Franceschetti told TechCrunch that international markets contribute over 30% of revenue. He mentioned that the sleep tech company plans to expand into other regions of Asia and Latin America. Franceschetti noted that the company is keeping a keen eye on the component crunch in the electronics sector, but didn’t say whether it will impact pricing.

“We definitely see the market changing a little bit because AI companies are requesting a lot of different components. We are adjusting our supply chain [to counter that]. It’s definitely something that we need to watch out for, particularly as our devices become more and more, I would say, compute-heavy and intelligent to be able to provide AI features to our users,” he said.

Tech.title: YouTube releases new AI features for creators within its Studio app
Tech.content:
At its Made On YouTube annual event, YouTube announced new tools for YouTube Studio, the app creators use to manage their channels, aimed at helping them analyze their videos and grow their audiences. The updates include expanding Ask Studio, its AI-powered Q&A feature, to iOS and Android, as well as new features that provide feedback on drafts and create dynamic thumbnails.

The draft-feedback feature uses AI to look at a creator’s unpublished video and provide suggestions about pacing, structure, and storytelling. YouTube is also debuting a new research feed in the Studio app that shows creators what kind of content is working on the platform, so they can apply their own take on it.

Creators are typically picky about the preview images and titles they use for their videos. The Studio app will now let them generate thumbnails and titles based on a video’s content and matched to their style. Creators can also use a new dynamic thumbnail feature to generate three options and show each one to a different segment of their audience.

Image Credits:YouTube

YouTube said creators have used its A/B testing feature to run more than 40 million tests on titles and thumbnails. Soon, the company said, users will be able to test up to three video cuts to see which opening hook works best. Later this year, YouTube Studio will also automatically monitor thumbnail performance and change one proactively if it doesn’t perform well.

YouTube also said it’s updating its analytics to go beyond raw numbers, explaining why videos perform the way they do and providing advice about how to make content more engaging.

Image Credits:YouTube

Besides the Studio app revamp, YouTube also introduced other tools for creators, including conversational editing in Shorts and the YouTube Create app.

Tech.title: YouTube’s new ‘Shorts series’ feature brings episodic viewing to Shorts
Tech.content:
As microdrama apps gain traction, YouTube is clearly betting that episodic short-form storytelling will stick around. And that the format belongs on Shorts.

At its Made On YouTube event on Wednesday, the company announced “Shorts series,” a new tool that lets creators organize their Shorts into TV-style seasons and episodes. The feature brings a more traditional episodic structure to YouTube Shorts, complete with custom thumbnails and playback.

With Shorts series, viewers can watch a selection of Shorts as a continuous story rather than simply scrolling from one stand-alone clip to the next. The series will live on a creator’s YouTube channel.

The feature is rolling out to creators in the YouTube Partner Program across web, mobile, and connected TVs.

The move comes as no surprise, given that YouTubers have already been experimenting with microdramas and, increasingly, they’re considering it a serious business venture.

For instance, internet personality Hannah Stocking has crossed into vertical drama, starring in the musical microdrama “Playback,” which premiered on Holywater’s My Drama platform. Then there’s Joshua Ovenshire (The Jovenshire), a longtime YouTube creator who has moved away from traditional YouTube videos. He now works as an executive producer, making shows for vertical platform ReelShort, including a “Love Island”-inspired series called “Secrets and Soulmates.”

The format has even become popular enough to attract recognizable Hollywood names, with celebrities including James Franco, Issa Rae, and Jesse Tyler Ferguson getting involved.

YouTube’s new feature also puts the platform more directly into competition with a growing collection of microdrama apps. TikTok recently launched PineDrama, its own microdrama app, while others such as ReelShort and DramaBox have also grown in popularity.

For YouTube, Shorts series could be a way to keep viewers engaged without sending them off to other platforms for episodic vertical storytelling. Instead, they’re providing a way to access it all directly on YouTube.

The company adds that Shorts series builds on “Creator Shows,” which it announced at its annual upfront event last year. This gave select creators the tools to organize their content into a viewing experience designed for TV. Creators, including Michelle Khare and Rhett & Link, used the tools to structure their content into seasons and episodes, making it easier for viewers to binge on the big screen.

Other Made On YouTube announcements are also designed to help creators grow and engage audiences. This includes “Live Showdowns,” which let creators pair up for interactive team challenges; expanded video A/B testing to compare different cuts or opening hooks; “Dynamic Thumbnails” to allow YouTubers to select the most engaging option from up to three creator-provided thumbnails for different audiences; new shopping features; and more.

Tech.title: YouTube adds new creator tools like video A/B testing, dynamic thumbnails, and live dubbing
Tech.content:
In a bid to help creators reach more people, YouTube on Wednesday unveiled a slew of new tools, many of which use AI to try out different tactics on videos to find what makes them perform best.

The new Ask Studio feature allows creators to share draft videos with AI to get personalized feedback based on their previous content and user comments. The feature will propose alternative titles and thumbnail options, analyze the creator’s channel analytics to explain the performance of their videos, and offer advice for improving metrics. Ask Studio is expanding to YouTube’s mobile apps, too.

Image Credits:YouTube

YouTube already allows creators to A/B test titles and thumbnails, and from 2027, this feature will let creators upload and test three different cuts for Shorts. There’s also a Dynamic Thumbnails feature, with which creators can upload multiple thumbnails and leave it to YouTube to determine which thumbnail to show viewers that is most likely to spark their interest.

Creators can also apply these tools to their existing catalog. If a creator allows it, Ask Studio will be able to autonomously monitor thumbnail performance and create tests to refine older videos.

On the shopping front, YouTube will now use AI to auto-tag products, which it says will help creators earn money through affiliate programs. The company is also expanding its Amazon affiliate program beyond the U.S.

Image Credits:YouTube

Some creators are understandably skeptical of using AI to support their content, worrying that just one AI-generated mistake could harm their credibility. For such features to succeed, they will need to be accurate enough to assuage creators’ concerns.

The platform is also giving creators new ways to go live. Early next year, YouTube will pilot auto-dubbing on live videos to translate creators’ speech into other languages in real time. The company is also launching a “live showdown” feature, which lets creators co-host streams together, and even get paired with other creators currently streaming through “live creator matchmaking.”

“Co-hosts can kick off friendly head-to-head matchups, where viewers send chats, gifts, and Super Chats to push their creator’s score forward on-screen in real time,” YouTube Live product manager Barbara MacDonald wrote in a blog post.

Image Credits:YouTube

Hopefully these impromptu collaborations with strangers won’t turn into a hotbed of bad behavior.

YouTube also shared data that provides insight into how people are using the platform. More people continue to watch YouTube on household TVs, and more than half of the top 100 YouTube creators have “living room” as their most watched interface.

YouTube’s data also confirms what we know about the growth of the microdrama industry: In the first half of 2026, microdramas on YouTube surpassed 6.5 billion views, and their watch time rose 50% year-over-year. People even seem to be watching these episodic, vertical video series on the big screen, with views of microdrama content on TVs increasing 90% year-over-year.

Tech.title: YouTube’s Custom Feeds Give You More Control Over the Algorithm
Tech.content:
My YouTube algorithm is sacred, with years of data about my preferences and viewing history fermenting into whatever videos it picks for my home screen. YouTube’s algorithm, while not perfect, sure knows what I want to see. The current top three videos on my front page are an Apple Watch analysis, a Big Brother season 28 update, and something called “I Lost to the Muppets” from comedian Chris Fleming. Click. Click. Click.

As part of its Made on YouTube event Wednesday, Google released several new features, including a Custom Feeds button for adjusting what videos pop up on your front page. It’s a rare chance for users to directly tweak their algorithmic feed on YouTube, in ways that go beyond just pressing thumbs up on a video or blocking a creator.

To try it out, users can click the Your custom feeds button below the search bar and type a request for the feed they’d like to see. YouTube uses large language models to process your request and whip up a freshly personalized homepage. “I want a rainy Shanghai vibe: café jazz, street food, and vlogs,” read one of my suggested prompts.

Courtesy of YouTube

YouTube tested Custom Feeds as an experimental feature earlier this year, before deciding that it was a good fit. The company plans to roll it out soon as an option for all US users, whether viewing on mobile, desktop, or TV.

“Users are always telling us that they want more control,” says Emily Moxley, YouTube’s vice president of product management. “They want more ability to steer their algorithm. With custom feeds, we're giving them a natural-language way that they can do that. They can tell us exactly what they want.”

So, I told YouTube exactly what I wanted to see: “Gooey macaroni and cheese recipe videos, Caleb Hearon clip compilations, and crystal singing bowl videos under 15 minutes.” And the feed it generated was exactly that. My perfect zen blend for rotting on the couch after a long day. YouTube suggested potential additions to expand my prompt, like “uploaded this month” and “without talking or commentary.” Not bad.

The Custom Feeds button sits next to other topic tabs below the search bar, like “Music” and “Podcasts.” Experimenting with this tool doesn’t replace your standard homepage, which you can access anytime by clicking the “All” button. Users can save multiple custom feeds.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse AI Assistant Rolled Out With a Serious Security Flaw
Tech.content:
Meta founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has gone to great lengths to hype the security of its new AI assistant, Muse, claiming it is “built from the ground up for privacy and security.” A zero-day vulnerability that gives locally run apps and terminal commands complete control of the agent raises serious doubts. Further raising questions, Amazon on Sunday began blocking Muse from its site.

Meta introduced Muse a few weeks ago. The assistant “books appointments, fills out forms, and handles customer service,” “proactively takes tasks off your plate,” and can “make purchases, generate images, create documents, and connect with your favorite apps and services.” The macOS app (curiously, there’s no Windows version) also works with a user’s WhatsApp, email, calendar, and social media accounts. When a task requires a tool that doesn’t exist, Muse creates one on the fly.

Meta Doth Hype Muse Security Too Much

Of course, for Muse to do any of these things, users must first give it access to their accounts. This includes authenticating the assistant to each service and, because the app runs on macOS, giving it permissions to a broad range of operating system-restricted device resources, like writing files to disk, accessing the mic and camera, and monitoring location and calendars. Apple has spent years developing these defenses to prevent installed apps or commands entered into the terminal from accessing these resources, clearly because the company considers them a security threat. Muse completely undoes these default measures.

The zero-day allowed any app or terminal command to gain access to the token that authenticates users to their Muse account. Meta developers designed the assistant so that any locally installed app or executed code, regardless of the macOS permissions it has, can change a long list of undocumented settings. Most of them are fairly innocuous, such as controlling dark mode. One setting, however, was anything but innocuous. It allowed processes to change the end point where transcription occurs. Normally, it’s a server address operated by Meta. Attackers could have exploited this flaw by changing the location to their own end point. If that happened, the attackers would have had the token that gives complete control over the Muse account.

“We can manipulate the agent and leverage its privileges to do whatever we want,” Patrick Wardle, the macOS security expert who discovered the zero-day, told Ars ahead of the hotfix. “So instead of us having to write a very comprehensive Mac malware stealer, we can just leverage the AI assistant itself.” Wardle said he has developed several proof-of-concept attacks that do things like writing malicious files to disk and snapping pictures, in many cases with no indication to even an alert user.

More than 12 hours after this post went live, Meta said it released a hotfix that patched the 0-day.

Meta has published two posts in as many weeks documenting the design decisions that went into ensuring an assistant with such extraordinary access to user data and resources is secure and private. The posts come amid revelations that internal testing of models from Anthropic and Google has resulted in security breaches of external, third-party networks that the engineers involved never intended to target. In traditional human-only hacking, these actions could likely result in the filing of criminal charges. The Meta posts are likely mindful of the resulting blowback and the calls to slow down AI development in response.

Wardle said that Meta developers made several design decisions that made his exploit possible. One is the choice for Muse dictation to occur in the cloud, where Meta can log it. macOS has long provided a simple means for apps to handle dictation and transcription in processes that stay securely on the device. Had the developers chosen this safer alternative, the attack wouldn’t have been possible.

Tech.title: The Best Samsung Phones of 2026: Ultra, Fold, Budget
Tech.content:
Other Samsung Phones to Consider

If you don't see a Samsung phone mentioned in this guide, it may be because it isn't sold in the US and is a little harder to source for testing. But here are a few other Samsung phones we've tested.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra for $2,100: An incremental upgrade over the Z Fold7, the Z Fold8 Ultra is for foldable phone fans who want the best and are willing to pay for it. The familiar book-style form factor offers a 6.5-inch cover screen, like a regular candy bar phone, and opens to give a tablet-sized 8-inch display with a fainter crease than before and a stronger hinge. Naturally, you get top-notch performance, all-day battery life, and Samsung’s best camera in a folding phone, with a 200-megapixel main shooter, 50-megapixel ultrawide, and 10-megapixel telephoto lens.

Photograph: Simon Hill

Samsung Galaxy S26 FE for $700: The Samsung Galaxy S26 FE is a perfectly decent phone with good battery life, a lovely big display, and a solid triple-camera system, but nothing about it justifies the extra $100 over last year’s almost identical S25 FE. The processor is slightly better, but that’s about it. In fact, Samsung downgraded the USB-C port to USB 2.0 in the S26 FE, so we think you’d be better off buying the S25 FE above while it’s still available.

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Z Fold7 for $2,000 or Z Flip7 for $1,100: If you want a Samsung foldable without the eye-watering price tag, consider 2025’s Galaxy Z Fold7 or Galaxy Z Flip7 if you can find them discounted. The Fold7 is a little thicker with a more prominent crease in the screen. The battery life isn’t great, and the ultrawide camera is weaker, but there isn’t a huge difference between it and the Fold8 Ultra. It’s a similar story for the Flip7, with the Flip8 bringing minor hinge improvements, a refined, lighter design with a less noticeable crease, a faster processor, and more useful software features for the outer display.

Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge for $1,300: Have you ever wanted a really thin and lightweight phone? No? Well, Samsung has an option for you anyway. The Galaxy S25 Edge was a unique one-off last year (it's doubtful we'll see a successor) and matches several features of the Galaxy S25 Ultra, like a titanium frame, stronger front glass, and 4K 120 frames per second video recording. All the cameras even have autofocus. But it made several sacrifices to achieve its amazingly slim 5.8-mm frame (for context, the S25 Ultra is 8.2-mm thick). There's no stylus, no telephoto camera, and worst of all, the battery capacity has been slashed. We've seen this before—thin phones have always compromised on battery life, and this is no different. We constantly had to baby this phone's 3,900-mAh battery with mixed usage, and that's just not acceptable. (The iPhone Air did it better.) If you find yourself constantly near a power source and think you'll enjoy the slim and light design, then go for it.

Galaxy A17 5G. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Samsung Galaxy A17 5G for $249: On paper, the Galaxy A17 seems like a really great deal. It offers six years of software support, an AMOLED screen, expandable storage, and a decent camera. Unfortunately, it's held back by lackluster performance. The problem is the very limited 4 GB of RAM in the US model, which ruins the overall experience. If you had to use your smartphone in an emergency, I would not trust the A17 to be reliable. But if your needs are extremely minimal, it may suffice.

If you're looking to save some cash, it's fine to buy Samsung's Galaxy S24 range from 2024, as long as the prices are a good deal lower than the original MSRP. (They're hard to find at most major retailers.) These phones will still get support for a while, and they're pretty great. I don't think it's worth buying anything older.

Should You Invest in Samsung’s Ecosystem?

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Samsung is one of the few smartphone manufacturers that can match Apple's hardware ecosystem. The company makes smartphones, but you can also expand your experience with a Galaxy Watch8 smartwatch, Galaxy Buds4 Pro earbuds, Galaxy Ring fitness ring, Galaxy Tab S11, and even a Windows-powered Galaxy laptop.

There are perks, like some features on the Galaxy Ring and Watch8 being available only when paired with a Samsung phone, and its earbuds automatically switching between Samsung devices based on what you're using. There aren't many exclusive features when using a Galaxy phone with a Galaxy laptop, but capabilities like Quick Share let you send photos and documents between your devices (even to iPhones via AirDrop!).

Again, it's not necessary, and these other devices might not be the right ones for you within their respective categories, but if you're chasing hardware parity, you have that option with Samsung.

What Is Galaxy AI?

Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

With the Galaxy S24 series, Samsung launched “Galaxy AI," a selection of artificial intelligence features, many of which are powered by Google's Gemini large language models. These enable smart features that may be helpful in your day-to-day, like real-time translations during phone calls, real-time transcriptions in Samsung's Voice Recorder app, the ability to summarize long paragraphs of text in the Samsung Notes app, or changing a sentence's tone with the Samsung Keyboard.

In the Galaxy S25 series, Galaxy AI expanded to include Gemini as the default voice assistant and the ability for Gemini to work with multiple apps simultaneously. It also debuted Drawing Assist, which lets you sketch or enter a prompt and get an AI-generated image. Now you can also use video in real time with Gemini, even from the cover screen of the Galaxy Z Flip7.

And in the Galaxy S26 series, the AI features got even more helpful. The Document Scanner built into the camera app can now erase fingers and creases and minimize distortion before converting the photo into a PDF. Audio Eraser is now available in any media app to reduce distracting background sounds in videos, so you can hear the subject clearly. And there's now built-in call screening to better filter out robocalls. Samsung also debuted Google's Task Automations in the Gemini assistant, allowing you to ask Gemini to book you an Uber or order something from DoorDash, Uber Eats, or GrubHub, though it's pretty slow.

You can find many of these features in Settings > Galaxy AI to toggle them on or off. We also have an explainer on how to limit Galaxy AI to on-device processing.

What Is Samsung DeX?

Courtesy of David Nield

Samsung's DeX (short for “desktop experience”) launched in 2017, and it lets you plug your Samsung phone into an external monitor and launch a desktop version of Android, all powered by the phone. You can find a list of compatible Samsung phones here—the Flip7 is the first Galaxy Flip to support DeX—and you'll need a monitor, mouse, and keyboard, plus a cable to connect the phone to the monitor. (You can also cast DeX to select screens wirelessly.)

In DeX mode, you can resize Android apps and open them all in separate windows. It's a proper computing platform, though you probably won't want to use this as a permanent laptop replacement or anything of the sort. It's great if you're visiting another office, or working out of a coffee shop or airplane (if you have a portable display). We have a whole guide to setting up and using DeX here.

What Happened to the Galaxy Z TriFold?

PHOTOGRAPH: Julian Chokkattu

I have not tested Samsung's Galaxy Z TriFold, and it seems I never will. (I had some brief hands-on time with it at CES 2026, but Samsung did not provide WIRED with a test unit.) This folding phone, which had an MSRP of $2,800, officially went on sale in the US at the end of January, but three months later Samsung discontinued it because of high manufacturing costs.

Yes, unfolding it from a fairly compact phone to a massive 10-inch tablet was amazing and the stuff of dreams, but it didn't justify the high price; you can buy a killer phone and excellent tablet for way less than $3,000. The luxury of having them in one pocket is incredible, but more than a $1,000 incredible? I think the TriFold is the true “phablet” Samsung promised so long ago, and the folding mechanism is novel and a marvelous feat. Hopefully, when the smartphone market picks back up, Samsung will revisit this design. It's great for productivity junkies who frequently juggle multiple apps. Alas, it's just a dream now. You'll have to stick with the standard Z Fold. —Julian Chokkattu

How We Test Phones

WIRED has been covering Samsung smartphones since they entered the market. With each Samsung smartphone we test, our reviewers always put their personal SIM card inside and spend as long as they can (a few weeks) using the phone as their own. We do camera testing and compare the results with similarly priced devices; we benchmark performance and play graphically demanding games to see how they fare; we try out all the new features; and we even take calls to make sure they go through and that voice quality is fine.

Tech.title: A Startup Wants to Power Data Centers With ‘Supercritical’ Carbon Dioxide
Tech.content:
A new company has a plan to make the dirty gas turbines powering data centers more efficient: liquid carbon dioxide.

American Supercritical came out of stealth Wednesday, announcing $8 million in funding. It wants to retrofit inefficient gas turbines that many data centers rely on for power with units that can generate more power, without adding more emissions (though the gas-fired turbines will continue to emit carbon pollution). The technology can also theoretically be used on a wide variety of energy sources at a time when power demand is skyrocketing.

“We want to start with gas turbines but eventually expand beyond that,” says cofounder Simon Shuham.

Most large gas-fired power plants in the United States use an array of heat engines in what’s known as a combined-cycle process: First, turbines generate electricity from burning compressed air and natural gas, then a separate engine uses the hot exhaust to make steam and create additional energy. But for a variety of reasons, data centers across the US have opted to power their operations with what are known as simple-cycle turbines, and exclude the steam component.

These turbines are much less efficient than combined-cycle plants. Usually, only about 35 percent of the energy from simple-cycle turbines is converted to electricity, while the rest escapes as exhaust. (In combined-cycle plants, that figure hovers closer to 60 to 65 percent.) That exhaust includes greenhouse gases, making plants that run on simple-cycle turbines a much worse choice for the environment than combined-cycle plants.

Tech.title: This App Makes Your Laptop Screen Look Like Paper
Tech.content:
Tech is so sterile now—everything lives on the same shiny screens. It's nice, then, when you find an application that exists mostly just to add a little grit to these devices.

That's how I'm interpreting Paperman, which makes everything on your computer screen look like it’s printed on paper. The application, from Finnish developers DoublOne, does this by adding a textural overlay onto everything you see on the screen. I'm typing this on my MacBook, but everything on my screen looks like it's on premium stationery.

Fans of old video games know about CRT filters, which emulate the look of old convex displays. Paperman is like that, but it mimics paper instead of a retro television. Just open the application, choose which kind of paper you want, and your entire display gets overlaid with a pleasing texture.

The goal is to help you focus on your work and to make the screen more pleasing to look at. The developers have collected a bunch of academic research, collected on a page on Paperman’s website, that points to studies showing that matte surfaces and paper texture help with visual fatigue. Can a virtual matte or paper layer on your screen help in the same way?

Courtesy of Justin Pot

Zoé Kilperti, half of the two-person DoublOne studio behind the application, admits she isn't sure. “A lot of that research looks at why reading on physical paper feels so restful,” she tells WIRED. “Its texture breaks up harsh light and softens sharp edges. Modern displays are the opposite: an intensely uniform, razor-sharp grid of backlight.” Paperman's filter is built to break up that uniformity.

The app offers a variety of textures, from Classic Matte to Sunbaked Parchment. I'm partial to Whisper Weave, the recommended texture. You can toggle how much intensity there is to the effect, and I recommend that you do.

I find this application works best when I'm reading, writing, or otherwise working with text. But you should know that everything on the screen is textured, including images, videos, and even some games. You can set Paperman to not apply the texture when certain applications are open, which is useful if you're doing something like graphic design work or browsing photos.

If you use multiple screens, you can also toggle Paperman to apply the texture effect to the content of one display and not the other. There are also customizable keyboard shortcuts, meaning you can toggle the effect on and off on the fly. You're always going to want to have some method of turning the effect off, so it's good there are so many options.

Tech.title: SmartLabels QR Code Organizing System Review (2026): AI Made Sense of My Junk Drawer
Tech.content:
A key ingredient to feeling organized is having a space that’s organized. That logic also helps explain the ubiquity of the junk drawer. It’s simply not realistic to have a dedicated spot for every item you own, so assigning a single destination where you can house all the leftover stuff makes sense. That is, until you can’t find your utility scissors or flashlight or stamps or favorite highlighter or double-sided tape when you need any of those things.

Regular organizing conventions won’t help you keep track of everything in your junk drawer—or any other storage area, for that matter. For example, nicely labeling your boxes is great, but if you lose track of where you put them, you’re toast. Also, that box labeled “kitchen stuff?” You definitely don’t know every item that’s inside. The clever SmartLabels system, which uses a QR code sticker for the outside of a bin, box, drawer, or other location and a companion app to keep a digital inventory of its contents, could help with each of these organizational pitfalls.

The system is simple to use, but its value in functioning as an up-to-date digital inventory of your belongings depends heavily on how often you update the app. The app won’t know, for instance, if you absentmindedly stow away your double-sided tape with your wrapping paper instead of putting it back in the junk drawer where it is cataloged. You’ll also need to remember to add new items to the app as you add them to a bin in question. But if you’re a gold-star user of SmartLabels, they do stand to help you keep track of your treasures.

Photographic Memory

Photograph: Alexis Berger

Each package of SmartLabels includes 48 unique QR-code stickers (four sheets of 12 codes each). After you download the free SmartLabels app (compatible with iOS and Android), fire it up and select the QR code sticker you want to use for the bin in question. The app will prompt you to take a photo of the QR code, then it’ll ask you to photograph the contents that you’re going to store. Every item must be clearly visible, so you can’t simply dump random products in a box and snap a photo. If the camera can’t see an item, the app won’t be able to catalog it. The app is free, but you can opt for a premium subscription ($15 per year) that offers exportable PDFs and spreadsheets of your SmartLabel inventory, among a few other benefits. Businesses might be interested in this capability, but the average home organizer doesn’t need it.

Tech.title: Kate Tolo Says Her Quest to Be ‘the Female Bryan Johnson’ Is ‘for Women’
Tech.content:
Kate Tolo got her first period at 13—an experience she says left her lying prostrate on the floor, debilitated by cramps and breaking out into a full-body sweat.

When she told her dad why she was home from school early, she remembers him saying, “We don’t talk about that female stuff.” Then he walked away.

For most of her teenage years, that was how Tolo thought about her period—as something “you just didn’t talk about.” When she was in her early twenties and experienced extreme pain while defecating, sending her to the emergency room, a doctor suggested Tolo may have endometriosis, a chronic disease believed to affect an estimated 10 percent of women of reproductive age, according to WHO data.

Caused by an overgrowth of endometrium-like tissue (uterine lining), endometriosis is primarily characterized by extremely heavy and painful periods, as well as pelvic floor dysfunction, bowel issues, and dyspareunia (pain during sex). The doctor recommended Tolo have a laparoscopy, an invasive surgical procedure required to get an official diagnosis and remove endometriosis tissue. But she refused: “I wasn’t going to undergo an invasive surgical procedure, or cut myself open,” she says. “That just wasn’t an option for me.”

Then in early 2026, Tolo started developing a concierge health service with her boyfriend Bryan Johnson, the technologist-cum-multimillionaire-cum-biohacker known for his quest to become immortal via rigid self-optimization and wellness protocols. During a clinical intake, she shared her lifelong struggle with suspected endometriosis—and he became obsessed with finding a cure.

Tech.title: AT&T Is Automating Away Jobs—and Its Old Telecom Empire
Tech.content:
AT&T, which already shed more than half of its workforce over the past decade, says it's going to continue laying off staff as it gears up for the AI era. The telecommunications giant is also doing away with its old-school landline service and using artificial intelligence to automate some internal processes. All this downsizing is resulting in tangible benefits, including a considerable decrease in electricity usage, AT&T chief technology officer Jeremy Legg tells WIRED.

“We’re not going to have the same headcount in five years as we do today,” Legg says, adding that comparing its staffing levels to that of peers plays a role in its decisionmaking. According to public financial disclosures, AT&T generated less revenue per employee last year than its competitors Verizon and T-Mobile, both of which have let go of workers in recent months.

If AT&T continues cutting jobs at the same pace as last year, when it shed 8,000 people, its workforce could approach 85,000 employees by 2030. A person familiar with the matter, who was not authorized to speak publicly, described that number as the company’s target. AT&T called the figure inaccurate. In the first half of 2026, the telecom giant cut some 2,100 jobs.

By the end of the decade, AT&T wants to be seen as a “dramatically different” company with a “fantastic” fiber internet service and “kickass wireless network,” AT&T CEO John Stankey said at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference in San Francisco earlier this month.

Got a Tip? Are you a current or former AT&T employee with more to say? We'd like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at peard33.24.

AT&T’s transition provides a window into how legacy companies are trying to rebuild their operations as artificial intelligence tools become increasingly capable. AT&T has been around for 150 years, and it still plays a major role in the global economy. Legg says it handles about 15 percent of the world’s internet traffic, and the company employed nearly 131,000 people as of June. The question is whether it can drive innovation while also shedding costs and trying to keep up with the likes of Elon Musk.

Some of AT&T’s decades-old systems still run on paper records and require workers to do things manually, such as when a customer wants to disconnect their phone service. Some of that work is now being automated.

The telecom giant is using AI systems for customer service, to help identify locations for new cell phone towers, and to find maintenance issues on existing ones. A generative AI system AT&T calls GeoModeler adjusts network settings on the fly during rare events like extreme weather. And like many companies, AT&T is using AI to generate software code and help manage service issues.

Starting next year, AT&T will replace physical hardware at thousands of central hubs with cloud software from Israeli startup DriveNets, in which AT&T is an investor. The change will allow technicians to make adjustments remotely, such as when a customer requests faster internet. As more tasks are automated, a number of middle management and junior developer roles are expected to disappear.

Jobs in the US telecommunications industry have been declining for 25 years, according to government data, but the potential for AI to accelerate the trend and boost profits has captivated investors.

At the same time, AT&T is decommissioning the energy-intensive copper wire network that has long powered its landline telephone and DSL internet networks. Dropping these services generally requires approval from state and federal regulators, since rural areas may not have access to alternatives, and the company’s plans have been met by local protests in some communities. But by the end of this year, AT&T expects it will no longer have to offer copper in more than 85 percent of its existing footprint.

Tech.title: What iOS 27.2 Could Bring to Your iPhone Later This Year
Tech.content:
About a week after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released the first public beta of iOS 27.2 on Sept. 22. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, this early look at iOS 27.2 shows Siri AI expanding to other languages and a few upgrades in other apps, such as FaceTime.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, Apple has said the foldable iPhone Duo will launch on 27.1 next month, and all devices will be able to update to 27.2 sometime later.

Since this is a beta, I recommend downloading it only on something other than your primary device. This isn’t the final version of iOS 27.2, so the update might be buggy and battery life may be short — it’s best to keep those troubles on a secondary device.

Also, since this isn’t the final version, more features could end up landing on your iPhone when Apple releases iOS 27.2.

Here are some features developers and beta testers can try now in the first iOS 27.2 public beta.

Siri AI in more languages

Siri AI is available on iOS 27 now. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

In iOS 27, Siri AI is only available in English. But the beta of iOS 27.2 expands Siri AI to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in Facetime

In the iOS 27.2 beta, you can use your front and rear facing cameras at the same time in Facetime calls. This allows you to Facetime call with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame in order to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

An anti-snatching feature

According to 9to5Mac, code within the iOS 27.2 beta shows a feature called AutoLock. This is reportedly an anti-theft feature that can lock your device if it detects it’s been snatched out of your hand. For example, AutoLock could lock your iPhone if it detects a sharp acceleration, as if it was snatched out of your hands, or if your device has been unlocked for an extended period of time.

It’s important to note that this feature is not a user-facing option on your iPhone in this beta. Rather, 9to5Mac has reportedly seen internal code related to the feature. That means this feature may not be available when Apple releases iOS 27.2 in October.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in the iOS 27.2 beta. The beta introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of what podcasts are new and what podcasts you still have to finish.

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In the beta of iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with.

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in the iOS 27.2 beta is Multiview. Developers and beta testers who subscribe to Apple TV can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racecourse while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

Updated Health app

The Apple Health app just got a refresh. Apple

Developers and beta testers can see a redesigned Health app in the iOS 27.2 beta. The redesigned app introduces some new features and changes some others.

The Insights tab can give you a look at your daily metrics, such as sleep and fitness activity, and personalized summaries near the top of the page.

The new Longevity tab analyzes health from your devices, like your Apple Watch and iPhone, and creates visualizations for that information. You can also try new movement assessments in this tab, like for flexibility and hearing health. Some of these assessments require you to perform an activity for a few minutes on camera so the app can analyze your movements.

Apple

The redesigned Health app also lets you see your Health Age, which reflects how your daily habits might influence your body. So depending on your habits, this number could go up or down relative to your actual age.

You can also order labs via Quest Diagnostics for $119 through the app.

However, the redesign is expected to launch sometime later this year, despite being featured in this beta.

Those are a few of the new features developers and beta testers can try now with the first public beta of iOS 27.2. There will likely be more betas before the OS is released to the public. Apple has not said when exactly it will release iOS 27.2 to the general public, but we expect it to land on devices in October.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1.

Tech.title: YouTube Is Expanding Its AI Search to Be More Like Google’s
Tech.content:
Platforms like YouTube have used machine learning tech for years to build your social media feeds. Now, in the age of generative AI, YouTube is building on that technological foundation and introducing a new way to use AI to build custom video feeds, the company announced at Made on YouTube on Wednesday.

You will soon be able to build multiple custom feeds of recommended videos by prompting YouTube like you would a chatbot, using plain language. So you can have feeds dedicated to specific subjects, like photography or college football, and YouTube creates dedicated tabs on your homepage for each feed. This will be rolling out across desktop, TV and mobile in the US next month.

YouTube’s experimental Ask YouTube tool lets you search for videos with AI, and it’s expanding its capabilities. Now, if you search for information about a new product, like the new iPhone Duo, the Ask YouTube AI can compile information from videos and outside sources. It uses that information to build comparison tables, among other things. You can click on a video that the tool surfaces and continue asking questions on the video’s watch page.

It is somewhat similar to how a chatbot can search the web for information, compile it and cite its sources. But similar to the decline in traffic that digital publishers have seen with the rise of generative AI, there is a risk that YouTube’s AI-enhanced search may eliminate the need for people to click on video links and consume original content.

“Our goal is to connect viewers with the right video faster. With Ask YouTube, we expect watch time to remain steady or improve,” a YouTube spokesperson told CNET. Other AI features, such as chapters and AI-generated summaries, “showed no negative impact on watch time; instead, they helped retain viewers.” Videos included in the AI search’s answers will “prominently display the video title and channel name,” the spokesperson said.

The AI takeover of YouTube has been an ongoing project for its parent company, Google, in recent years. While creators have been using AI to edit and create videos, leading to an onslaught of AI slop, the platform has been integrating new tools powered by Google’s Gemini models. Now, YouTube is focusing its AI efforts on personalization, both for viewers and creators, to ultimately keep us scrolling and monetize content. It is also adding Gemini as a content creation assistant to Shorts and the YouTube Create app.

YouTube has been under fire this year as a landmark court decision found that Meta and Google designed their sites to be intentionally addictive to children and teens, harming their mental health. YouTube has denied this, saying it’s a streaming platform, not a social media platform. Many child safety researchers and advocates are worried about social media sites adding more AI features. We’ve already seen how AI features can harm kids, such as in the case of Reuters’ 2025 investigation that found Meta’s AI chatbots on Instagram would engage in sexual and romantic roleplay with children.

Creator-specific tools coming to YouTube

YouTube is introducing a dedicated tool for episodic content, called Shorts series. This will let content creators designate videos as part of a dedicated series, with season and episode numbers. As more content creators are investing in serialized content — think Sydney Jo’s The Group Chat series or microdramas — this tool will allow people to separate and highlight these videos from the rest of their posts. Viewers will be able to more easily find and watch these videos. The series will live on a creator’s page as a playlist. Only creators in YouTube’s partner program will have access at launch, available on web, mobile and TV.

YouTube is also offering creators two new ways to personalize content for their viewers. Creators will be able to test multiple thumbnails and preview clips for their videos. YouTube will serve the video to real viewers, and depending on each thumbnail and video cut’s performance, it will match a viewer with the version YouTube thinks they will be most likely to click on. This kind of personalization is a key part of AI’s promise for digital marketers.

Auto dubbing, or real-time audio translation, will be available for livestreams, starting with English and Spanish, with plans to expand to additional languages in the future. YouTube is also expanding how creators can monetize their content with a new affiliate partnership with Amazon.

Tech.title: New Phishing Attack Promises Claude Max, but Steals Your Google Credentials Instead
Tech.content:
The offer is for access to about $200 worth of Anthropic’s Claude Max service. But the real price could be giving scammers access to everything in your Google accounts.

A new phishing scam reported by the cybersecurity service Malwarebytes works like this: The scam claims that Anthropic is celebrating attracting 100 million users by giving 10,000 people a free month of Claude Max with x20 limits. The offer, which includes “extended thinking” and “priority access to Opus and Sonnet, no caps,” is actually all cap. It’s a fake offer that leads to a Google login page meant to steal login and password information, which could in turn open up access to Gmail, Google Docs and other non-Google accounts that use your Google information.

The fake giveaway, Malwarebytes said in its report, is different from many other phishing attempts because of how convincing it looks.

“The presentation is careful, down to the real logo and colors, invented five-star reviews, and a long footer whose links lead almost entirely to genuine Anthropic pages,” wrote Stefan Dasic, senior malware research engineer at Malwarebytes. The page also includes a running counter showing how many of those fake 10,000 accounts have been given away.

For those who fall for the scam, clicking on the offer leads to a login page to upgrade a Claude account. An Apple login option is disabled, leaving only the option to “Sign in with Google.” The login page employs a browser-in-a-browser trick that Dasic said is convincing enough to fool those who don’t look carefully. “The page draws a browser window inside the existing tab, complete with a padlock and a correctly spelled Google sign-in address. It can even be dragged around the page.”

In a message to CNET, Dasic said that the login prompt might convince those who don’t take the time to examine the login page. “The overlap matters because Claude has no password of its own: You get in either by continuing with Google or by a login link sent to your email. So if someone’s Claude account is tied to the Google account that was phished, the attacker reaches it either way.”

How to spot fake browser scams like this

Dasic told CNET that it’s too early to tell how widespread the scam has gone or how many people it’s reached. So far, he said, an investigation has traced the site to a UK-registered company, but the server is rented, “which tells us where the server was rented, not who rented it.”

The web page has components that contain developer comments written in Russian; it could, however, be part of a tool built by someone who isn’t necessarily the scammer involved in this campaign.

“Language in code is weak evidence on its own and has been planted before to misdirect,” Dasic added.
